Online peptide craze fuels risky self-optimization
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
16:42:56 UTC
01:42:56 KST

Thomas’ phone alarm buzzes at 9:30pm — it is time for the aspiring bodybuilder to start injecting himself in the stomach with several banned peptides.
He takes vials from his refrigerator of GHK-Cu, which he says would give him “beautiful skin,” and Retatrutide, which would help him “feel less hungry.”
After adding a liquid to reconstitute the synthetic peptides, he disinfects the syringes and shoots both into his lower abdomen. Thomas, whose name has been changed, takes GHK-Cu daily and Retatrutide three times a week.
Photo: AFP
“It takes a little organization, but it’s become a routine,” said Thomas, who goes to the gym almost every day.
He is one of a growing number of people attempting to “optimize” themselves by using peptides, a class of substances being widely promoted online by influencers, celebrities and the wellness industry.
Viral social media posts claim peptides can offer a range of seemingly miraculous benefits including glowing skin, stronger muscles, deeper sleep, a more alert mind — and even provide an avenue to prevent aging.
However experts warned there is little evidence to support these claims, and that because these peptides have not been studied properly, they can pose serious health risks.
That is why these peptides remain banned in many countries, including in France where Thomas lives.
However, in the US, a panel recommended loosening restrictions on a range of peptides last month. The decision outraged many medical experts, who accused US Secretary of Health Robert F. Kennedy Jr — an avowed fan and user of peptides — of packing the panel with people who have strong ties to the peptide industry.
Peptides are short chains of amino acids that assemble to form proteins, which are the body’s building blocks.
They occur naturally in the body, helping dictate processes such as repairing tissue.
Peptides reproduced in a lab are the active ingredients in many common medications including insulin and GLP-1 weight-loss drugs.
However, unauthorized forms of synthetic peptides sold online have increasingly been promoted by influencers and gyms promising a more effective workout.
Thomas was already using steroids when he was introduced to peptides six months ago.
Along with GHK-Cu and Retatrutide, he sometimes injects himself with Selank for help with anxiety and BPC-157, which promises to more quickly repair soft tissue such as ligaments.
As these peptides are not authorized for sale in France, there are no official guidelines for how to use them. In online discussion forums such as Reddit and Discord, communities of mostly men exchange advice on how much and how often they should inject themselves.
“You read the studies, you look at the lab tests, and you see all the positive effects,” said Thomas, who believes that the risks are “rare and not serious.”
However, neuroscientist Armelle Rancillac at the French Institute of Health and Medical Research (INSERM) said that knowledge on how to use these peptides remains limited, because they “have often not been tested on humans.”
Earlier this year, INSERM said that “no large-scale, randomized controlled clinical trial has confirmed” the promised benefits of peptides, warning that some pose “very real health risks.”
“We are not giving research enough time to prove its worth,” Rancillac said, adding that “scientifically worthless” accounts of self-experimentation were being given too much credence.
Numerous nations have reported people being hospitalized after using peptides. In June, the Australian government reported six cases of acute liver injury linked to products labeled Retatrutide.
It is difficult to determine how many people are using peptides, but the recent increase to exposure is enough to “raise alarm,” said Fabien Ohl, a sports sociologist at the University of Lausanne in Switzerland.
Ohl criticized the “biological view” being pushed online that the human body is “capital” to be exploited by taking chemical substances to improve one’s physical appearance.
For example, one Web site selling peptides promised to provide “the chemical architecture for those seeking absolute biological optimization.”
Self-proclaimed experts online also sell advice vowing to help men “optimize” their physique.
Ohl criticized this view of masculinity as problematic, saying that it normalized an idea of “the biological male who is potentially more violent and aggressive.”

Taiwan to host Premier12 group stage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
16:42:52 UTC
01:42:52 KST

Taiwan is to host the group stage and Super Round of next year’s World Baseball Softball Confederation (WBSC) Premier12, as well as the 2028 Los Angeles Olympic Baseball Final Qualifier, the Chinese Taipei Baseball Association (CTBA) announced on Friday.
The announcement came after CTBA president Jeffrey Koo Jr. (辜仲諒) visited Shanghai and met with WBSC president Riccardo Fraccari and executive director Michael Schmidt on Thursday.
At the meeting, Koo presented Taiwan’s bid to host the two tournaments and received Fraccari’s approval.
Photo: I-Hwa Cheng, AFP
Koo said he was pleased to accomplish the mission and hoped that hosting two top-tier international tournaments would unite the nation and allow Taiwan’s baseball to continue shining on the world stage.
He also said that he looks forward to seeing Team Taiwan in the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
Three remaining spots in the 2028 Summer Olympics are to be decided through next year’s WBSC Premier12 and the final qualification event.
Taiwan can qualify directly by finishing as the highest-ranked Asian team at next year’s Premier12. If the team fail to do so, they would have another opportunity to earn a berth by winning the final qualification tournament.
Rakuten Monkeys manager Tseng Hao-jiu (曾豪駒), who led Team Taiwan to their 2024 Premier12 title, said that playing at home would give the team an advantage.
“The players are more comfortable in a familiar environment, and the support of home fans is the biggest source of motivation,” Tseng said.
However, he acknowledged that hosting also brings added pressure because of heightened expectations from fans.
Since everyone is aiming for good results, the most important thing for the team is to perform as it hopes to and stay composed, the coach said.
Tseng also said that, unlike the World Baseball Classic, the Olympic baseball tournament is held in the middle of the professional season, making player selection more difficult.
However, there is a possibility that Major League Baseball would release their players to participate in the 2028 Olympics, which would raise the level of competition, he said.
“It will also have a major impact on how we build our roster,” Tseng said.
Since hosting the inaugural WBSC Premier12 in 2015, Taiwan has hosted group-stage games of every edition of the tournament. Taiwan also hosted the 2008 Final Qualifier of the Olympics.

Photo: CNA

Women’s sport shouldn’t have to bend to the trans delusion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
16:42:52 UTC
01:42:52 KST

Women’s sport shouldn’t have to bend to the trans delusion
Despite the conspicuous difference in size, speed, and strength between the sexes, a debate is now raging in women’s professional basketball in the United States whether to let men compete alongside the ladies.
Nobody would ever confuse Royce White, 35, with a woman. The man with stands 6 feet 8 inches tall, weighs 260 pounds (118 kg), sports a bushy beard, and is bald. He has an ex-wife and two children. In other words, not exactly somebody you would expect to find in the glossy pages of Playboy magazine. But what would never sell at the newsstands may eventually sell at professional women’s basketball games.
Coming out of college, White was selected by the Houston Rockets in the first round of the 2012 draft, although he never played for the team due to a severe fear of flying. But apparently he has recovered from that condition because now he has said he would welcome the chance to play in the Women’s National Basketball Association (WNBA).
White, who was a Republican candidate in Minnesota’s Senate primary, admitted to Fox News that he’s transgender and identifies as a woman “sometimes … for [the] purpose of basketball, professional basketball.”
“I think I’d be unstoppable,” White candidly admitted with no apparent shame. “I’ll do whatever the coach needs me to do. I’ll do whatever the girls need me to do… I think it’s only fair.”
Yes, you heard that right. White thinks it’s “only fair” that he be allowed to play in a professional female league where the average height of the players is just 6 feet 0.8 inches (184.9 cm), whereas the average height for male players is 6 feet 7 inches (200 cm).
While much of the WNBA has been strangely silent over White’s career ambitions, Indiana Fever superstar Sophie Cunningham was a rare brave voice in an age of fear and intimidation.
In a lengthy ESPN piece on the WNBA superstar, Cunningham said: “I got a lot of negative feedback about me hating trans. And I’m like, ‘I never once said that,’” she says. “I think that I am here to extend love. But I also think with that love is truth, being honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn’t have to go against biological men.”
The comment reverberated through the world of sport like a category 8 earthquake. After all, with over 3 million followers on TikTok, Cunningham carries a lot of clout. When she talks, people listen.
Regrettably, however, Cunningham’s comment has turned a regular evening of basketball into a political circus, with half the audience condemning the woman while the other half declaring its support. A popular T-shirt for Sophie supporters is emblazoned with XX-XY, referring to the female and male chromosome pairs and pointing to the inescapable biological differences between men and women. On the other side of the debate, Minnesota Lynx head coach Cheryl Reeve wore a shirt that carried the caption “Trans Kids belong,” when the conversation involves grown men, not children.
The furor was so loud that the White House even remarked on it. White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt defended Cunningham during a press briefing.
“The backlash she is receiving from Democrats and left-wing figures across the country is astonishing. They are clearly very out of touch with the American public on this issue, which again, is an 80/20 issue. It’s common sense,” she said.
Clearly, this is a conversation that America needs to have, regardless of the emotions it stirs up. After all, let’s fast forward ten years and pretend that biological males were given a free pass to play on any women’s sport team they desired. It’s not difficult to imagine biological men, who perhaps weren’t good enough to play alongside other males, dominating the women’s league. This has all the power to make female contenders endangered species in their own sport.
Some progress has been made. The US Supreme Court has ruled that states can lawfully ban transgender women and girls from competing in female school and college sports teams. In the 6-3 decision, the court upheld restrictive laws from Idaho and West Virginia, concluding that separate teams based on biological sex do not violate the Constitution or Title IX, the law against sex-based discrimination in education.
Meanwhile, transgender women have been barred from competing in the female categories of the Olympic Games. The International Olympic Committee (IOC) announced an eligibility policy restricting the female category to biological females, verified via a one-time gene screening, starting with the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
The US world of professional sport may wish to take a cue from the National Collegiate Athletic Association, which recently updated its guidelines to restrict participation in women’s sports categories strictly to athletes assigned female at birth. Athletes assigned male at birth may practice with women’s teams or play in the transgender category, but they cannot compete in women’s collegiate events.
It’s time for women to speak up and show solidarity with their fellow athletes in the realm of professional sport, lest the entire feminist movement has been for nothing.

Taiwan has produced 2,577 missiles over the past five years, passing a key test of the nation’s capability to surge military production, a high-ranking defense official said yesterday.
The National Chungshan Institute of Science and Technology (NCSIST) achieved the figure by manufacturing missiles at capacity in the race to fill the orders authorized under the Sea-Air Combat Power Improvement Plan, the official said on condition of anonymity.
The orders included the land-and ship-based versions of the Hsiung Feng (雄風, “Brave Wind”) II and III anti-ship cruise missiles, Wan Chien (萬劍, “Ten Thousand Swords”) air-to-ground cruise missiles, Tien Kung (天劍, “Sky Sword”) II and III air defense missiles and Chien Hsiang (劍翔, “Rising Sword”) loitering munitions, the official said.
Photo: Chen Yi-kuan, Taipei Times
The Wan Chien missiles had a three-year production run, while Hsiung Feng IIE extended-range missiles and the Chien Hsiang attack drones had four-year production runs, they said.
The NCSIST overcame three critical production bottlenecks to pass the stress tests the orders posed, the official said.
The institute optimized assembly lines in anticipation of the high volume of orders, and obtained a domestically sourced 300-gallon (1,136 liter) industrial mixer at its missile propellant factory and high-powered X-ray equipment, they said.
The NCSIST’s acquisition of a mixer manufactured entirely in Taiwan was significant, as stringent foreign export controls prevent Taiwan from procuring the equipment overseas, the official said.
The mixer, capable of more than 80 production cycles a year, has boosted production capacity since going online in July last year, they said.
The upgraded X-ray equipment, which is capable of penetrating heavy-displacement rocket motors, accelerated the quality control process by 36 percent, the official said.
The Ministry of National Defense said in a report to the legislature that the NCSIST could produce up to 150 Wan Chien missiles, 96 Tien Kung III missiles, 70 Hsiung Feng III supersonic anti-ship missiles and 131 Hsiung Feng II missiles per year, with no delay if upgraded variants are produced instead.
The institute can produce up to 50 Wan Chien missiles and 48 Chien Hsiang drones a year, the report said.

Creating a non-red ‘Intermarium’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
16:42:44 UTC
01:42:44 KST

President William Lai (賴清德) late last month received a delegation of Polish members of the European Parliament at the Presidential Office — the first single-party, single-nation delegation from the EU legislature to visit Taipei in nearly two terms.
The group, led by former Polish prime minister Beata Szydlo, also met Legislative Yuan Speaker Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜), a gesture spanning Taiwan’s political divide.
For most Taiwanese observers, this was a pleasant, if minor, diplomatic event. It was much more than that — and the timing matters.
Within the same fortnight, Hudson Institute senior fellow Ken Moriyasu said in the Washington Examiner that deterring an invasion of Taiwan means squeezing the overland trade corridors China is building as insurance against a naval blockade — corridors whose western end lies in Central Europe.
Poland’s Ministry of Digital Affairs also confirmed that four months after its new cybersecurity law took effect, not a single high-risk vendor proceeding has been opened. Add to that the Taiwanese investments announced in Poland since spring, and three unrelated headlines start to look like one story.
To understand it, readers need to learn one Polish word: Miedzymorze — or the Intermarium.
A century ago, Marshal Jozef Pilsudski, the founding father of modern Poland, proposed a bold geopolitical concept: The nations squeezed between the Baltic, Black and Adriatic seas — Poles, Lithuanians, Ukrainians, Czechs, Romanians and others — could survive alongside imperial Russia only by standing together as a belt of free states too costly for any empire to swallow.
History gave Pilsudski’s idea no chance, as the region was carved up by Adolf Hitler and Joseph Stalin, then locked behind the Iron Curtain for half a century. However, the logic never died. It returned after 1989 and today has an institutional form: the Three Seas Initiative, which links 13 EU member states in Central and Eastern Europe, with Poland as its largest economy and leader.
The Intermarium was conceived as a shield against Russia. What is new — and should interest readers in Taipei as much as in Washington — is that the same belt could become a shield against Beijing.
Moriyasu wrote that deterrence works like acupuncture. You do not press where it hurts; you press the points connected to the person’s nervous system.
The main brake on Chinese President Xi Jinping’s (習近平) calculus over Taiwan remains the economic cost of war. An invasion would prompt the US Navy to close the Strait of Malacca, thereby strangling China’s seaborne trade. That is precisely why Beijing has been feverishly building overland backup corridors through Russia and Central Asia.
For Moriyasu, the acupuncture points lie in the South Caucasus; the western ends of those same corridors, where they finally enter the EU, deserve equal attention. Those corridors all terminate in the Three Seas region, and the Malaszewicze terminal on the Polish-Belarusian border handles the lion’s share of rail trade between China and the EU.
Decisions made in Warsaw therefore feed directly into Beijing’s war calculus. Poland does not need to send frigates to the Pacific to matter in the Taiwan Strait; it needs to control its own section of China’s economic lifelines — and to show up in Taipei.
Since early last year, Lai has been urging democracies to build “non-red supply chains” — production networks linking free nations, with no links controlled by Beijing. To a Polish ear, this sounds instantly familiar. It is the Intermarium logic translated into economics: a belt of states making themselves collectively too resilient to coerce.
Pilsudski’s belt was made of borders and bayonets meant to hold back Moscow. Lai’s belt is made of semiconductors, servers and battery plants, and it holds back Beijing.
These are no longer two separate threats. China is the principal sponsor of Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war machine — buying the oil and gas that fill the Kremlin’s coffers and supplying the dual-use components that keep Russian missile production running.
A joint investigation by The Insider, Der Spiegel and Le Monde revealed last month that the two militaries have been holding secret annual technology forums since 2020. Whoever underwrites Russia’s war on Europe is not a neutral trading partner of Europe. Central Europe sits in both belts — and increasingly, they are one.
Over the past few months, Poland has become the point where the non-red supply chain touches European soil. A Taiwanese consortium, organized by the Taiwan Electrical and Electronic Manufacturers’ Association and led by Hon Hai Precision Industry Co (Foxconn), is to build a technology park in Miekinia near Wroclaw — on the very site Intel abandoned last year.
The Czech Republic, Germany and France competed for that investment, but it was Poland that won.
Weeks earlier, after China’s Geely walked away from Poland’s national electric vehicle project, state-owned ElectroMobility Poland signed an agreement with Foxconn to develop an electromobility center in Jaworzno. A car that was to have a Chinese heart would have a Taiwanese one instead. None of this fell from the sky: Poland opened a trade office in Taipei in 2018 and has patiently built the relationships that made these announcements possible.
The July delegation matters, because it addresses the one question every Taiwanese investor and official quietly asks about a European partner: Would this survive a change of government?
Poland’s administration announced the Foxconn deals; the visiting delegation came from the conservative opposition, which governed until 2023 and might govern again. Its members stood in the Presidential Office and called peace in the Taiwan Strait a strategic matter for Europe.
Whatever divides Polish politics — and much does — Taiwan is becoming one of the few points of cross-party consensus. For a country living under permanent coercion, predictability across election cycles is the most valuable currency a partner can offer.
There is a message here for Washington, too. US strategists debate how Europe can share the burden of Indo-Pacific deterrence, usually concluding that it cannot.
The Intermarium suggests otherwise. A Central Europe that screens Chinese investment, keeps Chinese hardware out of critical infrastructure, polices the overland corridors on which Beijing’s war insurance depends and anchors
Taiwanese high-tech manufacturing on NATO’s eastern flank is not a spectator in Pacific deterrence. It is a participant — it is pressing, as Moriyasu would put it, an acupuncture point far from the Taiwan Strait, yet wired straight into Beijing’s nervous system.
Poland has the assets to lead a technological Intermarium: the region’s largest economy, the corridors, the investments and a cross-party consensus on Taiwan that is being built. What it must still prove — to itself and its partners — is consistency.
Poland’s amended cybersecurity law, in force since April, empowers the government to designate high-risk vendors and requires that their equipment be removed from critical infrastructure within four years.
Yet as of this month, the ministry confirmed that no proceedings have been opened and no vendors designated, while Huawei threatens international arbitration over the mere possibility.
A law never used is a law untested. Warsaw must also build a rigorous mechanism to screen Chinese investment in critical sectors and turn the recent agreements with Taiwanese partners into operating factories rather than framed memoranda.
Its partners have homework of their own. If the non-red Intermarium is to become real, Taipei should treat Central Europe as a destination for technology, not just assembly — bringing research and development, chip-packaging know-how and training programs to Poland, as it has begun to in Japan and the US, and widening the door for Central European firms in the Taiwanese market.
Washington, for its part, should explicitly put the Three Seas region on its economic security map: coordinate export controls and investment screening with Warsaw, as it does with The Hague and Tokyo, and back the region’s infrastructure with financing, so that the corridors of the Intermarium are built with US and allied capital rather than left open to Chinese money.
A century ago, Pilsudski imagined free nations between the seas standing together so no empire could pick them off one by one. His idea failed for a lack of partners. Its heirs now have partners he could not have imagined — in Washington and 9,000km away in Taipei.
Taiwan, which knows better than anyone what it means to live next to an empire that calls its neighbors its own, has every reason to make sure that this time, the belt holds.
Hanna Shen is a Taiwan-based journalist and foreign correspondent for Polish media.

On a 0.8 hectare farm outside Bengaluru, India, Billy, Jessie and Banu put on their gear, enter a laboratory packed with samples and clock in for a shift detecting early signs of cancer.
Their most important diagnostic equipment is their noses.
Billy, Jessie and Banu are part of a team of beagles, labradors, Dutch shepherds and other dog breeds being trained by start-up Dognosis to sniff out traces of cancer in human breath.
Photo: Reuters
Dognosis is repurposing the canine sense of smell — traditionally used to detect drugs or explosives — for low-cost health screening and aiming to make early detection accessible to far more people.
Dogs have previously been shown to detect illnesses ranging from cancer to COVID-19, and the two-year-old company aims to apply that capability at scale in India. It joins a small set of start-ups harnessing dogs’ olfactory abilities to develop a non-invasive diagnostic tool.
Patients breathe into masks sent to the company’s facility, where dogs are exposed to the sample. Sensors and artificial intelligence (AI) then interpret signals including the animals’ movements, respiration, brain activity and body language to determine whether the sample carries signs of cancer — without imaging scans, blood tests or biopsies.
“It is like finding a needle in a haystack of who in a population has an undiagnosed case of cancer,” cofounder Akash Kulgod said.
Its backers include early stage investors such as Accel India and San Francisco-based Caffeinated Capital. They raised US$1.5 million via a preseed round in 2024 and then an undisclosed sum recently. This is enough for the next two years if the firm sticks to its planned growth trajectory, Kulgod said.
The dogs live together at Dognosis’ farm and laboratory, are given walks and playtime, and spend 30 minutes to an hour a day on the detection platform, where the work is designed as a game. Their reward: treats.
During one recent session, two-year-old beagle Whiskey worked through 10 samples, bounding past the first five. At the sixth, she paused, sniffed, moved away and returned, circling for several seconds before the system marked it positive.
In a Phase 2 study published in the Journal of Clinical Oncology, Dognosis reported about 90 percent sensitivity for early-stage cancers across seven broad groups spanning more than 20 cancer types.
The dogs also seem capable of expanding their detection abilities: Trained on the scent of 10 cancer types, they identified an 11th they had not encountered before, Kulgod said.
The bigger test now is proving that performance holds up outside controlled trials. India has the third-highest prevalence of new cancer cases globally, while routine screening remains exceedingly rare, the International Agency for Research on Cancer said.
The agency estimated 1.5 million new cancer cases and more than 900,000 deaths from the disease in India in 2024.
About one in 10 Indians are at risk of developing the disease before age 75. Breast cancer was the most commonly diagnosed type, followed by cancers of the lip and oral cavity, lung and cervix.
Yet only 1.9 percent of Indian women surveyed in 2019-2021 said they had ever been screened for cervical cancer, while 0.9 percent had undergone exams for breast or oral cancer. Among men, just 1.2 percent reported having undergone oral cancer screening.
Against the backdrop, Dognosis plans to launch an at-home, multi-cancer prescreening test in India next year.
Dognosis aims to process 1 million tests a year, double its canine workforce to 30 and halve turnaround times to one week. It is also eyeing the US, where Kulgod said it could open a facility by late next year or early 2028.
New Jersey start-up SpotitEarly has reported similar results from canine cancer-detection trials, although such testing has yet to be commercialized.
Getting there would mean showing that accuracy holds across larger, more varied populations, while building the logistics to move and process huge numbers of breath samples. It would also require persuading doctors and patients to trust a screening system built around dogs.
Emerging technologies “offer exciting opportunities, but they should strengthen — not replace — existing screening programs,” said Pankaj Chaturvedi, deputy director of the Centre for Cancer Epidemiology at Tata Memorial Centre in Mumbai.
Dognosis is forging ahead, having started its Phase 3 trial in April with 10 hospitals — and plans to recruit about 10,000 people over 12 months. The study would test asymptomatic people at higher risk of cancer and survivors at risk of recurrence, and those flagged would receive conventional follow-up including imaging and biopsy.
If the results stand, it plans to launch in Bengaluru next year before expanding across India through partnerships with diagnostic chains and healthcare providers. Kulgod said the test does not need Indian regulatory approval as it’s a prescreening tool, rather than a diagnostic device. Only the latter is regulated in India.
“A lot of people recognize we are already depending on dogs in life and death situations,” he said. “The bottleneck all along was: How do you standardize and scale the dog’s nose?”

US allows ‘pirates’ to fight cybercrime
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
16:42:41 UTC
01:42:41 KST

The US is to allow private companies to hack foreign cybercriminal groups after US President Donald Trump on Wednesday signed a memorandum that directed the US Department of Justice and the US Department of Homeland Security to allow some US firms to spy on and attack transnational criminal organizations.
The White House said that the damage caused by ransomware, “sextortion” and online fraud cost Americans more than US$20 billion last year.
The memorandum calls for authorizing private partners to take down hackers’ servers or to infiltrate their machines with spyware.
Photo: AP
Each operation requires prior government approval and companies have to post a bond of at least US$1 million. Any action that could cause death or injury is excluded, as is anything that would meet the threshold of “use of force” under international law.
The effort has parallels with 18th-century “privateering,” when governments would authorize private ships or sailors to carry out raids on enemy vessels.
“The private sector holds the data. The public sector holds the authorities,” and the new memorandum “puts them together,” said Ari Redbord, a former federal prosecutor who is now head of policy and government affairs at TRM Labs, an analytics firm that works with US authorities.
Redbord embraces the historical comparison to maritime privateering.
“Privateering broke down because there was no way to watch a ship once it left port,” he said. “We live in a very different world than 1812... Oversight that used to end at the dock now runs alongside the operation from start to finish.”
Other experts are not convinced.
“You can hand out a commission. You can’t hand out obedience,” University of Surrey professor of cybersecurity Alan Woodward told reporters. “History’s verdict on privateering wasn’t that it was immoral. It was that it became more trouble than it was worth.”
The effort marks a reversal for the White House, after a senior US official in March said that it was “not interested in fighting pirates with pirates,” according to The Record news site.
US National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross also previously ruled out using the private sector for such efforts, according to another site called CyberScoop.
It was unclear what prompted the U-turn.
However, the program appears to have some guardrails, said Jason Healey, a Columbia University researcher and former cybersecurity official under former US president George W. Bush.
“They’re backing this by the rule of law, and so I don’t feel like this is something crazy,” Healey said.
His concern lies elsewhere.
“This administration has systemically weakened those organizations that might provide oversight, like the Office of the Director of National Intelligence,” Healey said.
US tech giants are already heavily engaged in cybersecurity efforts to defend their own products.
The White House program would allow them to go further and operate without judicial oversight, under government oversight alone.
Microsoft declined to comment.
Google did not respond to a request for comment.
Any company that participates in government-sanctioned hacking “stops being a neutral defender and becomes a target” itself, Woodward said.
The Trump administration has 60 days to finalize the program’s details, although some aspects are classified.
Washington will have to decide if the costs of the effort are worth it, such as “a slow accumulation of misattributed targets, foreign prosecutions and diplomatic headaches,” Woodward said.
Cybercrimes proliferate nonetheless.
“Short of victims getting funds back, none of the rest counts for much,” Redbord said.

Severe constipation cause floating blood clots in eyes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
16:42:41 UTC
01:42:41 KST

An ophthalmologist in Kaohsiung on Friday said that severe constipation during menstrual periods could result in calcified blood clots in the eyes.
Hung Chi-ting (洪啟庭) issued the warning, citing a recent case, in which a female patient in her 20s complained of eye irritation, and discovered what appeared to be a small stone growing beneath her eyeball.
The woman had no history of blood diseases, kidney stones, hypertension or diabetes, and had not exhibited any signs of eye injuries before visiting the clinic, Hung said.
Photo courtesy of Hung Chi-ting
Hung quoted the woman as saying that over a span of two months, she noticed there appeared to be a small, grayish-black stone that was growing under the iris of her right eye, adding that when the woman visited the clinic, doctors found no external injuries on her eyes.
Upon examination of the stone-like mass after a surgical removal, it was found to contain intracellular yellowish-brown granules and brown deposits of hemosiderin and melanin, Hung said.
The lesion was believed to have resulted from an intraocular hemorrhage, followed by gradual mineralization and formation of a mineralized mass surrounding the hemosiderin and melanin pigments.
As the woman had no history of eye trauma, Hung said he asked her to return during her menstrual period, and found that the woman’s right eye suffered from mild anterior chamber hemorrhage.
As such conditions usually heal over time, Hung discussed the issue with the woman and learned that she usually suffered from severe constipation during her menstrual periods, and straining had caused the eye to hemorrhage.
Hung said that menstrual periods could lead to unstable hormones and fibrinolytic system activation, which could result in nosebleeds, coughing up blood, bloody stool, bloody urine or bruising.
Calcified clots in the eyes are rarer, but people should not be alarmed if they experience similar symptoms, he said, adding that the symptoms would not affect eyesight.

New technique for using incense cedar developed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
16:42:39 UTC
01:42:39 KST

The Taiwan Forestry Research Institute said it is promoting full utilization of Taiwan’s incense cedar to develop a high-value circular economy for forest resources.
Incense cedar is an endemic species of Taiwan and is one of Taiwan’s five major coniferous tree species, the institute said.
It is distributed in mountainous areas of northern and central Taiwan at elevations of 300m to 1,900m, it said.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Agriculture via CNA
Taiwan incense cedar is the primary tree species used for reforestation in warm forests between 500m and 1,800m above sea level, the institute said.
While Taiwan incense cedar wood is popular with consumers thanks to its distinctive aroma, surplus materials generated during the process of forest tending, pruning and wood processing are usually used as fuel or disposed of, it said.
The institute’s Chiayi Research Center promoted research on the reutilization of Taiwan incense cedar surplus materials at the Yunshui Experiment Station (澐水試驗站) from last year to this year, the institute said.
Water distillation was applied to extract Taiwan incense cedar oil from surplus materials, while the remaining materials would be ground into scented powder or made into incense cones, it said.
The institute said that water distillation is a well-established extraction technique.
It uses high-temperature steam to release volatile aromatic compounds from plants, which would then be condensed and separated to obtain natural essential oils, the institute said.
Water distillation can preserve the plant’s aroma and active compounds without adding organic solvents, it said.
That helps meet modern consumers’ demand for natural, safe and environmentally friendly products, the institute said.
Taiwan incense cedar essential oil is rich in compounds such as ferruginol, alpha-pinene and limonene, it said.
Ferruginol is highly antibacterial and antioxidant, the institute said, adding that it can inhibit skin disease-associated pathogens and tyrosinase, a key enzyme involved in skin pigmentation, it added.
The institute said the full utilization of Taiwan incense cedar would maximize the use of forest resources.
Techniques could be transferred to forest farmers, forest product processors or local revitalization teams, the institute said.
That would help them more efficiently utilize forest by-products to increase revenue, it said.

Taiwan High Speed Rail Corp (THSRC) yesterday received a N700ST high-speed train from Japan, the first in a set of 12 ordered by the state-supported corporation.
The train arrived at the Port of Kaohsiung to fanfare, with THSRC chairman Shih Che (史哲) co-hosting an event celebrating its arrival at the port alongside senior government officials.
Shih confirmed that THSRC is considering raising train fares for the first time in 20 years on July 1 next year, when the N700ST is anticipated to enter into service.
Photo: CNA
The price increase would facilitate the planned safety, ride comfort and service quality upgrades under the Taiwan High-Speed Rail 2.0 plan, he said.
Minister of Transportation and Communications Chen Shih-kai (陳世凱) said price adjustments depend on the new bullet trains’ reception by the public, and that he hopes THSRC would continue its tradition of excellent service.
The new train was originally scheduled to embark and get under way on Aug. 6, but Typhoon Dolphin and Tropical Storm Chan-hom delayed the departure by five days, THSRC said.
The rolling stock is being unloaded for the next two days and then transported overland to the Yenchao Main Workshop over three more days, it said.
THSRC expects to complete assembly and static testing by November, it said.
The dynamic test, which consists of 68 sub-trials for drive systems, brakes and onboard amenities, is to be completed by April next year, it said.
The other 11 trains are on schedule to be delivered from this year through 2028, with all sets scheduled to enter service by September 2028, it said.
The Kaohsiung City Government has changed its lighting to the THSRC color scheme at scenic locations throughout the municipality until this evening to honor the train’s arrival.

S Korean tycoon appeals divorce ruling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
16:42:38 UTC
01:42:38 KST

A South Korean tycoon has appealed a court ruling ordering him to pay US$666 million to his former wife in the country’s largest-ever divorce settlement, his lawyers said yesterday.
Chey Tae-won, 65, is the chairman of SK Group, which owns world-leading memory chipmaker SK Hynix — a pillar of South Korea’s tech-led economy.
The Seoul High Court in 2024 told him to pay 1.38 trillion won (US$974 million at the current exchange rate) to his ex-wife, Roh Soh-yeong. The sum — equal to more than US$1 billion at the exchange rate at the time of the ruling — led local media to dub it the “divorce of the century.”
Photo: EPA
Chey appealed to the South Korean Supreme Court, which told the High Court to reconsider its 2024 decision and led to the tycoon’s reduced divorce bill of 944 billion won in July — still the largest divorce asset settlement ever awarded in South Korea.
The High Court last month ruled that Roh was entitled to a cash payout worth one-third of the couple’s marital assets, including Chey’s SK shares, citing her family role and support for SK Group activities.
The tycoon has appealed the July ruling, his lawyers said yesterday, which brings the case to the country’s highest court again.
“After careful consideration of various factors, Chairman Chey Tae-won has filed an appeal to the Supreme Court,” his lawyers said in a statement. “We will approach the upcoming procedures with a commitment to minimizing any negative impact on shareholders and the group’s management.”
Roh’s legal team declined to comment.
The appeal could extend a closely watched legal battle that has drawn attention to Chey’s control of SK Group as the artificial intelligence boom boosts the value of its chip assets.
SK Group shares have more than tripled in value since December 2015, when Chey publicly disclosed an extramarital affair.
South Korean newspaper Money Today reported that Chey offered Roh a mix of stock and cash to settle the asset division to limit market impact, but she reportedly demanded full payment in cash, which would require him to sell a large amount of shares — prompting his appeal.
Chey and Roh — daughter of a former South Korean president — married in 1988 and have three children together, but the couple are believed to have lived apart for more than 15 years.
The 2024 ruling ordering the payout to Roh cited a 30 billion won slush fund her ex-president father, Roh Tae-woo, used to propel SK Group’s growth.

Organizer SEMI on Friday said the event would bring together executives from major global technology companies and five key segments of Taiwan’s electronics supply chain.

Photo: Ritchie B. Tongo, EPA

The exhibition would run from Sept. 2 to 4 at halls 1 and 2 of the Taipei Nangang Exhibition Center, while related programs would be held from Aug. 31 to Sept. 4.

====================================================================================================

Peptides should not be China’s next fentanyl moment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
16:42:36 UTC
01:42:36 KST

China has demonstrated time and again that when its leaders make something a priority, they usually get results. A decision to ban all forms of the powerful drug fentanyl seven years ago under US pressure showed how quickly authorities can mobilize against an illicit trade. They should now bring that same attention to the export of unregulated peptides.
These compounds are short chains of amino acids that work as chemical messengers that activate or inhibit various biological functions in the body. While some peptides such as insulin and the active ingredient in Ozempic are legal and widely prescribed, there is a vast array of injectables that have become wildly popular among Western biohackers looking to build bigger muscles, get smarter or look better.
However, there are two main issues with products such as BPC-157 and TB-500, which purportedly help speed recovery, and melanotan, a synthetic tanning agent. First, the molecules have not been adequately tested for safety or efficacy in humans. Some were banned three years ago by the US Food and Drug Administration over those concerns. Misuse of peptides can upset the body’s hormonal and metabolic balance, increasing the risk of serious side effects including organ damage. Secondly, the proliferation of a booming gray market means they are often sold by online merchants without meeting basic quality standards.
China, with its vast chemical and pharmaceutical industries, appears to be the main source — creating public-health risks that demand Beijing’s urgent attention. The country has about 1,000 online sellers targeting buyers abroad, the Financial Times said.
While no one should equate unlicensed peptides with fentanyl, the synthetic opioid responsible for the bulk of about 40,000 overdose deaths in the US last year, there are obvious parallels.
Both compounds can be manufactured cheaply at scale and shipped across borders in small parcels, making them difficult for regulators to track. Like fentanyl, peptides are being marketed widely over social media or e-commerce sites to overseas buyers while remaining off-limits at home due to tighter regulations.
The clandestine nature of the business has fueled a boom in the use of digital assets by first-time users. Because banks and credit card processors generally eschew transactions involving unlicensed substances, buyers have made cryptocurrency the backbone of the industry. Crypto payments to peptide vendors jumped 700 percent to US$32 million in the first quarter of this year, analytics firm Chainalysis wrote in June.
Some of the biggest vendors are Chinese chemical manufacturers that were, until recently, mainly supplying the building blocks of fentanyl and amphetamines to drug cartels, blockchain records show. This on-chain peptide economy is expected to exceed US$100 million annually, driven by endorsements from celebrities such as podcaster Joe Rogan and actress Jennifer Aniston. Industry insiders estimate the unregulated market is worth US$1 billion to US$3 billion, compared to tens of billions of dollars for fentanyl.
The trade is strikingly one-sided. Unauthorized peptides attract little interest in China. “Looksmaxxing,” an online subculture focused on maximizing one’s physical attractiveness that can escalate to extreme measures including using peptides to change skin tones or body composition, has failed to gain traction. Disenchanted Gen Z have instead responded to a slowing economy and high jobless rates with silent rebellion in the form of ugly work outfits or vows to “lie flat” (躺平). Self-improvement is not on the agenda.
The country also has highly reputable peptide manufacturers. Companies such as WuXi AppTec Co have benefited from soaring demand for the ingredients used in blockbuster GLP-1 diabetes and weight-loss drugs, including the active ingredient in Eli Lilly & Co’s obesity treatment Zepbound.
It might seem like Beijing has little incentive to crack down on a shadow business that barely affects its citizens, but that view is shortsighted. Similar to fentanyl, the gray peptide market creates reputational, regulatory and geopolitical risks. Singapore has declared it illegal to sell the unregulated products, while Australia has warned of serious side effects including liver damage and severe allergic reactions requiring hospitalization. The US is bucking the trend, with outside advisers to the FDA recommending relaxing restrictions on some peptides last month.
More than most countries, China understands the national trauma that can accompany the unchecked spread of potentially dangerous substances. That history has shaped decades of tough anti-drug policies at home. Allowing it to become the world’s main source of unregulated peptides would sit uneasily with that legacy.
It has something else to protect: an ambition to become a global pharmaceutical leader. World-class manufacturers should not have their reputations tarnished by a gray market flourishing alongside them. Bringing unauthorized exports under tighter control would only reinforce that goal.
Juliana Liu is a columnist for Bloomberg Opinion’s Asia team, covering corporate strategy and management in the region. She was previously CNN’s senior business editor for Asia, and a correspondent at BBC News and Reuters. Parliamentary staffers from 12 European countries are visiting Taiwan to exchange views on democratic governance, resilience and digital government as part of a Taiwan-organized exchange program, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said yesterday.
The delegation is the second group to visit Taiwan this year under the European Valued Important Partnership (EVIP) program, jointly organized by the ministry and the Taiwan International Cooperation and Development Fund.
The visitors, from Austria, the Czech Republic, France, Germany, Italy, Lithuania, Montenegro, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia and the UK, are in Taiwan from Wednesday through Friday next week, the ministry said.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs via CNA
Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Francois Wu (吳志中) hosted a reception for the delegation on Thursday, during which he stressed the importance of closer Taiwan-Europe cooperation amid growing global instability.
Despite international challenges, Taiwan has maintained peace and stability while delivering strong economic performance, Wu said, citing nearly the 14 percent economic growth in the first quarter and the nation’s stock market becoming the world’s fifth-largest by market capitalization.
Taiwan’s semiconductor industry success was partly due to long-term cooperation with European partners, particularly the Netherlands, France, Germany and Belgium, he said.
The visitors were from different countries and backgrounds, but shared a commitment to democracy, freedom, human rights and the rule of law, the ministry cited delegation leader Matej Stevove as saying.
As authoritarian states expand their influence and challenge the international order through coercion and other means, Europe should deepen cooperation with Taiwan on economic, technological and security issues, Stevove said.
He also praised Taiwan for demonstrating the resilience of its democracy and expressed hope that the EVIP program would deepen exchanges and partnerships between Taiwan and Europe.
This year’s program focuses on digital governance, and includes visits to government agencies and private organizations.

A magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck off the coast of Indonesia early yesterday, killing at least 38 people, and collapsing buildings and homes.
Authorities said that more than a dozen residents were injured.
Authorities issued a tsunami warning and urged coastal residents to move to higher ground, but later lifted the warning when the Indonesian Meteorology, Climatology and Geophysics Agency said monitoring showed no significant sea-level changes that would pose a threat to coastal communities.
Photo: EPA
The US Geological Survey said the quake hit Indonesia’s Flores region with a depth of 10km at 5:58am. Its epicenter was 68km north-northwest of the city of Ende in East Nusa Tenggara Province.
The initial quake was followed by several aftershocks.
Suharyanto, the head of the Indonesian National Disaster Management Agency, said rescuers had recovered at least 38 bodies, mostly in the three devastated regencies of Sikka, Manggarai and East Manggarai, including 16 bodies that were pulled from a landslide in the village of Reok in Manggarai.
At least 13 people were rushed to nearby hospitals, including two with serious injuries.
Suharyanto, who like many Indonesians uses a single name, said three helicopters and a rescue vessel were deployed to assist with logistics and support emergency response operations, including possible evacuations if needed, given East Nusa Tenggara’s geography, which consists of numerous islands and presents significant transportation and access challenges.
About 2,000 villagers in Nagekeo regency fled their homes to temporary shelters, he said.
East Nusa Tenggara Police Chief Rudi Darmoko said the earthquake caused severe damage.
Power outages hampered the flow of information, and complicated rescue efforts, he said.
“We are continuing to collect reports of damage and casualties, but there are communication disruptions,” Darmoko said.

S Korea’s fortune-tellers losing business to AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
16:42:30 UTC
01:42:30 KST

Clients have drifted away from Song Oh-soon’s fortune-telling village on the edge of Seoul, preferring online artificial intelligence (AI)-powered divination to the centuries-old prophesying tradition still practiced there.
At 86, Song is one of the last members of a community of visually impaired practitioners that drew generations of South Koreans seeking answers and advice about everything from illness and money to love and fate.
In one of the world’s most AI-connected societies, the village’s greatest challenge is not fading belief in fortune-telling, but the way it is consumed.
Photo: AFP
Song remains adamantly offline, relying on the “Four Pillars of Destiny” astrology in Braille and on her four decades of experience in careful listening — a skill her automated competition cannot match.
“There were people who came here wanting to die,” Song said in northern Seoul’s Mia village. “I persuaded them to keep living.”
“I also once wanted to die, but I found this work and survived,” she said.
Today, silence is often Song’s only visitor. The community was once home to 70 or 80 practitioners, but fewer than 20 remain.
Many have died. Their shops down narrow alleys sit dark behind faded signs advertising “traditional fortune-telling houses.”
“When I go outside for a walk, it’s quiet,” Song said in her tiny room that serves as home and consulting space. “It feels lonely.”
Figures show South Korea’s fortune-telling business is growing — worth 1.4 trillion won (US$988.2 million) as of 2024, according to start-up analysis firm InnoForest.
Many now turn to mobile apps and AI chatbots such as ChatGPT and Gemini for readings, a survey by market researcher Embrain said this year.
However, occasionally someone still seeks out a human intervention.
University professor Oh Ji-hye for years walked past the village without going inside, opting instead for AI readings during her commute.
Only recently, anxious about her career, did she turn to Song for a phone consultation.
“It felt good that someone rather than AI was concentrating on and listening to my story,” the 44-year-old said.
Mia village emerged in 1966 after the first blind fortune-teller settled there, said the Seongbuk Cultural Centre, which researches the district’s history.
As Seoul boomed in the 1970s and 1980s the neighborhood enjoyed cheap rents and a constant foot traffic of potential customers by the time Song arrived in 1984.
She lost her sight in a childhood illness before the Korean War and by 11 was studying Korean fortune-telling — predicting subjects’ futures based on their birth dates and times.
She was a professional by 16, working in an industry where many people with disabilities — especially women — have been historically confined owing to discrimination.
“Nowadays, if a visually impaired person is musically talented, they can pursue a career in music,” she said. “But back when I lost my sight, there was nothing else I could do besides this job.”
Over her lifetime, South Korea has witnessed the devastation of the 1950-1953 war, periods of military rule and the 1990s financial crisis.
After periods of hardship and loss, the nation has emerged as a global financial powerhouse — with recent astronomical profits from manufacturing AI microchips.
Those gains have lifted the nation’s fortunes. Clients who once came for advice about medical ailments can now head to hospital instead.
However, the technology has drawn away clients from Song’s 50,000-won sessions in favor of free or affordable AI readings.
Most of the remaining practitioners have little online presence, and many cannot be found through major search platforms.
“I don’t think people are less interested in fortune-telling,” Song said. “But these days, they look online, so they do not come all the way to us.”
Despite the village’s decline, Song believes no fate is set in stone.
“If you put in the effort and make wise judgements, good fortune will come your way three times in your life,” she said.

What should have been a discussion about the marriage of their children resulted in a brawl between the two fathers due to a disagreement over the dowry and wedding arrangements, according to documents from Keelung District Court.
A July 29 ruling said a man surnamed Chang (張) and his girlfriend registered their marriage at a household registration office, and on Dec. 8, 2024, they invited both sets of parents to their home to discuss plans for a wedding ceremony.
However, the two fathers disagreed over the dowry and arrangements for the wedding, leading to a heated argument and a tense atmosphere, the ruling said.
Photo: Lin Chia-tung, Taipei Times
During the argument, Chang’s father lost his temper and grabbed his son-in-law’s father by the neck. In the ensuing struggle, Chang’s father pushed the other man into a nearby glass partition, causing bruises to his neck, left shoulder, right upper arm and upper back, the ruling said.
The parents left the gathering on bad terms, with the injured father going to the hospital for a medical examination and filing an assault charge with the police, the ruling said.
Chang’s father countersued the victim for assault and the Keelung District Prosecutors’ Office dismissed the case after investigating the incident, it added.
Chang’s father-in-law, however, was prosecuted on suspicion of assault following the complaint filed by Chang’s father-in-law.
During the trial, Chang’s father admitted to grabbing the victim by the neck and engaging in a physical struggle, which was consistent with statements from his wife, Chang, daughter-in-law and the victim’s wife, as well as the medical examination.
The judge said that Chang’s father assaulted the victim over a trivial matter and had failed to reach a settlement, showing a lack of remorse. He was sentenced to 20 days in detention for assault, which can be commuted to a fine of NT$20,000.
The ruling can be appealed.

EDITORIAL: What are Han Kuo-yu’s ‘dark forces’?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
16:42:27 UTC
01:42:27 KST

It was shocking to hear Legislative Speaker Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜) say that the legislative branch is somehow now under the control of “dark forces.”
Frustrated at the glacial pace of the passage of the government’s annual budget for this year — it was finally passed at 6:08pm on Friday after a record delay of 266 days — Han had lost his temper during a cross-caucus negotiation meeting on Tuesday. The target of his ire was Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) caucus whip Fu Kun-chi (傅崐萁), who was absent that day.
Fu had failed to attend the cross-caucus negotiations on a total of five occasions since July 30, including Tuesday. He has excused his behavior by saying that it had been a silent protest at the way the Executive Yuan had “disrespected” the legislature.
Others have said that Fu was disrespecting Han. There are apparently tensions between the two men that stem from Han’s reluctance to have Fu as the deputy legislative speaker.
Han’s outburst, and the “dark forces” comment, could well have been a result of the pressure of having to pass the much-delayed budget, Fu’s absence being the last straw, tinged with the tensions between them. That does not absolve him of his inability to bring the respective caucuses together to pass the budget in a more timely fashion; it is his job to do so. Nor does it absolve Fu of his immature dereliction of responsibility; neither does it answer the question of whom Han meant when he used that ominous term.
Han did not elaborate at the time, neither was it obvious within the context in which the remark was made, and he has not clarified what he meant by the outburst in the days since. This has left it open to interpretation, and interpreted it has been, unreliably yet predictably so, through the filter of differing political agendas.
In a Facebook post, the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) pointed to the increasingly pro-China, Chinese Communist Party (CCP)-adjacent rhetoric of KMT Chairwoman Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文) and the large delegation of KMT legislators that Fu had led to Beijing in 2024 — shortly after he took the reins as KMT legislative caucus whip — where the group met Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference Chairman Wang Huning (王滬寧) and China’s Taiwan Affairs Office Director Song Tao (宋濤).
The post also pointed to the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP), whose former legislator-at-large Xu Chunying (徐春鶯), a Chinese immigrant, was sentenced on Tuesday for contravening the Anti-Infiltration Act (反滲透法), among other crimes.
The post did not explicitly say that Han’s “dark forces” comment was a reference to the CCP’s infiltration of the legislature and influence over KMT and TPP figures, but it strongly insinuated that it was, leaving readers to come to their own conclusions. This insinuation would certainly cohere with concerns that many Taiwanese have.
At the speaker’s podium in the legislative chamber on Friday evening, after striking his gavel to signify the passage of the long-delayed budget, Han shook his head in a show of exhaustion and delivered closing remarks to the legislators present.
He called on the opposition to demonstrate more maturity in providing legislative oversight, and on the central government, and Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) in particular, not to jeopardize the rule of law or the smooth operation of a constitutional government by refusing to countersign or implement laws that the legislature had passed after three readings.
Han also called on the opposition and governing parties to be more open to compromise in negotiations.
The KMT and the TPP have jumped on his criticisms of Cho and the Executive Yuan, saying that these were the targets of Han’s “dark forces” comment.
The attribution of blame is pure politics. For the DPP, it was an easy conversion. For the KMT and the TPP, it was more problematic, and doubtless required careful coordination regarding messaging, to distract from the obvious connection of “dark forces” to CCP influence and infiltration.
Surely, Han would have known, in the current political environment, how saying that “the legislature had come under the control of dark forces” would be open to interpretation from the political rivals of the KMT, to which he belongs. This makes it doubly surprising that he has not since clarified to the public what he meant by the term.

Scam targeted Taiwanese abroad, police say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
16:42:26 UTC
01:42:26 KST

A Taiwan-based scam ring allegedly funneled more than NT$5 billion (US$156 million) a year to China while targeting Taiwanese and Chinese in the US, Japan and Canada, police said yesterday.
Police revealed the case after more than a dozen people were arrested for allegedly transporting cash in a scheme targeting a Taiwanese woman surnamed Hsu (徐) living in California.
Amid a surge in the stock market last year, the group targeted Hsu, who is in her 80s and has been living in California for nearly 30 years, although most of her family lives in Taiwan, police said in a statement.
Photo courtesy of the Taipei City Police Department
The group sent members to California, who operated in teams of three on a rotating basis, police said.
They rented accommodation near Hsu’s home, from where they monitored her, police said.
Whenever the group deceived Hsu into handing over cash or gold, the members in California would collect it, police said, adding that between September last year and Jan. 8, three or four teams made trips to the US.
Each team stayed in the US for about a month, with about 17 in-person pickups conducted in total, collecting NT$89.26 million (US$2.79 million) in cash and gold, the statement said.
Hsu in May returned to Taiwan and reported the case, as the men she had interacted with had Taiwanese accents and issued receipts written in traditional Chinese, it said.
The Taipei City Police Department and the National Police Agency’s Criminal Investigation Bureau said they formed a joint task force, which found more than 10 fingerprints on 17 falsified receipts provided by Hsu.
The fingerprints showed that several of the suspects had backgrounds with the Bamboo Union, or they had been convicted of fraud, the statement said.
Three suspects were arrested in June in an initial round of raids, it said.
In a large operation conducted last month, police arrested more than 20 other suspects in Taipei and central Taiwan, it said.
The suspects who collected the money would convert it into cryptocurrency in California and transfer it in batches to Taiwan, China or Cambodia, it said.
They would not carry much cash when flying, making it difficult to track the flow of the cash, it said.
Once a target was identified, the group would dispatch members posing as investment advisers to collect money, police said.
Hsu was not the only target, with communication records showing that Taiwanese living in the US, Japan and Canada were defrauded of more than NT$10 million combined, the task force said.
Based on nearly a year of financial records gathered during the investigation, most of the funds — totaling more than NT$5 billion — were transferred to China, it said.

KMT defends cuts, while DPP calls them irrational
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
16:42:24 UTC
01:42:24 KST

The Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and the Cabinet traded barbs over cuts to the central government budget, with KMT caucus whip Fu Kun-chi saying that the 1.689 percent reduction to this year’s central government budget should be seen as a gesture of “great goodwill,” while the Cabinet described the cuts as “irrational.”
Lawmakers from the KMT and the Taiwan People’s Party, who together hold a majority in the legislature, passed the cuts on Friday amid strenuous objections from the central government and Democratic Progressive Party lawmakers.
The cuts included NT$10 million (US$312,051) from President William Lai’s (賴清德) confidential state affairs fund, with an additional NT$20 million from the fund frozen until Lai promulgates several bills passed by the legislature.
Photo: Chen Yi-kuan, Taipei Times
The legislature also eliminated funding for the Cabinet’s Department of Human Rights and Transitional Justice, halved the operating budget of the Ill-gotten Party Assets Settlement Committee and cut NT$684 million from the NT$1.379 billion funds for central government agencies’ policy promotion, including NT$69.32 million requested by the Cabinet and NT$47.38 million by the Ministry of Culture.
Fu said the opposition had shown its “greatest goodwill” by passing this year’s central government budget with NT$48 billion in cuts, or just 1.689 percent of the original proposed expenditures.
More than 1,700 proposed cuts had been reduced through negotiations, resulting in 98.4 percent of the Cabinet’s proposed budget passing and allowing the government to operate normally, Fu said.
Fu also criticized the central government for failing to implement laws passed by the Legislative Yuan, including: allocating more tax revenues to local governments; raising pensions for police, firefighters and civil servants; and increasing military salaries.
However, Cabinet spokeswoman Michelle Lee (李慧芝) said such “irrational” cuts could seriously impact government operations, as well as hamper Taiwan’s progress on human rights.
Reduced funds for policy promotion risked allowing disinformation to spread, Lee said, adding that a NT$52.54 million cut to the Department of Information Services’ operating budget could fall on the shoulders of contract workers, whose salaries were now uncertain.
Moreover, cuts to the confidential state affairs fund two-thirds into the year had effectively rendered it unusable, depriving the president of necessary flexible resources for public engagements, military inspections and other state affairs operations, she said.
The basic resources needed by the Executive Yuan to conduct on-site disaster assessments have also been completely cut, she said, adding: “Disasters will not disappear simply because funding has been cut.”
The budget cuts are no longer about individual programs, but about whether the government can continue to function normally, the spokeswoman said.
From the National Communications Commission and the Ill-gotten Party Assets Settlement Committee to funding for the Executive Yuan’s policy outreach and implementation, human rights and transitional justice, and the president’s official and confidential affairs, the cuts are no longer simply a matter of “how much money is being cut,” she said.
Rather, they raise questions about whether the government can maintain basic operations, respond promptly to public needs, and constitutional bodies can fulfill their legal duties, she said.
In response, KMT caucus deputy secretary-general Hsu Yu-chen (許宇甄) said that Taiwan is a democratic country, not one where the Executive Yuan has the final say.
Accusing the DPP of labeling legislation and budget measures “irrational” or “unconstitutional” whenever they fail to conform to its wishes, Hsu said the Executive Yuan refusing to countersign or implement laws passed by a legislative majority is what truly harms the nation’s democracy.

KMT’s Cheng facing election, party woes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
16:42:23 UTC
01:42:23 KST

Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Chairwoman Cheng Li-wun’s (鄭麗文) controversial cross-strait statements aim to cover up her inability to resolve divisions within the party ahead of the November elections and gain media exposure amid a lack of support from within the KMT, a Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) figure said on condition of anonymity.
Cheng in an interview broadcast online on Friday last week said Taiwan has never been independent and has never been a country.
The Constitution of the Republic of China is a “one China” constitution, she said, citing the so-called “1992 consensus.”
Photo: Taipei Times
The “1992 consensus,” a term former Mainland Affairs Council chairman Su Chi (蘇起) in 2006 admitted making up in 2000, refers to a tacit understanding between the KMT and the Chinese government that both sides of the Strait acknowledge there is “one China,” with each side having its own interpretation of what “China” means.
Asked if the KMT wants to negotiate “peaceful unification” with China, Cheng said her ideas would “be truly introduced and implemented as policy once the KMT retakes power,” and that it would bring warmer ties between the two countries.
The DPP figure said Cheng’s remarks amounted to a denial of Taiwan and was an insult to Taiwanese, calling her views “unacceptable” and “mind boggling.”
Since Cheng became chairwoman and held a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) earlier this year, a bubble of “rising radical unification forces” has emerged, they said.
However, major KMT local figures, such as Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安), Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen (盧秀燕) and Taichung mayoral candidate Johnny Chiang (江啟臣), have largely kept their distance from these forces, the figure said, adding that Cheng’s position on key issues, including arms procurement and drone-related legislation, were given the cold shoulder within the party.
These signs indicated that the KMT is acutely aware that Cheng’s hardline stance is highly detrimental to the party’s prospects in the upcoming elections, they said.
Cheng was reviving controversial cross-strait rhetoric to bolster her standing within the party and distract from her inability to resolve internal divisions over party nominations ahead of the year-end elections, they added.
Asked whether Cheng’s “pro-China” rhetoric would affect the KMT’s electoral outlook in the Nov. 28 elections, a KMT candidate running for office, on condition of anonymity, said the pan-blue camp would proceed cautiously and respond to situations as they arise.
Many swing voters saw Cheng’s visit to China as proof that cross-strait peace was achievable, but as soon as that shift took shape, the DPP resorted to its usual tactic of framing cross-strait relations as a choice between being “pro-US” or “pro-China,” they said, calling it a very effective political move.
Rhetoric about being pro-US or pro-China might seem harmless, but it carries hidden dangers, the candidate said.
Taiwan’s elections are highly competitive and can be swayed by a small number of issues in the final week of campaigning, they said, adding that even parties leading in local races could not afford to be complacent.
Meanwhile, a member of the KMT’s Central Standing Committee said Cheng has gained significant political momentum following her meeting with Xi and subsequent visit to the US in June.
Cheng’s growing profile and foreign policy initiatives have unsettled anti-Cheng factions within the KMT, which fear that her influence could shape the party’s direction heading into the 2028 presidential election, the party insider said.
Opponents have sought to portray Cheng as excessively pro-China and said that her approach would make it hard for the KMT to retain its local governance footholds — potentially losing three to five cities or counties — and weaken its chances of defeating the DPP in the presidential race, they said.
However, such rumors have had a limited impact on Cheng’s leadership, they added.
A former KMT official critical of Cheng said that while she claims to advocate for peace, her approach was unrealistic, because Beijing’s “one China” principle refers exclusively to the People’s Republic of China and leaves no room for the Republic of China.
Such a position would not help the KMT’s electoral prospects in the year-end elections, they added.
