Taiwan in Time:  An Indian revolutionary’s mysterious final hours in Taipei
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
16:42:20 UTC
01:42:20 KST

Aug. 17 to Aug. 23
Subhas Chandra Bose was meant to be in Taiwan for no more than two hours. After refueling at today’s Songshan Airport in Taipei, the Mitsubishi Ki-21 bomber carrying the Indian independence leader took off for Japan — and crashed almost immediately.
It was Aug. 18, 1945, three days after Japan announced its surrender to the Allies. Bose, who advocated armed struggle to free India from British rule, had worked closely with Imperial Japan. He was attempting to reach the Soviet Union via Manchuria in the hope of gaining support for India’s independence when the accident occurred.
Photo courtesy of Wikimedia Commons
While the pilot, copilot and Japanese lieutenant general Tsunamasa Shidei were instantly killed, Bose was relatively uninjured. However, with the rear of the plane blocked by luggage, he tried to escape through the flames of the wreckage. But since his clothes were soaked with petrol, he was soon engulfed in fire and suffered severe burns.
Bose and other survivors were rushed to the Nanmen Branch of Taipei Army Hospital (today’s Heping Hospital), where he remained mostly conscious before succumbing to his injuries that night. His body was reportedly cremated at the Taipei Crematorium (near today’s Linsen Park) and his ashes were taken to Japan, where they were later placed at Renkoji Temple in Tokyo.
From official accounts, it appears to have been a straightforward tragedy. But many still refuse to accept that explanation.
Some allege that the Japanese had meant to assassinate him rather than risk handing him to the Allies; others claim they staged his death to help him escape to the Soviet Union, while some maintain that Bose secretly lived on in India as an ascetic.
In 1956, the Indian government appointed the Shah Nawaz Committee to investigate, sending investigators to interview eyewitnesses in Japan. It concluded that Bose had died in the crash, but the controversy surrounding his fate continued.
THE DEADLY CRASH
Known for the quote “Give me blood and I will give you freedom,” Bose is widely regarded in India as a national hero who fought British rule; Kolkata’s international airport bears his name. But his willingness to ally with Nazi Germany and Imperial Japan remains controversial.
After being placed under house arrest in India for his anti-colonial activities, Bose escaped in 1941 and made his way to Nazi Germany. There, he sought German support for India’s independence and organized the Indian Legion from prisoners of war and expatriates.
Curiously, major newspapers erroneously reported in 1942 that Bose had died in a plane crash.
Disappointed with Germany’s limited support, Bose traveled to Japanese-occupied Southeast Asia in 1943, where he launched the Indian National Army (INA) and headed the Japanese-backed Provisional Government of Free India. The INA fought alongside Japanese forces during their disastrous 1944 invasion of India from Burma.
Bose fled Yangon as the British retook it in May 1945. Japan’s surrender greatly affected his plans, and he hoped to find a new ally in the Soviet Union. On Aug. 17, 1945, he left Saigon (today’s Ho Chi Minh City), stopping briefly in today’s Da Nang before landing in Taipei around noon the following day.
After a lunch of sandwiches and bananas, he set off again. Mechanics had noticed something wrong with one of the engines, but they resolved the problem and deemed it safe to fly.
Bose’s chief of staff, Habib-ur-Rahman, recalled that the plane had cleared the runway and begun to climb when he heard a “noise like a cannon shot.” The aircraft began wobbling before crashing on its nose. Rahman later found that the propeller of the port engine had broken off. The two men pushed their way out of the burning wreckage.
The two collapsed, and Rahman later recalled Bose telling him, “When you go back to the country, tell the people that up to the last I have been fighting for the liberation of my country; they should continue to struggle, and I am sure India will be free fore long. Nobody can keep India in bondage now.”
They woke up in the only military hospital still running in Taipei, reportedly due to Allied air raids. According to a Japanese report, Bose remained conscious for much of the time, even offering to be treated last. He died that night.
After his cremation, a small funeral ceremony was held at Nishi Honganji Temple near today’s Ximending. It was reportedly kept low key to avoid attracting Allied attention. His remains, along with his belongings, were sent to Japanese Army headquarters in Tokyo and transferred to Renkoji temple.
STILL ALIVE?
A decade after the accident, many Indians still refused to accept Bose’s death.
“The rumor is persistent and deep-rooted among people of India to the effect that Chandra Bose is still alive,” stated a 1956 article by the Indo-Japanese Friendship Association.
That year, the Indian government sent a three-person investigation team led by Shah Nawaz, and included Bose’s brother, to Japan to examine the circumstances of his death. Also in question were the jewels Bose was reportedly carrying to fund his operations, of which only a small portion was found.
The committee repeatedly requested permission to visit Taiwan, but the Indian government refused, having broken diplomatic ties with Taipei in 1950 in favor of Beijing. Triloki Nath Kaul of the Ministry of External Affairs wrote to the Indian ambassador to Japan: “We do not recognize that government and they are likely to put obstacles in the way of the committee.”
However, in 1946, Indian journalist Harin Shah visited Taipei and interviewed a Taiwanese nurse at the hospital named “Tsan Pi Sha,” who confirmed that she looked after him and was present when he died.
During the investigation, the Indian government also obtained a copy of the Taipei cremation permit from Japanese authorities. Curiously, the document gave the name of the deceased as Ichiro Okura, rather than Bose. Japanese officials explained that the name had been used to keep Bose’s death confidential. This would later become an important point for those who reject the conclusion that Bose died in the crash.
The Shah Nawaz Committee report noted that the Japanese remained secretive and delayed publishing the news, and also produced no convincing proof of Bose’s death, which raised initial suspicion among Indians. However, it partially attributed this to things being “out of gear” after the Japanese surrender, and found no convincing reason to reject the fact that Bose had died in the crash, with his ashes taken to Japan where they still remain today.
However, the theories continue. In 2005, a commission headed by retired Supreme Court judge Manoj Kumar Mukherjee concluded that Bose had not died in the crash and that the ashes in Japan were not his. The Indian government rejected these findings.
Taiwan in Time, a column about Taiwan’s history that is published every Sunday, spotlights important or interesting events around the nation that either have anniversaries this week or are tied to current events.
It is forest fire season in Europe and North America, and the news is filled with harrowing images of disastrous fires filling the air with smoke. What about Taiwan? Taiwan has a unique forest fire profile. Unlike other nations, where the threat peaks in the dry summer months, that period is wet. Instead, major forest fires typically occur during October to April, when the country is drier. Moreover, “high temperatures are not the primary drivers of forest fires” as a study in Theoretical and Applied Climatology noted. Rather, the consensus is that dryness is the trigger of forest fires here, with
When Gary Melyan, a longtime Taiwan resident who died on July 7 at age 83, arrived in Taipei for the second time in 1971, he was a graduate student trying to complete a doctoral thesis on the Taiping Rebellion. Wanting to assemble some fellow academics for a regular meal, he initiated a Saturday lunch, which quickly shifted to Saturday dinner. Then, sometime in 1974 or 1975, it became a weekly Wednesday night meal. Melyan never finished his PhD, but the weekly Wednesday dinner, now known as the Wednesday Night Old Farts (WNOF), has continued for more than half a century

Erdogan says Egypt could join Turkiye-Saudi-Pakistan defence pact

Erdogan says Egypt could join Turkiye-Saudi-Pakistan defence pact
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said Egypt could join the joint defence agreement recently signed by Turkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, describing Cairo’s accession as “possible” and the pact as open to further members.
Speaking to Al Jazeera in an exclusive interview for Al Muqabala (The Interview), which will air on Sunday evening on Al Jazeera Arabic, Erdogan said the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement commits signatories to taking unified steps should any one of them come under external attack.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Turkiye’s AK Party turns 25: A journey of change and renewal
- list 2 of 3Saudi Arabia announces start of Red Sea defence alliance: Will it work?
- list 3 of 3Mutual defence: The alliances that preceded Turkiye-Pakistan-Saudi pact
“This agreement has sent an important message to the world,” Erdogan said, adding that Egypt’s participation was among the options for its future expansion.
The deal, also known as the Mecca Pact, was signed in the holy city last Friday by Erdogan, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Pakistan’s Prime Minister, Shehbaz Sharif. It stipulates that an armed attack against any one of the three would be treated as an attack against them all, a collective-deterrence provision that analysts have compared to NATO’s Article 5. However, officials in Islamabad have cautioned against interpreting it as a NATO equivalent or as being directed at any single country.
Erdogan spoke on a range of regional issues, including tensions over the Strait of Hormuz and the wars in Syria, Gaza and Lebanon.
The Turkish leader said reopening the strait was a priority for Ankara, arguing that its continued closure served no one’s interests. He credited Qatar with playing an important role in mediation efforts to halt fighting in the region.
Syria, Gaza and Lebanon
Erdogan pledged that Turkiye would not leave its neighbours to face regional turmoil alone, singling out Syria, Gaza and Lebanon.
He said Ankara would do everything in its power to support stability in Syria, noting his plans to visit the country, and that Syria’s Kurds would have “a share of peace and stability”. Turkiye would also continue to strengthen ties with Kurdish communities and safeguard their rights across the region, he added.
Concerning Gaza, Erdogan said Turkiye “cannot leave Gaza alone” and would do whatever was necessary to support it. He said Hamas was meeting its commitments in good faith, while Israel continued its war.
Turning to Lebanon, the Turkish president said continued Israeli attacks were a source of serious concern for Ankara. He said he had raised the need to end the war on Lebanon with the US president during Donald Trump’s recent visit to Turkiye, stressing Washington’s role in bringing the fighting to a close.
Erdogan said Turkiye would continue to support Sudan and described his relations with the head of its Sovereignty Council, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, as good. He said Ankara’s relations with Libya were stable and that Turkiye would not abandon it.
On Europe, Erdogan said the European Union did not appear willing to admit Turkiye, adding that membership was no longer a priority for Ankara and that Europe would be “the loser” as a result.
He also said he had received a promise from Trump regarding F-35 fighter jets and was waiting for it to be honoured.
Turkiye was removed from the multinational F-35 programme in 2019 after taking delivery of the Russian-made S-400 air defence system, which Washington argued could compromise the stealth jet’s technology. Standing beside Erdogan during the NATO summit in Ankara last month, Trump said his administration would lift the CAATSA sanctions imposed on Turkiye in December 2020 over the S-400 purchase, and said a return to the F-35 programme was “something certainly we’d consider”.
Any sale, however, still faces resistance in Congress and a 2020 law bars the Pentagon from transferring F-35s to Turkiye for as long as it retains the S-400 system.

Zelenskyy signed a decree establishing the status of national shrines of the Ukrainian people
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
19:37:58 EEST

Zelenskyy signed a decree establishing the status of national shrines of the Ukrainian people
Kyiv • UNN
The President signed a decree establishing the status of national shrines for heritage sites. The Cabinet of Ministers is to prepare a law by August 24 providing for protection and liability for their destruction.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed Decree No. 726/2026 on August 15, “On the National Shrines of the Ukrainian People,” which provides for the creation of a separate status for unique sites of Ukraine’s historical, spiritual and cultural heritage. This is stated in the president’s decree, UNN reports.
Details
By August 24, the Cabinet of Ministers is to prepare a draft law on the protection of national shrines. The document is to define the criteria for granting the relevant status and the procedure for compiling a list of such sites.
The list is proposed to include, in particular, national heritage monuments and UNESCO World Heritage sites that are prominent centers of the historical memory, spirituality and culture of the Ukrainian people, as well as of the formation of the Ukrainian political nation and statehood.
National shrines to be protected through separate state programs
The future law is also to provide for additional measures to protect such sites, the powers of government bodies regarding their protection, and liability for the destruction or ruin of national shrines.
The government was also instructed to step up preparations of Ukrainian nominations for the UNESCO World Heritage List and improve state policy on the protection of national heritage monuments amid Russian aggression.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs is to strengthen efforts to inform the international community about Russia’s crimes against Ukraine’s cultural heritage and facilitate bringing the Russian Federation to justice.
In addition, the MFA was instructed to attract international aid and investor funds, as well as reparations and other payments collected from Russia, for the protection, preservation and restoration of Ukrainian monuments.

The death toll from the earthquake in Colombia rose to 294, the National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD) wrote on Saturday on US social media company X.
The figures as of 6.30 am local time (1130 GMT) are up by six from Friday’s toll.
The UNGRD said 3,935 people were injured and 320 remain missing.
Search and rescue teams are continuing operations as authorities work to locate the missing, provide medical assistance and assess damage caused by the disaster.
The UNGRD is coordinating the national emergency response and collecting information from authorities and emergency agencies as officials assess the effect of the quake.
The number of people reported missing remains a key focus of rescue efforts, with emergency teams working to establish their whereabouts.
Authorities are also assessing damage to infrastructure and determining the needs of communities as response operations continue.
Emergency services have deployed personnel and resources, while local authorities are assisting residents and coordinating relief efforts.
Response teams are working to identify and address the most urgent needs of communities, while authorities continue to gather information on the extent of the damage.
Authorities have urged residents to follow instructions from emergency services and remain alert as rescue and assessment operations continue.
The casualty figures remain provisional and could change as rescue teams make progress and authorities verify information received from affected areas.
The UNGRD has continued to receive and compile information from authorities and emergency agencies on the ground to update the reported number of deaths, injuries and missing people.
The latest figures represent the most recent toll released by the disaster management agency, but additional changes are possible as individual cases are verified.
The UNGRD is expected to provide updates as new information becomes available.

A magnitude 7.7 earthquake on the island of Flores has claimed the lives of 47 people, and more than 150 homes have been damaged. Rescuers continue their search, and the number of victims may rise.
The death toll from the 7.7-magnitude earthquake on Indonesia’s Flores Island has risen to 47. This was reported by Indonesia’s National Disaster Management Agency, according to the BBC, writes UNN.
Details
The earthquake struck on the morning of August 15 at a depth of about 15 km. Dozens of aftershocks were recorded in the region following the main tremor, including one measuring 6.1. Rescuers continue search operations, so the number of victims may rise.
According to local authorities, more than 150 houses were seriously damaged. Public facilities and infrastructure were also affected, including the port in Maumere.
Residents evacuated en masse
After the earthquake, authorities issued a tsunami warning, prompting about 2,000 people to evacuate or leave dangerous areas on their own. The warning was canceled approximately three hours later because no significant rise in sea level was recorded.

Iraq moves to retake Jurf al-Sakhar, return displaced Sunnis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
16:29:46 UTC
01:29:46 KST

Breadcrumb
Iraq moves to retake Jurf al-Sakhar, return displaced Sunnis
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi is moving to restore state control over Jurf al-Sakhar and allow its predominantly Sunni population to return nearly 12 years after they were displaced, as Baghdad pushes armed factions to surrender weapons outside state control.
Iraqi political sources told The New Arab that Zaidi had ordered a review of the security and logistical situation in the town, around 60 kilometres south of Baghdad in the country's Babil province, which has remained largely emptied of its residents and under the control of Iran-aligned armed factions since 2014.
The government is examining mechanisms for regular security forces to deploy around Jurf al-Sakhar and at its entrances before beginning a process to restore state control.
Zaidi has also ordered the area to be reopened, its residents allowed to return and state institutions restored.
"The government is not considering storming the area, but rather reclaiming it through understandings and by gradually applying pressure on the factions," sources told The New Arab.
The move could coincide with the expiry on 30 September of a deadline given to Iraqi factions to surrender their weapons.
Sources said the government's plan includes gradually evacuating some faction headquarters in Jurf al-Sakhar, including those belonging to groups formally affiliated with the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) and others operating under its umbrella.
They would be replaced by forces from the Iraqi army, Counter Terrorism Service, National Security Service and intelligence agencies, alongside some PMF brigades regarded as disciplined. "Zaidi wants to use the deadline given to the factions to surrender their weapons to resolve outstanding issues, including displacement," the sources said.
Twelve years of displacement
Jurf al-Sakhar was a predominantly Sunni Arab town and a stronghold of the al-Janabi tribe before the Islamic State group seized the area in 2014.
Iraqi forces and Shia armed factions retook it in October that year, but its civilian population was not subsequently allowed to return.
The New Arab's sources put the town's displaced population at around 180,000 people, many of whom remain scattered across camps and other areas of Iraq despite repeated promises by successive governments to facilitate their return.
The town has since remained largely isolated from the rest of Iraq, with even government and military officials facing restrictions on entering because of the presence of Iran-backed armed groups.
The issue returned to the political agenda over the past two weeks after Adnan al-Janabi, sheikh of the Janabi tribe in Babil, described Jurf al-Sakhar as still "occupied".
"The people of Jurf al-Sakhar consider 25 October 2014 to be the day the area was occupied, not the day it was liberated," Janabi said at a press conference.
He accused militias of refusing to hand security responsibility back to state forces and demanded accountability for "forced displacement and the crimes of kidnapping, torture, enforced disappearance and extrajudicial killings".
Janabi also said residents remained unable to access their land and alleged that property, including water wells, had been stolen or looted.
His comments prompted the Babil Provincial Council and provincial government to file a legal complaint against him, accusing him of presenting false information and making statements that could provoke sectarian tensions.
Babil governor Ali Turki, a senior figure in Asaib Ahl al-Haq, rejected the return of Jurf al-Sakhar's displaced residents in June, claiming their land consisted of agricultural leases whose legal status had expired.
Sunni Sovereignty Alliance leader Khamis al-Khanjar responded by describing Turki's position as "an explicit declaration of a sectarian demographic change project".
The dispute now risks becoming part of a wider confrontation over the power of Iraq's armed factions.
A member of the Sunni National Political Council told The New Arab that Zaidi faced the challenge of restoring state authority over areas not under its full control "after disarming or expelling the factions controlling depopulated areas, including Jurf al-Sakhar".
The official argued that Iran-aligned factions were significantly weaker than in previous years and said the local population would support moves to end militia control.
"Zaidi faces a major challenge and must restore the state's authority in the face of gangs and rogue groups," the official said.

US and Türkiye opening ‘Pandora’s box’ with Ukraine arms deal – Moscow
The planned transfer of US-made missiles and other weapons from Türkiye to Ukraine will “inevitably undermine mutual trust” with both Washington and Ankara, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova has warned.
The US State Department notified Congress earlier this month that it was prepared to authorize the re-export of weapons from Turkish stocks to Ukraine. The package reportedly includes 70 M39 ATACMS tactical ballistic missiles, 12 M270 multiple-launch rocket systems, more than 2,500 M26 rockets with cluster warheads, and 47,000 203mm cluster artillery shells.
The total value of the proposed transfers is estimated at around $280 million.
“Attempts to use peacemaking rhetoric while simultaneously supplying weapons to Ukrainian Nazis inevitably undermine mutual trust,” Zakharova said, noting that Turkish officials had repeatedly maintained that Ankara was avoiding deliveries of “lethal” weapons to Kiev.
The circumstances surrounding the planned transfer remain “extremely contradictory,” according to the spokeswoman, who said it was unclear who had initiated the re-export or how and when the munitions would reach Ukraine.
Zakharova also questioned why Washington and Ankara had decided to open another “Pandora’s box” while both countries claim a special role in efforts to resolve the Ukraine conflict.
“The issue is not only the casualties and destruction that the authorities in Kiev seek to increase, but also the serious damage to our bilateral relations with Washington and Ankara,” she said.
Because the weapons were manufactured in the US, their re-export from Turkish stocks requires authorization from Washington. The State Department submitted the relevant documents to Congress on August 6.
Under US law, Congress has 15 calendar days to review the proposed transfer. No separate approval vote is required; unless both chambers adopt a joint resolution blocking it, the administration’s authorization automatically takes effect.
Moscow has repeatedly condemned Western weapons deliveries to Ukraine, arguing that they prolong the hostilities and make the US and other NATO countries direct participants in the conflict.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said last month that Western weapons supplies, military advisers, and satellite intelligence provided to Kiev amounted to “direct participation” in the war against Russia. 
Russian officials have also repeatedly accused Kiev of using Western-supplied long-range weapons against civilian targets. Moscow has specifically pointed to a June 2024 ATACMS strike on Sevastopol, in which Russian authorities said four people, including two children, were killed and more than 150 injured. The Kremlin said at the time that the sophistication of the US-made missiles meant Washington was directly involved in their targeting and operation.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has similarly claimed that NATO military specialists provide Kiev with intelligence and help coordinate precision strikes, including attacks that have hit homes, energy facilities, schools, and hospitals.

Bonnie Tyler fans line the streets of a Welsh village as her coffin is brought home

Bonnie Tyler fans line the streets of a Welsh village as her coffin is brought home
LONDON (AP) — Hundreds of fans lined the streets of a seaside Welsh village on Saturday to bid farewell to late singer Bonnie Tyler as her coffin was brought home.
The Grammy-nominated Welsh pop star, beloved worldwide for her 1983 chart-topping power ballad “Total Eclipse of the Heart,” died last month in a hospital in Portugal. She was 75.
Tyler was hospitalized in May in Faro, where she had a home, for emergency intestinal surgery.
Locals and fans from around the United Kingdom and beyond took to the streets of Mumbles, near the city of Swansea, to see the hearse, which carried her coffin, draped in a Welsh flag. Dozens waited outside the singer’s former home or left floral tributes there.
“She was always coming home and making sure that she came back to her fans in Wales,” said Carys Edwards, 18. “Her songs really did touch a lot of people here in Wales; we loved her a lot.”
Tyler was born Gaynor Hopkins, a coal miner’s daughter in public housing with an outside toilet in Skewen, Wales, about 7 miles (11 kilometers) outside Swansea. She grew up with three sisters and two brothers.
The singer earned three Grammy nods and in 2013 represented Britain at the Eurovision Song Contest, where she came in 19th. She was honored as a Member of the Order of the British Empire in 2022 for her services to music by Queen Elizabeth II, thanks mainly to “Total Eclipse of the Heart.”
The ballad shot to the top of the charts in Britain and the United States and has had more than 1 billion streams, boosted by real eclipses in 2017, 2024 — and most recently during this week’s solar eclipse.
She was also known for other hits including “It’s a Heartache” and “Holding Out For a Hero,” from the soundtrack of the film “Footloose.”
A celebration of Tyler’s life for family and friends will take place at a church in Swansea on Monday, before the singer makes a final journey through her hometown of Skewen.

Remains of 21 Palestinians retrieved from homes destroyed during Israel’s genocidal war

2026-08-15

01:22:27 KST

Gaza’s civil defence teams recovered the remains of 21 Palestinians on Saturday from beneath two homes destroyed by Israeli attacks during the genocidal war in Gaza, according to a spokesman.
They began searching for the remains of 40 more people believed to be trapped under a third house.
Mahmoud Basal told Anadolu that rescue teams recovered the remains of 12 Palestinians from beneath the Batniji family home near the Asqula area in eastern Gaza City after completing search operations at the site.
He said crews also recovered the remains of nine Palestinians from the Gharbiyah family home in the Katiba area in western Gaza City.
Basal said teams later moved to the al-Maghribi family home in the Zeitoun neighbourhood in eastern Gaza City after receiving reports that the remains of 40 Palestinians were buried beneath the rubble.
He renewed warnings about the severe challenges facing civil defence teams due to acute shortages of heavy machinery, equipment, logistical supplies and fuel needed for recovery operations.
The shortages have significantly slowed search efforts and limited the ability of crews to reach the large number of destroyed buildings, he said, as he urged the international community to provide the necessary equipment.
The recovery operations are part of the second phase of a project launched by the civil defence on July 19 to retrieve bodies from beneath destroyed buildings.
At the launch of the second phase, Basal said the operation would cover 147 destroyed homes in Gaza, North Gaza and central Gaza, where the remains of an estimated 1,072 Palestinians are believed to be buried under the rubble.
The first phase of the project, launched in November 2025, recovered 333 bodies and human remains from 54 destroyed homes and buildings. Civil defence officials said limited resources prevented teams from reaching 226 other bodies trapped beneath the debris.
Around 9,500 Palestinians have been reported missing since the start of the war, including many believed to be under the rubble of destroyed buildings, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office.
Israel has continued its military offensive in Gaza since October 7, 2023. Palestinian authorities said more than 73,000 people have been killed and over 174,000 injured, most of them women and children, while about 90% of the enclave’s infrastructure has been destroyed.

Sudan’s al-Burhan pledges immunity for dialogue, rules out Hemedti return

Sudan’s al-Burhan pledges immunity for dialogue, rules out Hemedti return
Al-Burhan said the army was ready to engage with any serious peace initiative but would not accept what he called an ‘incomplete peace’.
Sudan’s Sovereign Council chief and army commander Abdel Fattah al-Burhan has pledged temporary immunity and legal, political and security guarantees for participants in a Sudanese dialogue to be managed by an independent national mechanism.
Speaking early on Saturday during celebrations marking the 72nd anniversary of the Sudanese Armed Forces, al-Burhan said criminal proceedings against participants facing charges would be temporarily suspended while they take part in the dialogue, without affecting the rights of those who filed complaints against them.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Sudan’s war threatens an ‘entire generation’s’ future, UN warns
- list 2 of 4Sudan’s army chief holds unannounced talks on national dialogue
- list 3 of 4Sudan army says RSF advance on key town bordering Ethiopia
- list 4 of 4How a Sudanese refugee became a head teacher in a Chadian camp
Al-Burhan said measures taken by the state regarding any dialogue participant would not amount to a pardon, but rather a temporary suspension of criminal proceedings against those facing charges. He said this would grant them temporary immunity while taking part in the dialogue without affecting the rights of those who had filed complaints.
He said the national dialogue should be an open-ended process conducted in a public space that allows society to express opinions and criticism without fear or restrictions.
He also pledged legal protection for the opinions and positions expressed by participants, saying statements made during dialogue sessions would not be used as grounds for legal prosecution.
Al-Burhan said a group of Sudanese figures had independently proposed the initiative and would oversee the dialogue. He stressed that the state would not organise the process or determine its agenda or outcomes.
Sources told Al Jazeera that the national mechanism is expected to hold a news conference in the coming days to present its vision and plans for the political process.
No ‘incomplete peace’
On the war, al-Burhan said the army was ready to engage with any serious peace initiative but would not accept what he called an “incomplete peace” that returned the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), led by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti, and its supporters to power.
Al-Burhan said the army would continue what he described as the “completion of the cleansing of the country from the terrorist militia”.
He said the path to peace must begin with RSF forces withdrawing from cities and gathering in designated areas, followed by the return of displaced people and refugees to their homes.
Discussions could then take place over the status of RSF fighters and the possible integration into the regular forces of those who had not committed crimes, he said.
Separately, al-Burhan said he had begun talks with national forces that had supported the state and its institutions during the previous period, with the aim of involving them in completing the institutions of government.
He said this would include representation in a legislative council, or parliament, whose formation is currently under discussion.
African Union delegation
Meanwhile, a delegation from the African Union’s Peace and Security Council is expected to arrive in Khartoum on Saturday for a three-day visit, its second since the war began.
The delegation includes representatives of the council’s 15 member states and is headed by Algeria’s representative, as Algeria holds the council’s rotating presidency for August.
According to Sudan’s Al-Muhaqiq news agency, the African delegation’s visit will last three days and include talks with al-Burhan, Prime Minister Kamil Idris, political groups and civil society organisations.
In July, the African Union’s special envoy to Sudan, Mohamed Belaiche, discussed the political and security situation in Khartoum, African mediation efforts and the reopening of the African Union’s office in the capital.
Sudan has formally asked the council to lift its suspension from African Union activities, imposed after al-Burhan dissolved the Sovereign Council and cabinet and declared a state of emergency in October 2021.

London tribute honours Anas al-Sharif, condemns media silence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
16:15:45 UTC
01:15:45 KST

Breadcrumb
London tribute honours Anas al-Sharif and Gaza’s killed journalists as speakers condemn media silence
A year after the killing of the Palestinian journalist Anas al-Sharif, fellow reporters gathered in London on Friday to remember a broadcaster who became one of Gaza’s most recognisable witnesses, and to confront what speakers described as a systematic campaign to erase Palestinian journalism.
The event, "Bearing Witness: Tribute Panel for Anas al-Sharif & Gaza’s Murdered Journalists," was held at Palestine House and organised by Youth Movement Palestine.
It brought together Ahmed Al-Naouq, a Palestinian journalist at Palestine Deep Dive; Mariam Al-Sayeh, a journalist and media researcher at Al Jazeera; and Malak Tantesh, a Guardian reporter formerly based in Gaza. Abubaker Abed, a Palestinian journalist who evacuated Gaza for Dublin, joined remotely.
The panel took place as Palestinian media workers continue to face a devastating toll. The Palestinian Journalists’ Syndicate says that 264 journalists have been killed, 572 injured and 38 detained since October 2023, while 150 media institutions and infrastructure sites have been destroyed.
Al-Sharif, 28, was a prominent Al Jazeera Arabic correspondent whose broadcasts from northern Gaza made him an essential source of information for Palestinians and audiences abroad during Israel’s genocidal war.
He was killed on 10 August 2025 when an Israeli strike hit a tent used by journalists near al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City. Five other Palestinian journalists were also killed in the attack: Al Jazeera correspondent Mohammed Qreiqeh; camera operators Ibrahim Zaher, Mohammed Noufal and Moamen Aliwa; and freelance photojournalist Mohammed al-Khaldi.
At Friday’s event, the speakers unanimously agreed – the incident was not murder, but a mass assassination.
Israel acknowledged targeting al-Sharif and alleged he was linked to Hamas. Al Jazeera rejected the claim, while the Committee to Protect Journalists said the allegations against him were unsubstantiated and called for accountability. The killing followed months of threats and public accusations against the reporter, who had become known for reporting from areas subjected to intense bombardment, displacement and starvation.
For Tantesh, who began reporting from Gaza in 2024 at the age of 20 and was displaced 13 times during the genocide, al-Sharif’s standing was evident in the response he received from ordinary Palestinians.
"I met Anas just once, just a few days before he was killed," she told The New Arab. "I was reporting about the situation at Al-Shifa Hospital in northern Gaza. His smile was shining the place and everyone was happy to see him, especially the patients, who saw him as the messenger who would deliver their suffering to the outside world."
Abed called al-Sharif "a giant of a man", describing his work as "very extensive, very thorough, very professional, indispensable, and instrumental in shedding light on the genocide in Gaza, particularly on the vast destruction and catastrophic famine levels in the northern parts of the Strip."
"He is the best in our lifetime," Abed told The New Arab.
Reporting and surviving
Much of the discussion focused on the impossible conditions confronting Palestinian journalists, who have had to report on Israel’s assault while enduring the same hunger, displacement, loss and threat of death as the people they cover.
"Our work as journalists was extremely difficult and exhausting," Tantesh said. "We were experiencing fear, hunger and displacement, just like everyone else in Gaza. At the same time, we continued reporting and risking our lives to tell the truth and share our suffering and our voices with the outside world."
She described the fear of being killed while working, and of the consequences for her family. "I clearly remember how scared I was of being targeted while working," she said. "I was afraid that my family would not be able to recognise me, or that they would not even be able to find my body. I was also afraid that my family and the people around me would be killed, leaving me alone."
Abed, who said he felt compelled to leave Gaza after receiving repeated threats on social media, likened the labour expected of Palestinian reporters to “the work of a superhuman”.
Yet, he said, journalists continued because of their attachment to their homes and communities. "We did it because we loved our homeland," he said. "Because we love our homeland, we love our people, we love justice to be served, and we want our human rights and dignity and freedom, as any other human being around the world."
Speakers also emphasised the dignity with which journalists such as al-Sharif worked amid extreme deprivation. They recalled the difficulty of preparing to go live while facing queues for bathrooms, unstable communications and shortages of food.
Al-Sharif, they said, often refused food aid himself, accepting only food offered directly by others even as people phoned urging him to eat.
A struggle over the narrative
The panel framed the killing of journalists not as a series of isolated wartime deaths, but as part of a broader effort to restrict Palestinians’ ability to document their own reality.
"The killing of journalists has been systematic," Abed said. "I’m so lucky to have survived, and I also feel sorry and contrite that other people, other journalists, have been killed. I feel a lot of guilt."
"It’s a tactic," he added. "It’s not some sort of aberrational activity. It is a tactic, and it is something that Israel deliberately did because [journalists] expose the unbelievable magnitude of what they have perpetrated in Gaza."
The speakers argued that the pressure on Palestinian journalists has changed over the course of the war: from threats, online discrediting and attempts to constrain live reporting, to the killing of media workers.
They said the attacks have also stripped Gaza of established reporters whom Palestinians had long relied on, leaving younger and less experienced journalists to fill the gap.
Mariam Al-Sayeh argued that the media’s failure was not limited to under-reporting mass casualties. "Mainstream media still cannot accept what happened," she said, criticising coverage that focuses on spectacular moments of violence while neglecting the conditions that make daily life unliveable, including heatwaves, deprivation and the continued deaths of children after ceasefires.
"Every day, the media chooses to ignore what is happening in Palestine," she said, as the speakers expressed outrage at the censorship reserved for Palestinian journalists who would refer to Israel's deadly campaign as a "genocide".
Al-Naouq urged journalists and media institutions to resist an audience-driven approach that prizes novelty over necessity. "We should not actually care what the audience wants, but what the audience needs," he said. "And the people need to see what’s going on in Gaza."
Abed was equally critical of political and media institutions beyond Israel, telling The New Arab: "What we are seeing is something that has been enabled by Western media outlets, by Arab media outlets, and by Western and Arab regimes. They have enabled all this. They stayed silent. Not all they stayed silent, but they funded the genocide."
On accountability, Abed said he had little faith in the international community, noting that al-Sharif had appealed for protection after receiving threats. "If you want to achieve accountability, which I don’t see in a complicit, rude world who has been standing by for the past few years, you go to occupy Palestine," he said. "You take the soldiers responsible. You put the Israeli military under the pressure and under the accountability umbrella. Other than that, this won’t happen."
A serious response requires more than condemnation. UNESCO called for a "thorough and transparent investigation" after the killings, while press-freedom organisations have called for answers from Israel and accountability for attacks on media workers.
"Do not forget Gaza"
Towards the end of the evening, al-Sharif’s will was read aloud. Speakers noted that many journalists in Gaza had prepared similar messages because of the persistent danger they faced.
"If these words reach you, know that Israel has succeeded in killing me and silencing my voice," al-Sharif wrote.
"I have lived through pain in all its details. Tasted suffering and loss many times. Yet I never once hesitated to convey the truth as it is, without distortion or falsification."
He left behind his daughter Sham, his son Salah and his wife, Umm Salah, whom he described as remaining "steadfast as the trunk of an olive tree that does not bend" despite the separation imposed by Israel's war.
Al-Sharif’s final appeal was directed beyond the journalists’ tent where he was killed: "I urge you not to let the chains silence you, nor borders restrain you. Be bridges toward the liberation of the land and its people, until the sun of dignity and freedom rises over our stolen homeland."
"Do not forget Gaza," he wrote, "and do not forget me in your sincere prayers for forgiveness and acceptance."

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs refuted rumors about mandatory Reserve+ for 18-year-old Ukrainian women in the EU
Kyiv • UNN
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs called rumors about the mandatory presentation of "Reserve+" for 18-year-old Ukrainian women in the EU manipulative. The ministry confirmed isolated requests for information due to the EU's new rules.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine called manipulative the claims that 18-year-old Ukrainian women in EU countries are allegedly required to show the "Reserve+" app to obtain temporary protection. At the same time, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed isolated cases in which Ukrainian citizens, including women, were asked to provide information from "Reserve+," UNN writes.
Details
The ministry explained that such situations are related to the European Union's introduction of new rules for obtaining temporary protection in accordance with Council of the EU Decision 2026/1912 of July 30, 2026.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs is aware of cases in which, in certain EU member states, Ukrainian citizens, including women, were asked for information from Reserve+ while applying for temporary protection. This situation is related to the EU's introduction of new rules for obtaining temporary protection (Council of the EU Decision 2026/1912 of July 30, 2026)
As the EU has not yet provided member states with uniform clarifications regarding the practical application of this decision, certain national authorities are using their own instructions. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs explains the requests for information from "Reserve+" by this circumstance.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs speaks of isolated cases
The ministry emphasized that the cases known to the Ukrainian side are not widespread. For the most part, they concern situations in which applicants could not confirm the legality of their departure from Ukraine.
The cases known to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs are not widespread and concern, for the most part, situations in which applicants were unable to confirm the legality of their departure from Ukraine—for example, by showing in their international passport a stamp from the State Border Guard Service confirming that they crossed the border when departing Ukraine
As an example, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs cited the absence from an international passport of a State Border Guard Service stamp confirming that the holder crossed the border when departing Ukraine.
If there is confirmation that the departure was lawful, there should be no need to provide information from "Reserve+." At the same time, due to the lack of a uniform approach in certain EU countries, such requests are currently possible.
The Ukrainian side expects the European Union to standardize the practice of applying the new rules as soon as possible, taking Ukraine's appeals into account.
Recall
Earlier the National Security and Defense Council's Center for Countering Disinformation stated that information about the mandatory presentation of "Reserve+" by 18-year-old Ukrainian women seeking temporary protection in the EU is manipulative.

Ghalibaf's comments come amid a tense period in negotiations between Iran and the United States. Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Iranian news outlet Shahrara News earlier on Saturday that Iran-US negotiations have not resumed despite the regime exchanging messages with mediating countries Qatar and Pakistan.
Ghalibaf, who is also Iran's top negotiator, insisted that both Hezbollah and Lebanon were included in the US-Iran Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), Al Arabiya added.
IDF strikes Hezbollah terror targets in Lebanon
Meanwhile, the IDF continues to strike Hezbollah targets in Lebanon following ceasefire violations by the terrorist group, with the latest strike targeting the southern Lebanese village of Ansar overnight between Friday and Saturday.
Aoun condemned the "ongoing Israeli attacks" in a post from his office’s X/Twitter account on Saturday morning, calling them a "violation of the Framework Agreement."
Hezbollah responded to the IDF strikes later on Saturday, saying they would be "met accordingly."
Hezbollah chief: No progress in Israel-Lebanon framework agreement
According to Al Arabiya, Hezbollah Secretary-General Naim Qassem said on Friday that the Israel-Lebanon ceasefire framework "has not achieved any progress," describing the establishment of pilot zones for the framework in southern Lebanon as a "novelty that serves Israel’s goals."
The report contrasted Qassem's comments with those of Lebanese Information Minister Paul Morcos, who emphasized the country's commitment to continued negotiations with Israel.

The Norman: A high-end, quiet corner of Tel Aviv - review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
16:08:31 UTC
01:08:31 KST

Tel Aviv never stops. The city is full of movement wherever you go, especially during the hot summer months when the streets can feel almost overwhelming. Cars, scooters, construction, people rushing between appointments, and the Mediterranean heat all contribute to the city’s particular rhythm.
As someone living in the city, I am often looking for somewhere a little quieter, somewhere that still feels connected to Tel Aviv without having to experience all of it at once.
The Norman, just off Rothschild Boulevard and adjacent to Nahalat Binyamin, provides that contrast.
The four-story hotel occupies two restored 1920s heritage buildings, with citrus gardens and Italian-style patios connecting them.
From the outside, the architecture is relatively understated. Inside, the atmosphere changes. The interior combines the character of an older European residence with contemporary design, marble surfaces, dark wood, and a collection of Israeli art spread throughout the hotel.
Our room had tall windows, which brought in the afternoon light, while the combination of marble and dark wooden furniture gave the space a sense of calm.
Hotel library transforms into cocktail bar, Japanese dining spot at night
In the evening, the hotel’s library serves as a cocktail bar, leading into the on-site Dinings restaurant, which features a Japanese izakaya-style menu. The venue offers standard selections like tuna sashimi with yuzu, sake-steamed chicken, and yellowtail crispy rice with jalapeño aioli, and one of the non-traditional options is goose liver sushi.
It is worth noting for prospective guests that the hotel is not kosher, which limits its demographic. Furthermore, premium ingredients and a luxury setting mean menu prices are significantly higher than average Tel Aviv dining options, making it an unlikely choice for budget-conscious travelers.
After dinner, we moved out onto the balcony with our sake. Looking down, the contrast was hard to miss. Down on the streets, the city was still moving at its usual pace. Up above, everything felt considerably slower. It was a distinctly Tel Aviv moment, although one with a Japanese accent.
The following morning, we had breakfast in the courtyard. The area manages to maintain a connection with the city without exposing you completely to it.
Greenery and shade offer a welcome escape from the city outside
The sounds of the streets are still there, the buildings are still visible beyond the hotel, and the heat is impossible to forget, but the greenery and shade create a welcome separation.
After checking out, we left our luggage with the hotel and headed to the rooftop pool. The view up there puts the hotel back into its surroundings. Skyscrapers stand around the pool, while the Mediterranean appears on the horizon. The city and noise are everywhere, but from up there it seems considerably further away.
Ultimately, The Norman does not try to replace Tel Aviv, nor does it completely disconnect you from it. Instead, it offers a different way of experiencing the city, one where you can step outside into the heat and noise, then return to a quiet courtyard, a drink at the bar, dinner upstairs, or a few hours beside the pool.
While it comes at a very high price point, The Norman serves those looking to experience Tel Aviv without being consumed by its pace.
Sometimes experiencing Tel Aviv means going out and seeing everything it has to offer. Sometimes it means finding somewhere quiet enough to watch the city from a distance.
The writer was a guest of the hotel.

The rural roots of religious-Zionist philosophy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
16:08:30 UTC
01:08:30 KST

Sunday, August 16, is 3 Elul. It is not only the yahrzeit of Rabbi Abraham Isaac HaCohen Kook, the first chief rabbi of Israel and the greatest spiritual architect of religious Zionism. It is also an invitation to travel. Not merely through his books, but through landscapes.
The winding country roads of Latvia and Lithuania, lined with silver birch forests and bordered by quiet rivers, still seem to whisper his story. The scent of wet earth after a summer shower, the rustling of flax fields in the wind, the silence of forgotten Jewish cemeteries, all preserve echoes of a man who believed that holiness was not hidden from the changing world but revealed through it.
To understand Rabbi Kook, opening his books Orot or Igrot HaRe’iyah is not enough. We must walk where he walked, breathe the same northern air, and stand before the remnants of the communities that shaped his soul. Several Israeli religious tour operators organize heritage journeys following Rabbi Kook’s footsteps. Their tours continue to attract Jewish travelers eager to discover not only the biography of a towering rabbinic figure but also the landscapes from which his revolutionary ideas emerged.
Griva
Nearly 160 years ago, a baby was born in the small town of Griva, today a neighborhood of Daugavpils in southeastern Latvia. His parents named him Abraham Isaac, but affectionately called him “Yatzki.”
When little Yatzki was only three, he attended the local cheder. There he invented a game: He lined up the children with their small satchels across their shoulders, as though preparing for a long expedition. Then he asked them to call out: “Where are we going?” And he would shout back: “To Eretz Israel!”
It was a child’s game, yet in hindsight it seems almost prophetic.
That game took place in the courtyard of the Kaddish Synagogue, which still stands today after careful restoration. Here, his parents used to pray, and the young prodigy astonished the community. At nine, he was already delivering sermons from its pulpit, and by 11 he had begun writing a commentary on the Song of Songs.
Visitors to the synagogue at Cietokšna 38 today will find commemorative plaques honoring Rabbi Kook on the synagogue’s exterior. Joining the Mincha prayer service inside these ancient walls is more than a religious experience. It feels like stepping into the opening chapter of a remarkable life.
At 15, Rabbi Kook continued his studies in the Panevežys Yeshiva. There, Rabbi Israel Meir Hacohen, known as the Chafetz Chaim, gathered a select group of exceptionally gifted students who were priests and assigned them to immerse themselves in Seder Kodashim, the Talmudic tractates devoted to the Temple service and sacrificial rites. His vision was that when the Messiah came and the Temple was rebuilt, the Jewish people would already have scholars thoroughly versed in its sacred service. Rabbi Kook was chosen to join this elite circle and devoted himself to mastering the laws governing the priests’ service in the Holy Temple.
The Chafetz Chaim later arranged his marriage to the daughter of Rabbi Eliyahu David Rabinowitz-Teomim (the Aderet), then the rabbi of Panevežys.
Žeimelis
After his marriage, Rabbi Kook became rabbi of Žeimelis, a quiet agricultural village in northern Lithuania.
The countryside has hardly changed. White stone cottages still line the roads. Orange brick farmhouses stand beside wooden barns. Vast flax fields shimmer beneath enormous skies, interrupted only by rows of trees tracing the edges of streams and small lakes. Now and then, herds of deer emerge from the forest and bound gracefully across the open fields.
Most of the town’s Jewish residents were farmers. For the first time, the brilliant scholar confronted the practical questions of daily agricultural life: The shemita (sabbatical) year restrictions, milking cows on Shabbat, and the countless legal dilemmas of families whose livelihood depended on the land.
These encounters profoundly shaped his halachic thinking. The famous heter mechirah, the temporary sale of agricultural land during the sabbatical year, grew from a deep understanding of hardworking farmers whose faith and survival depended equally on the fields before them. Not from abstract legal theory. For Rabbi Kook, Jewish law was never meant to remain confined within the walls of beit midrash. It had to walk through muddy fields, endure rain and drought, and accompany people where life actually unfolded.
His former home no longer survives, but its foundations are marked by white stones at Bauskes Street 7.
Across from his home, once stood the synagogue where Rabbi Kook studied the Jerusalem Talmud and wrote the first chapters of the book Itur Sofrim, a place that helped shape his intellectual and spiritual world. When I stood among the remaining stones, I found myself regretting that I had not brought a volume of Igrot HaRe’iyah. There seemed no more fitting place to read his words than the place where many of his earliest ideas first took shape.
Rabbi Kook lived seven years in Žeimelis, which also witnessed profound personal sorrow. His first wife died here at a young age. Her gravestone, discovered years ago lying abandoned on the ground, has since been restored. The small Jewish cemetery has become another stop for Jewish travelers.
Here he remarried. Here his son, Rabbi Zvi Yehuda Kook, was born, later becoming head of Mercaz HaRav Yeshiva and one of the foremost spiritual leaders of religious Zionism (and my rosh yeshiva).
Bauska (Boysk)
From rural Žeimelis, Rabbi Kook moved to Bauska in southern Latvia. It was an entirely different world. More than half the city’s residents were Jewish, yet not all observed Jewish law. Traditional scholars lived alongside merchants, intellectuals, Zionists, laborers, members of the Bund, and young Jews already drifting away from religious life.
Years earlier, Rabbi Kook had often traveled to Bauska to study with Rabbi Mordechai Eliasberg, one of the leading figures of the Hibbat Zion movement and an early founder of the Mizrachi movement.
When Rabbi Eliasberg passed away, the young Rabbi Kook delivered the eulogy. His words so deeply impressed the community that they immediately offered him the city’s rabbinate.
He declined.
Only five years later did he finally accept.
The Jews of Žeimelis loved him so dearly that they reportedly organized a wagon drivers’ strike in an attempt to prevent his departure. Eventually, Bauska sent its own drivers, and the young rabbi began the next chapter of his life.
The central square of Bauska still looks remarkably similar to photographs from Rabbi Kook’s era. Nearby stands a memorial built on the site of his synagogue. The synagogue itself was torched by the Nazis.
Currently, there are no Jews in Bauska, but Jewish public buildings such as the school and the slaughterhouse remain and are worth visiting.
It was in Bauska that one of Rabbi Kook’s most influential ideas fully matured. Ten years he was living in Bauska. He encountered Jews who no longer observed Shabbat and mitzvot, yet he recognized their idealism, their devotion, and their love for the Jewish people and their ancestral homeland. He refused to define them as enemies. To him, even the secular pioneers draining swamps and cultivating barren land were partners in redemption. Their language differed from his; their purpose did not.
Following the First Zionist Congress in Basel in 1897, a rumor spread claiming that the Congress had resolved that “Zionism has nothing to do with religion.” (It was later revealed to be fake news, circulated by those whose position had been rejected in the vote).
In response, most rabbinic leaders chose to distance themselves from the Zionist movement. Rabbi Kook, however, challenged this approach and argued that there was a better alternative: a religious Zionism that united Jewish faith with Jewish nationhood rather than separating them. The estrangement of today’s haredi (ultra-Orthodox) community from compulsory service in the army has its roots in that historic moment, when many came to feel that Zionism was “not ours.”
At the age of 39, Rabbi Kook stood at a crossroads. He had to choose between serving as the spiritual supervisor (mashgiach) at the prestigious Telshe Yeshiva, or becoming the rabbi of Jaffa. He chose to make aliyah to Eretz Israel, and the rest is history.
Rabbi Kook’s contemporaries recognized his extraordinary stature. When derogatory remarks were spoken against him, the Chafetz Chaim reportedly declared that such words warranted the traditional act of rending one’s garments in grief. The Chazon Ish likewise refused to join those who opposed Jerusalem’s chief rabbi, saying simply: “Know that he is holy and pure.”
Returning with different eyes
Something changes after completing this journey. Returning to Rabbi Kook’s writings, one no longer encounters abstract ideas alone, but the landscapes that shaped them. Griva inspired his vision, Žeimelis taught agriculture, and Bauska deepened his understanding of sociology. From these quiet towns, he carried to Jaffa and Jerusalem a spiritual vision that sought to unite heaven and earth.
Today, most of the synagogues have disappeared, the rabbis’ homes are gone, and the communities that once flourished have faded into history. Yet among the birch forests, quiet rivers, and weathered stones, their spirit still lingers. Following Rabbi Kook’s footsteps across Latvia and Lithuania is more than a heritage tour. It is a journey to the birthplace of an idea: that faith and modernity, Torah and daily life, can enrich rather than oppose one another.
Perhaps that is Rabbi Kook’s greatest legacy. Not only the books he wrote, but the hope he carried. His footsteps remind us that every generation can rediscover its past, draw strength from it, and continue the journey toward a brighter future.
The author is the creator of the JewishTraveler blog.

‘My One and Only’ is a muddled look at Jewish mysticism - review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
16:08:04 UTC
01:08:04 KST

The Israeli movie My One and Only, which just opened in theaters around the country, aims high as it attempts to combine Jewish mysticism and Torah study with the mysterious style of a director like David Lynch.
For some, that description will be enough to get them to order a ticket, and the more you are interested in Jewish holy books, the more you will get out of this film.
But for anyone who just wants to have fun at the movies, it’s a misfire.
That’s a shame because there are many well-acted, well-written scenes and an intriguing main plotline. It follows multiple stories, all of which, on some level, dramatize mystical concepts.
The central story is that of a young wife and mother, Shira (Talya Bartfeld Diskin, who gives a compelling performance), who turns to her rabbi’s wife, Miri (Navit Sitbon), with a complaint familiar to horror-movie viewers: Her husband, Noam (Nadav Antman Ron), is not her husband – he’s been replaced by an imposter who looks just like him.
Is Shira’s husband possessed, or is she simply imagining it?
Her reasons for suspecting this switch are very prosaic, and will be familiar to anyone who’s ever been married: He seems indifferent; he came home from the store without buying what she asked him to; he doesn’t remember what he said about her blouse a few months ago.
It seems as if, in the tradition of the classic Rosemary’s Baby, the director is leaving us to decide whether her husband is possessed or whether Shira is just neurotic, a new mother who feels dismayed that her husband has lost interest in her.
But then there is another detail: his dominant hand seems to have switched. Miri tells her husband (Shimon Mimran) about it, and he is skeptical that anything is genuinely wrong, and quotes various Jewish texts to her.
Miri wants Shiri to see a famous psychiatrist (Zohar Strauss), who turns out to have become a mystic who performs exorcisms, while Shira resists the notion that she needs mental help.
Miri is in touch with another young woman, Gaia (Inbal Raz), who is about to get married and who, although she is secular, has just become interested in studying Jewish texts.
Gaia asks her fiancé, Idan (Yoel Rosenkier), why he decided that she was the one, as the couple sit with their families tasting the food at the venue where their wedding will be held. This leads to a reminiscence by one of the couple’s fathers about how he fell in love, but when he tells the story, his wife says that it’s all about the girlfriend he had before her, continuing the theme of doubles and replacement.
There is also a waitress, Heli (Ella Armony), at the wedding hall, who is caring for her senile mother who may or may not be possessed by some kind of spirit.
Suddenly, and this is where the movie lost me and never got me back, the two actresses playing Heli and Gaia switch roles.
A familiar cinematic device that works better in theory than practice
This is not an unprecedented device, but frankly, it always annoys me.
The master director Luis Buñuel did something similar in his 1977 film, That Obscure Object of Desire, where he had two very different actresses, one elegant and chilly, the other fiery and sensual, playing the same character at different times, and there, it worked well.
But here, when these two pretty ingenues swap places, it doesn’t seem to mean anything. I imagine we are supposed to think about how the course of anyone’s life could change in an instant, or how we might all have easily ended up with a different partner under certain circumstances. But neither actress is distinctive, and it just takes you out of the action and makes you think about the director’s logic.
There’s also a sequence where Shira goes to visit her grandmother (the always entertaining Shosha Goren), who tells her that her own husband was replaced years ago, after trauma he experienced in combat. The grandmother, who is not observant, believes he was taken by aliens, rather than an evil spirit.
It goes on like this, and the biggest suspense is whether the actresses will switch back. Along the way, there are some interesting scenes and ideas, which make it seem that there is a well-constructed movie struggling to get out of this muddled script.
Tauber made the movie with his wife, producer Eliya Tauber – with whom he has four children – over a period of 10 years, and that’s a nice story.
I have a feeling it would be more fun to watch an interview with them talking about the ideas behind the movie than it is to actually see their film.

Australian lawyer makes aliyah just before October 7, quits job to launch babywear brand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
16:08:00 UTC
01:08:00 KST

I’m an Australian lawyer who made aliyah just before October 7, had my third baby here, then quit my NGO job during the war with Iran to launch a babywear brand,” says Miriam Agranat, the 33-year-old daughter of an Israeli-born mother and Australian father.
She had long harbored the dream of making aliyah, having been raised in a strongly Zionist home, attending a Zionist school, and participating in the Bnei Akiva youth movement in Sydney. In high school, she and several 10th-grade girls spent a school term in Israel. “The trip had such a profound impact on me that adjusting back to life in Australia wasn’t easy,” she says.
Until the time was right, she earned a law degree at Macquarie University and landed a job at a large corporate law firm. She married her high school sweetheart, Ori, in 2016. When their first baby came along six years ago, she shifted into venture capital and found it much more fulfilling than corporate law. Still, not all the pieces were exactly in place.
“Life in Australia is beautiful and comfortable, but it was missing something,” she says. “My husband and I talked about wanting more for our children. So we decided to make the move to Israel once we had a three-year-old and a less-than-one-year-old.”
On a pilot trip, they visited various communities and chose Modi’in because of its central location, not knowing where they’d be working. “It has turned out to be the best thing. It’s quite Anglo, with a mix of Americans, British, Australians, and South Africans, and we’ve been welcomed with open arms.”
One of her two younger sisters had made aliyah a few years before, and her parents followed a year later, also settling in Modi’in. “We’re all on a high here. I’m so thankful we are here, especially with what’s happening in Australia now,” Agranat says.
She recounts that when she tells people that they arrived in August 2023, “everyone says, ‘Oh my gosh, what bad timing!’ But it was one of the best decisions we ever made. We’ve created such incredible friends here; we’re in such a special community that became like family, and we landed very special jobs.”
Agranat discovers outlet for long-felt entrepreneurial desire
Her husband works for an energy company. She got a job in January 2024 as donor relations manager for Orr Shalom, a national organization for children and youth at risk. She loved her work there, but a year ago, after giving birth to her third child, she discovered an outlet for a long-felt entrepreneurial desire.
“I’d always had an itch to start my own business. When we made aliyah, it wasn’t the right time. The war started, and I was a new immigrant and didn’t know anything about anything here. So I opted to do something meaningful,” she explains.
“Then, when I was on maternity leave, I didn’t find baby clothing here that I liked, and I felt that I needed to bring the standard I know from Australia. The itch to start my own business came back full force.”
She spent time during her maternity leave developing the idea and researching the basics of how to turn it into a business for the Israeli market. She chose the name Tiftaf (Hebrew for “droplets”) “because it’s catchy, playful, associated with Israeli childhood, and filled with Israeli soul.”
Agranat built Tiftaf as a one-woman operation, teaching herself every part of the process from scratch: design, textile patterns, manufacturing, importing, marketing, filling orders, and brand-building. Her father, a serial e-commerce entrepreneur, supported her with the technical side of the business.
The first product is an infant onesie made of a stretchy blend of organic cotton and bamboo. It features a two-way zipper for easy diaper changing, fold-over feet that become socks, and fold-over sleeves that become protective mittens. These premium features blend Australian standards with Israeli creativity.
“I’m releasing the onesies in very limited drops and collaborating with Israeli local artists. They’re doing extremely bold, colorful prints,” Agranat says.
“For the next drop that’s currently live, I commissioned a Tel Aviv artist I met in Nahalat Binyamin. She painted two beautiful designs – a Tel Aviv landscape and a playground. Once that sells out, it will not come back, so it’s essentially a collectible,” she notes. “Tiftaf clothing is functional, beautiful, authentic, and unique.”
Despite launching the business during the war with Iran and the website in mid-May amid continuing geopolitical uncertainty, Agranat found the response “exceptional and mind-blowing. Within the first five minutes of going live, I had 40 people at checkout. After a week, I’d sold half my stock and realized I’m really filling in a gap.”
Social media influencers with tens of thousands of followers discovered the brand organically, including one who reached out after seeing Tiftaf shared in a local WhatsApp group and offered to help.
“Others began following before I had even approached them, and later chose to share the product as well. I felt truly supported by a community who genuinely wanted to back a small, female-led business.”
The challenges of starting a new business amid a war
Much as Agranat enjoys realizing her entrepreneurial ambitions, it hasn’t been simple in these extraordinary times.
“Shipping the first drop in wartime was very touch-and-go. I paid a huge amount for air shipping and was on the phone with FedEx and customs officials every day. I was lucky that it came through in time.
“The morning after the drop arrived, I had a photographer come to do a photo shoot, then we promoted it and went live. It was a fast and very stressful process. But it had a great response.”
Agranat says she believes that part of building a life in Israel is noticing where things can be better and feeling responsible enough to help improve them. She noted that she has taken to heart the phrase, “If not me, then who?” echoed in the words and diaries of fallen Israeli soldiers, including Capt. Daniel Perez.
“For me, it is not about focusing on what is different or difficult here,” she says. “It is about asking what I can contribute. If not me, then who? That idea really permeates me. We all have a responsibility, in whatever small way we can, to help build the country we want to live in.”
Miriam Di Veroli Agranat, 33
From Sydney to Modi'in, 2023

Catania Airport in Sicily resumed flights on August 15 after the aviation hazard level due to activity from Mount Etna was lowered from red to orange. Airport representatives reported this, Reuters reports, writes UNN.
Details

The academic was found dead a week after he quit his role as Cambridge University professor and Jesus College fellow after allegations he had plagiarised parts of his PhD thesis and embellished his life achievements.
The family of British academic Jason Arday, who was found dead at a South London address on Friday night amid a high-profile plagiarism storm, have denounced what they called years of "sustained abuse".
In an overnight statement following Arday's death, his family said he had been "subjected to a campaign of sustained abuse for more than three years since he accepted the role of professor at Cambridge University".
Arday had himself alleged a "racially motivated" campaign against him.
Speaking to reporters on Saturday, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said "it's a tragedy on so many levels, but particularly just for everybody who knew Jason, his family obviously, his friends."
Burnham also said it was not the time for "any rushing to judgement", and that now is "a moment for reflection... reflecting on how things came to this."
A 'campaign of misinformation'
Arday resigned from his post at the University of Cambridge last week shortly after it announced a probe into the various accusations against him.
He made headlines when the university appointed him as its youngest black professor in 2023, but subsequently faced growing claims he plagiarised parts of his PhD thesis.
Questions also emerged about some of his stated life achievements, including that he once ran 30 marathons in 35 days and raised millions for charities.
The allegations were seized on by British right-wing newspapers and commentators, who claimed he unfairly benefited from diversity, equality and inclusion (DEI) policies.
Media outlets including The Times, Guardian and the Telegraph have published several investigative articles into Arday's academic work and personal life.
In their statement following his death, Arday's family alleged "the campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone."
Diagnosed with autism, Arday said he was non-verbal until age 11 and only learnt to read and write at 18, before becoming Cambridge's youngest black professor at age 37, teaching sociology.
In an interview with The Times earlier this month, Arday admitted making academic "mistakes" but said he was being wrongly "portrayed to be a liar and a fantasist and an academic fraud".
He said that some errors in his early academic work were because of his autism, as he relied on using mimicry to understand information.
Simon Baron-Cohen, a Cambridge professor and director of the Autism Research Centre, told BBC radio that he spoke to Arday on Friday morning.
"He was being subjected to relentless scrutiny, including ridicule, discrediting absolutely every detail of his life," he said.
"He wasn't coping with the loss of his career, the loss of his reputation, and he felt he could not go on. He used those words in voice notes."

PARIS - British budget carrier easyJet has called off about 100 flights out of French airports on Aug 16 and 17 because of a strike by cabin crew furious over repeated changes to their schedules.
Unions said about half of the company’s 900 French-based cabin crew would join the strike, which would affect about half of the flights out of two Paris airports, Nice, Bordeaux and Lyon.
The airline’s management has called the action “opportunistic” as it falls on a major national holiday weekend when airports are busy.
France is a key market for the low-cost airline, which was recently taken over in a US$7.7 billion (S$9.8 billion) deal by US private equity firm Apollo.
Its passenger numbers in France are second only to Air France.
Most of the flights were cancelled on Aug 15, with the company saying it wanted to help passengers find alternative routes.
William Bourdon of the SNPNC-FO union said that cabin crew wanted “stability” in their duties.
He said some crew could see their hours and destinations changed 50-60 times a week.
“For anything to do with personal life or childcare, it makes things extremely complicated to organise because most of the changes come at the last moment – 24 to 48 hours before,” he told AFP.
“It is a permanent musical chairs,” Bourdon added.
The three unions involved in talks have warned of strikes between Aug 7 and Sept 2.
When easyJet lacks staff at an airport, they are called in from another base, which must then fill its own gaps, said Bourdon.
Ahead of the action, easyJet urged staff to call off the strike on such a busy weekend. It said it had made offers to change staff conditions and that talks were planned in September.
A previous strike in April had only a limited impact. Unions accused the company of offering bonuses of up to €700 (S$1,000) to work on that day of action.
Bourdon said he had warned the company against using a similar “illegal” tactic this weekend.
EasyJet declined to comment on this when reached by AFP. AFP
