Anthropic's revenue surged more than 14-fold in the second quarter from a year earlier, Bloomberg News reported Friday, underscoring the rapid growth of the Claude chatbot maker as it prepares for a potential blockbuster initial public offering.
The AI company reported preliminary revenue of more than $11.5 billion for its latest completed quarter, up from $787 million in the same period last year and $4.73 billion in the first quarter of 2026, according to documents viewed by Bloomberg News.

An IPO as soon as this fall could make Anthropic one of the first major private AI companies to tap public markets. That debut would unlock access to billions of dollars in additional capital, providing the immense financial runway required to fund escalating compute infrastructure costs, secure advanced hardware, and build specialized data centers.

‘No longer small dreams’: Modi’s message to India on Independence Day (VIDEO)

‘No longer small dreams’: Modi’s message to India on Independence Day (VIDEO)
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday outlined the country’s achievements and priorities for future growth as the world’s largest democracy marked its 80th Independence Day.
Addressing the nation after hoisting the Indian national flag at Delhi’s iconic Red Fort, Modi cited India’s rapid economic growth from being one of the ‘Fragile Five’ economies in 2013 to a $4.15 trillion, fast-growing major economy, and said the country is emerging in the eyes of the world as a widely accepted and respected nation.
The ‘Fragile Five’, was a term for Türkiye, Brazil, India, South Africa, and Indonesia, which were overly dependent on unpredictable foreign investments and large current account deficits to fuel their economic growth.
“Our country is not going to move forward with small dreams,” Modi said, noting the country rises through the “strength of its dreams, its resolutions, and its capabilities.”
📹🇮🇳 ‘We Can No Longer Move Forward With Small Dreams’: Modi’s Big Message From Red Fort
The prime minister urged Indians to “dream big,” saying a nation rises through the strength of its dreams, resolve and capabilities. https://t.co/F71jMC9sPTpic.twitter.com/GgzxMjxJmL
Fuel for growth
Listing India’s achievements in the last 12 years since his Bharatiya Janata Party came to power, Modi said the country’s defense production has increased fourfold, electronic manufacturing has increased sevenfold, and digital transactions have increased 100 times.
Modi pointed to the success of his Make-in-India initiative, and cited the three chip plants that the country has built, with plans to add eight more. “Chips are indispensable; without them, the world would come to a standstill,” he said, as Indian positions itself to benefit from the global demand for chips driven by the boom in artificial intelligence and data centers.
This, however, raises the demands for energy security, Modi acknowledged, stating that the South Asian nation will need electricity “on a very large scale.”
The Indian leader reiterated the country’s target of achieving a capacity of 100 GW of nuclear power by 2047 and highlighted the need for accelerating offshore exploration to find oil and gas that could replace imported energy that makes the national economy vulnerable to external shocks.
⚛️ AI Needs Power, PM Modi Wants Nuclear To Bring It
Pointing to GPUs, AI and data centres, Modi said, “Energy security is the need of our times,” adding that India will need electricity “on a very large scale” and is targeting 100 GW of nuclear power by 2047.
The SHANTI Act,… https://t.co/dIK8Pogw5hpic.twitter.com/Ihr51lv9xx
New Delhi in December 2025 passed the SHANTI Act (the Sustainable Harnessing and Advancement of Nuclear Energy for Transforming India Act), which modernizes India’s nuclear framework and opens the door to greater private sector participation in India’s nuclear energy industry, which has been lacking so far.
The country currently operates 24 nuclear power reactors across seven different sites with a total installed capacity of 8.78 GW. This includes Russia-built Kudankulam designed to house six VVER-1000 reactors with a total planned capacity of 6,000 MW. Units 1 and 2 were connected to the national grid in 2013 and 2016, respectively, while units 3, 4, 5, and 6 are at different stages of implementation and construction.
Overall, India currently has ten reactor units with a combined capacity of 8,000 MW are under construction, while pre-project activities for ten additional reactors are also underway.
Focus on self-relaence
“It is our conviction that India must not be dependent on other countries. We must become self-reliant,” Modi stated, calling for strengthening the country’s capabilities and protecting national interests.
Modi outlined seven broad areas that he said would be central to his government’s goal of turning India into a developed country by 2047. These included manufacturing, agriculture and food production, technology and innovation, connectivity – including high-speed rail – defense production, the green and blue economy – such as green hydrogen, renewables and energy storage – as well as the expansion of India’s soft power such as yoga, which he called “an energy for the world, and a major source of confidence for India.”
“India possesses a stable political mandate, a stable government, a vibrant democracy, a robust judiciary, and guiding all of us is the Constitution of India,” Modi said. He also noted that the youth are the “biggest beneficiaries” of India’s development, and said his government will run free online coaching networks for competitive exams for students. The move comes weeks after student-led unrest rocked the country’s capital and led to the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
Celebrating friendship
India achieved independence from British rule on August 15, 1947, through largely non-violent means and beginning the end of Western colonial rule over the world. Independence Day celebrations were held across the country, in state capitals and various offices.
In Moscow, Indian Ambassador Vinay Kumar raised the tricolor at the Indian Embassy as the Indian national anthem was sung. In a symbolic move, a group of Russian and Indian motorcyclists rode across the city to celebrate the decades of close ties, marked by cooperation and trust.

'Not a matter of ego': BCI chairman apologises to law students after row over NALSAR diktat
TOI News Desk / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 15, 2026, 20:37 IST
Comments

NEW DELHI: Bar Council of India chairman Manan Kumar Mishra on Saturday apologised to law students following the council's controversial decision to briefly halt the enrolment of National Academy of Legal Studies and Research (NALSAR) University of Law's 2026 graduating batch as advocates, Bar and Bench reported.In a letter issued on Independence Day, Mishra said he regretted any words or communication connected to the controversy that may have hurt the feelings of law students."If anything connected with the present controversy, any of my words, or letter, has hurt the feelings of our law students, I sincerely regret and apologise for the same. There should be no hesitation in saying so," the letter reads."An expression of regret is not a matter of prestige or ego. It is simply an acknowledgment that the feelings and concerns of our students matter," he added.The apology comes after the BCI directed all state bar councils not to enrol NALSAR's 2026 graduates as advocates until further orders. The council withdrew the directive within hours following an uproar on social media.The BCI had initially said it was examining allegations regarding a campaign against Chief Justice of India Surya Kant's participation in NALSAR's convocation and had sought a report identifying those responsible.
The council later modified its decision to allow the enrolment of the university's 2026 graduates before withdrawing the notification altogether. The revised notification said the "vast majority" of students were innocent and should not be made to suffer for the alleged "misconduct" of a few.The controversy began after around 450 graduating NALSAR students urged the university to reconsider inviting CJI Kant as chief guest at its convocation. The students cited his alleged refusal to hear pleas concerning "police brutality" against students who had marched to Parliament on July 20 seeking the resignation of then-Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the NEET-UG question paper leak in May.
The Supreme Court later expressed "strong disapproval" of the BCI's now-revoked order.A bench headed by CJI Kant, and comprising Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, said students have the right to protest peacefully and described the episode as a "dialogue" between him and the students."If students are protesting peacefully, who is BCI to take action? It is the right of the students to protest peacefully. It is a dialogue between students and me. No one else has to step in," the CJI said.The Supreme Court also stayed any coercive action against students or faculty by the BCI or state councils."It (the letter) was absolutely uncalled for," the bench added.

TV TIME: Best intense thrillers while awaiting ‘Fauda’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
14:39:40 UTC
23:39:40 KST

Fauda finally announced its Netflix international release date is September 8, when you will be able to stream its fifth season with English subtitles.
But that’s almost a month away, and what will you watch till then? One option, obviously, is to re-watch the previous season, which introduced new characters and spanned several continents. But I would recommend going back even further and starting with the first season, so you can see how the characters and themes develop.
Another suggestion is to watch a different thriller series in the meantime. Legends, the new Netflix series about British customs agents cracking an international drug ring, is one of the best recent ones and shows how drug cartels operate around the world, as does Narcos, which is also on Netflix.
On Apple TV+, Slow Horses is a good option, even though it’s far more comic than Fauda, but it really does build suspense. It was recently announced that the sixth season of Slow Horses will be released on September 16.
If you are looking for something a little lighter, a series that fits that sweet spot between too dark and too dumb, then check out Parenthood, which has just become available on Hot VOD and Next TV, and will be shown on Hot 3 starting at the end of August. The series is also available on Netflix.
I have recommended this series in the past because it helped me get through the pandemic and the early days of the war.
Parenthood brings three generations of a complicated family to life
Unlike other essentially feel-good series that were a bit more grandiose or contrived, like This Is Us, Parenthood tells the story of a loving but complicated three-generation family in Berkeley, California. It was based on a darker, more cynical movie of the same name starring Steve Martin, but aside from a few plotlines, it has little relation to the film.
Usually, in a series like this, you tend to like one generation, but here, they are all equally engaging. The oldsters are Zeke (Craig T Nelson), a demanding Vietnam veteran with an unpredictable side, and Camille (Bonnie Bedelia, who has never been more charming), an aspiring painter who gave it all up to be a supermom to her four children.
The adult children are the main protagonists, and the series gets going when prodigal daughter Sarah (Lauren Graham of The Gilmore Girls) moves home, years after running off with a musician, bringing along her two teenagers, Amber (Mae Whitman of Good Girls) and Drew (Miles Heizer from People We Meet on Vacation).
The rebellious Sarah learned far too late that her parents were right about her ex and is trying to build a new life for herself, which is a struggle since bartending is her only marketable skill.
Her brother, Adam (Peter Krause of Six Feet Under), encouraged her to make the move back to the family home. An executive at a shoe company, he is the good son, and he is the one everyone comes to with their problems.
But he is dealing with a big problem of his own when his son Max (Max Burkholder, one of the standouts in a great cast) is diagnosed with Asperger Syndrome.
Julia (Erika Christenson), a control-freak lawyer, and Crosby (Dax Shepard), an unreliable sound engineer who has to grow up in a hurry when a former flame returns, round out the Braverman second generation.
The supporting cast includes Michael B Jordan, who just won the Best Actor Oscar for Sinners; comic Ray Romano of the series Everybody Loves Raymond; and Xolo Mariduena, who starred in the Cobra Kai series.
Besides the likability of the entire cast, the series, created by Jason Katims, has several unusual aspects. One is that the writing is so much less predictable than on most television shows. Another is that the Asperger storyline, based on Katims’ own family, is just one story among many; it’s just part of life.
A third is the soundtrack, which features great indie and offbeat music, including a gospel version of Bob Dylan’s “To Make You Feel My Love” and dozens of other songs that may well end up on your playlist.
Two of the characters eventually team up to open a recording studio, and many real musicians drift through the show, including CeeLo Green recording a Janis Joplin song and Glen Hansard, the Irish musician who passed away recently.
Monster explores the origins of evil in post-Cold War Germany
I’ve watched quite a few anime series, and the only one I’ve ever been moved to re-watch is Monster, available with English subtitles on Netflix. I was introduced to it by one of my sons, and it’s really unlike anything out there, both in the anime world and in general.
Based on a famous manga series by Naoki Urasawa, the series brings Urasawa’s drawings to life, and they are beautiful.
This isn’t the kind of anime where everyone has exaggerated round eyes, but rather a far more realistic style.
Monster opens with a quote about the beast from the Book of Revelation, and it tells an ambitious story that grapples with no less a topic than the origin of evil. Set in Germany mainly during the decade after the fall of the Berlin Wall, its hero is a brilliant young Japanese neurosurgeon named Kenzo Tenma, who has come to Europe to finish his training.
Tenma is ambitious but has a strong moral compass. When Johan, a child whose life he saved, turns up years later, Tenma learns to his horror that the young man is a psychopathic murderer. Even worse, Johan frames the surgeon for his crimes, and Tenma must go on the run, determined to save the world from this monstrous killer.
The series provides a kind of snapshot of Germany in that era. The path to Johan leads to an East German eugenics project in an orphanage, whose creators tried to twist children’s minds using a frightening fairy tale.
There are a little over 70 episodes of Monster, and each runs about 20 minutes, so it will keep you busy for a while – and it’s hard to stop at just one. If you can watch the English version, you will get to hear Liam O’Brien as Tenma, which is considered to be one of the greatest performances in anime.
The bottom line is that Monster plays as if Alfred Hitchcock had come back to life and decided to direct an anime.
Shark Week may be over, but there’s still plenty to watch
Maybe you didn’t get your fill of shark content when Shark Week ran on the Discovery Channel, and Sharkfest was shown on National Geographic Wild. The good news is that there is still a lot of shark content out there, perfect to watch on mind-numbingly hot days.
Obviously, the great shark movie will always be Jaws, which is available to rent or buy on Apple TV+. People may not remember that there were multiple Jaws sequels that Steven Spielberg had nothing to do with. They are all beyond terrible, but the most unintentionally funny one is Jaws: The Revenge.
It is set mostly in the Bahamas and stars acclaimed actor Michael Caine, who has admitted he was having financial problems when he signed on to the role. Most of the Jaws sequels are available on Apple TV+, although Jaws fans will probably have more fun with the documentary, Jaws@50: The Definitive Inside Story, available on Disney+.
Disney+ is truly the king of shark content among the streamers, featuring over 20 shark documentaries, so there may be one you haven’t seen yet. You might enjoy the two newest documentaries, the Up Close series with the genial British researcher and filmmaker Bertie Gregory, Hammerhead Sharks: Up Close and Sharks: Up Close.
There’s also Sharkcano, a documentary that reveals that wherever there are active volcanoes, the nearby waters are filled with sharks. Could there be a connection, or was this documentary created mainly because the title sounds like Sharknado?
You’ll have to watch it to find out.

Rediscovering an ancient gift: What Nigerian Jews taught me about the meaning of Shabbat - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
14:39:18 UTC
23:39:18 KST

For the second year running, I had the privilege of teaching a remarkable group of young Nigerian Jews. They are primarily members of the Igbo ethnic group who believe that they are descended from the lost tribe of Gad. What struck me last year was their extraordinary sincerity.
These young men and women, many of whom are highly educated professionals, were not interested in the labels and divisions that so often preoccupy the established Jewish world. They simply wanted to learn Torah, understand Judaism, and deepen their connection to the Jewish people.
Last year, when I taught them, they made me rethink what it means to choose Judaism. This year, they made me think again about Shabbat.
I had been asked to give them four one-hour sessions. Their Jewish knowledge was enthusiastic but patchy, so I could not assume that everyone knew what kiddush was, why we light candles on Friday before sunset, what the prayer “Lecha Dodi” means, why there are three meals on Shabbat, or even why Jews refrain from doing certain things on the day of rest.
It was an interesting challenge. Where do you begin to explain Shabbat from scratch? Not with turning light switches on and off. Nor with cooking, carrying, mobile phones, or the 39 categories of prohibited activity. Those things matter, of course, and eventually we discussed them. But if your introduction to Shabbat is simply a list of things you are not allowed to do, you have missed the point.
So I found myself going back to the beginning. Literally.
The first Shabbat in the Torah is found in the opening chapter of human existence. God created the world in six days and then stopped on the seventh.
Shabbat does not mean collapsing exhausted onto the sofa after a difficult week. It means ceasing; stepping back from creating, manipulating, producing, and controlling.
Suddenly, I realized how radical that message has become. We live in a world that measures us by what we produce. How much have we earned? How many emails have we answered? How many tasks have we completed? How quickly did we respond to that WhatsApp message?
Our phones make us permanently available. Work follows us home. News follows us to bed. Even recreation becomes something to photograph, post, and share.
Then, once a week, Judaism says: stop. For 25 hours, the world can manage without you. That is an extraordinarily liberating idea.
The Torah gives another explanation for Shabbat in the second version of the Ten Commandments. This time, it tells us to remember that we were slaves in Egypt.
What does slavery have to do with Shabbat? Everything.
A slave does not own his time. Someone else determines when he wakes, when he works, when he eats, and when he may stop. Shabbat, therefore, is a weekly declaration of freedom. I may have an employer, responsibilities, bills, and deadlines, but ultimately I am not a slave to any of them.
Perhaps today we should add something else: I am not a slave to my screen. That does not mean technology is evil; far from it. I am writing these words on a computer, and I taught my Nigerian students using modern technology.
But something can be useful without being entitled to occupy every minute of our lives. There is something wonderfully subversive about a dinner table where nobody is looking at a screen.
Sacred and ordinary time
Teaching the practical structure of Shabbat reminded me of something else we easily overlook: Shabbat has theater.
Friday is spent preparing. Food is cooked. The house is made ready. We wash and change our clothes. Candles are lit. In synagogue, we sing “Lecha Dodi” and metaphorically go out to welcome the Shabbat bride.
We do not simply notice that Saturday has arrived. We welcome Shabbat as an honored guest.
Then there is kiddush, invoking the sanctification of the day and declaring that this piece of time is different from the time that preceded it. There are meals, singing, Torah, conversation, prayer, and community. At the end comes havdalah, when wine, spices, and flame accompany us as we distinguish between sacred time and ordinary time.
That distinction is crucial. Judaism does not teach that the ordinary week is bad. We need six days in which to work, build, trade, travel, and create.
But Judaism insists that not everything should be ordinary. We need sacred space, but we also need sacred time. And there is something particularly ingenious about sacred time. A holy building can be destroyed. A holy place can become inaccessible. A people can be driven from its land.
But Shabbat travels. Jews carried it to Baghdad and Berlin, Casablanca and Krakow, London and Lagos. Wherever Friday evening arrived, Jewish sacred time arrived with it.
Think about this: a Shabbat table throughout the millennia hasn’t changed! Candles, wine, challah, a white tablecloth, and our best tableware.
That is surely part of what Ahad Ha’am, the founder of cultural Zionism, meant when he famously wrote that more than the Jewish people have kept Shabbat, Shabbat has kept the Jewish people. For generations, it created a rhythm that said: whatever country you live in, whatever language you speak, whatever happened to you this week, you belong to an ancient story.
Where rediscovery begins
Teaching these young Nigerians also made me wonder whether we present Shabbat as an all-or-nothing proposition too often.
I am an Orthodox rabbi. I believe that Shabbat has a halachic structure and that its laws matter. I am not suggesting that we can simply rewrite them according to personal preference.
But there is a world of difference between saying, “I do not yet keep every aspect of Shabbat,” and saying, “Therefore, Shabbat has nothing to offer me.”
Imagine what would happen if Jewish families who currently do little to mark Shabbat decided that Friday night would become sacred family time. Phones away, no television, a proper meal, candles, wine, challah. Perhaps one song and one exchange of Torah. Perhaps simply two hours in which parents and children actually talk to each other.
Would that constitute full halachic Shabbat observance? No. Would it enrich Jewish lives? I find it difficult to believe otherwise. Perhaps that is where rediscovery begins.
My Nigerian students needed me to explain why Jews prepare their homes for Shabbat, why we sing to welcome a day, why we stop creating, and why we separate holy time from ordinary time.
As I was explaining it to them, I recalled that last year they reminded me that Judaism cannot merely be inherited – it has to be chosen. This year, they again reminded me that Shabbat must be chosen.
Perhaps in an age of permanent noise, permanent availability, and permanent distraction, that ancient choice has never been more modern.
For one day a week, stop. The world will survive. And we may discover that we are living again.
The writer is a rabbi and physician. He writes and teaches on Jewish ethics, leadership, and resilience. His work appears on rabbidrjonathanlieberman.substack.com and youtube.com. @rabbidrjonathanlieberman.

What is the connection between Zionism and planting trees in Israel?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
14:39:02 UTC
23:39:02 KST

The Torah prohibits the unnecessary destruction of resources. This principle is known as bal tash’hit, the ban against needless waste.
Of course, what constitutes waste depends on context. Behavior that is wasteful in one era or circumstance may not be considered wasteful in another. In a modern world where, thank God, food is abundant, discarding leftover food may not carry the same implications that it did in generations marked by scarcity.
What is striking is the setting in which this prohibition appears. The Torah introduces bal tash’hit, the prohibition against waste, amid warfare, rather than in the more predictable setting of agriculture or everyday life.
Ancient wars were fought by laying siege to cities, requiring enormous quantities of timber. Wood was needed for military camps, battering rams, siege towers, and fuel. Recognizing these genuine military needs, the Torah permits the felling of non-fruit-bearing trees for such purposes, while protecting fruit trees from wanton destruction.
Why do we plant trees?
When outlining this prohibition, the Torah offers an iconic analogy: ki ha’adam etz hasadeh, “man is like the tree of the field.” Just as human life must be carefully protected, a tree that produces and sustains life cannot simply be felled for utilitarian purposes.
The comparison reflects the unusual connection human beings have always felt toward trees. More than almost any other part of nature, we identify with trees and sometimes even personify them.
The 19th-century naturalist W. H. Hudson observed nature through an almost spiritual lens. In his memoir Far Away and Long Ago, he recounts the story of a landowner who possessed a “reverential feeling for his old trees.” Before retiring for the night, “he would walk round to visit them, one by one,” resting his hand on the bark and whispering good night. Hudson writes that the man believed his trees possessed “intelligent souls” and appreciated his devotion. To him, trees were alive, individual, and deeply personal.
Unlike this landowner, we do not believe that nature is animate, and trees certainly do not possess human souls. Yet the prominence of trees throughout Tanach suggests that our attachment to them is more than sentimental.
Human history begins among the trees of the Garden of Eden. Abraham receives his angelic visitors beneath a tree, and Jonah becomes deeply attached to his kikayon tree. Again and again, trees appear in Tanach as part of the human landscape.
Even the anatomy of a tree invites comparison to the human form. A mature tree has a clearly defined structure: hidden roots supporting a central trunk which rises and spreads into an intricate network of branches. There is something almost “bodily” about this structure, with a stable core and limbs reaching outward in different directions.
Our Sages drew on this structure in Pirkei Avot, comparing a person whose wisdom exceeds his deeds to a tree with many branches but few roots, easily overturned by the wind. The comparison works because we so readily recognize human qualities reflected in trees.
More than almost any other feature of nature, trees really do seem alive. As Shakespeare wrote, there are “tongues in trees.” Each tree has its own shape and something resembling a distinct personality. An old oak conveys strength, a willow gentleness, a cypress dignity. Trees grow and mature; they age and become scarred, and each develops its own shape and character.
The comparison between a tree and a human being reminds us to guard against wasting human potential. A productive tree still has fruit to bear; a person still has talents, abilities, and contributions to offer. Wasting either means cutting short what could still have been produced.
The connection between trees and war
However, there is a particular reason why the Torah draws this analogy between human beings and trees, specifically in the context of war. The qualities represented by trees carry special importance during wartime. Preserving sensitivity toward trees can help counter some of the pressures that war creates.
Planting for Israel's future
Trees teach us to think about the future. The Talmud in Ta’anit tells of a man planting a carob tree even though he will not live long enough to enjoy its fruit. When asked why he is planting for a future he will not see, he explains that he entered a world filled with trees planted by earlier generations and must do the same for those who will follow him.
Unlike crops that must be replanted each year, a tree planted today can continue producing fruit for decades. Trees naturally extend our vision beyond our own lives. We plant and nurture them, knowing that their fullest benefits may only be enjoyed by generations who had no part in planting them.
War demands that we extend our vision into the future. It is painful and exhausting, exacting enormous sacrifices at many levels. Without a clear vision of what we are fighting for, those sacrifices become much harder to sustain. A war without a larger purpose can easily become a succession of battles without hope.
During the past three years, we have endured an extraordinarily difficult war; the strain on our society has been enormous. The war has dragged on without a clear and decisive victory on the horizon.
We must keep reminding ourselves that our generation is struggling so that future generations will not face the violence and pogroms that we experienced on October 7. Sometimes a generation is called on to carry a burden whose benefits will be realized only by generations to come. We plant and nurture a tree today, knowing that others may sit beneath its branches and enjoy its fruit.
Every tree is different
Trees also possess remarkable individuality. No two mature trees are identical. Each develops its own shape and carries its own history. Trees are battered by storms, afflicted by disease, scarred by injury, and sometimes recover in ways that permanently alter their appearance. An old tree possesses something resembling a biography, with much of its history written into its trunk and branches.
War reduces individuals to numbers and statistics. Behind every person lies a world of relationships, dreams, achievements, and hopes. Every loss is the loss of an entire world. Every serious injury can radically alter a person’s life and the lives of those around them. Amid the scale and intensity of war, it is easy to lose sight of the individuality of each person and the unique story of every family.
The Torah’s concern for each individual tree reminds us to preserve that same sensitivity toward every individual human life.
Building, not destroying
Finally, trees remind us that humans are meant to be productive in this world. Trees are among nature’s great providers. They give us fruit, shade, shelter, fuel, and, through photosynthesis, the oxygen we breathe. Their presence sustains the environment around them.
War is fundamentally destructive. It destroys lives and what human beings have spent years building. Sometimes we are forced into war, but we should never develop a culture that celebrates war or destruction.
The comparison between people and trees reminds us of our deeper calling. We are meant to produce, build, and improve our world. War may sometimes be necessary, but destruction can never become our purpose. Man is meant to be a tree.
Planting again in Israel
From its earliest days, the Zionist movement viewed planting trees in Israel as an expression of confidence in our future. I remember collecting money as a child in the little blue Keren Kayemeth LeIsrael-Jewish National Fund boxes to help plant forests in Israel.
Trees have repeatedly been destroyed by war, fires, and other causes, but we have always planted again as an expression of Jewish resilience and rebuilding.
The writer is a rabbi and educator at Yeshivat Har Etzion (Gush). Find his latest book, Reclaiming Redemption, Vol. II: Faith, Identity, Peoplehood, and the Storms of War, at mtaraginbooks.com.

Liechtenstein's royal house said Saturday that the tiny country's rules of succession will be changed so that a woman could inherit the principality's throne in the future.
Hereditary Prince Alois announced the change in his speech marking the country's national day. He said it was approved on Wednesday by the necessary two-thirds majority of family members who can vote on such matters.
The prince said, according to a text of his remarks posted on the princely house's website, the vote allowed that "all female descendants of the Princely House will be granted the same participation rights in matters governed by the House Law as male descendants."
"The line of succession will be adjusted from male primogeniture to absolute primogeniture," Alois said. "That means that in the future, the first-born child will, regardless of sex, become the heir to the throne and later the princess or prince of Liechtenstein."
The change shouldn't affect the top of the line of succession in the immediate future.
Prince Hans-Adam II remains the head of state, but in 2004 handed over most of his powers to Alois, his eldest son, who is now 58. That was in line with a tradition of Liechtenstein monarchs giving up the reins to their heirs.
The eldest of Alois' four children is 31-year-old Prince Joseph Wenzel.
Liechtenstein, a wealthy nation of 40,000 people that borders Switzerland and Austria, has an unusually powerful monarchy by European standards. The ruling prince has the power to veto referendum results, appoint judges and fire the government.
The country is traditionally conservative and in 1984 became the last European country to grant women the right to vote in national elections. Male voters narrowly approved the change, which Hans-Adam had backed, in a referendum.
Last year, Brigitte Haas became its first female prime minister.

The next Yemen war might be different
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
14:32:07 UTC
23:32:07 KST

The next Yemen war might be different
Drones are no longer the advantage for only one side.
As the conflict in Yemen rages on and spills over into the Red Sea, developments in recent weeks reveal a new trend worth pondering. The Houthis group, which for years almost monopolised the advantage of drone warfare, has begun facing fire from the same weapon used by its opponents on multiple fronts.
This does not mean that the balance of power has shifted, or that the Houthis have lost their missile and drone superiority. However, the increasing use of this type of warfare by the forces loyal to the internationally recognised government may change the nature of the confrontation, especially if it shifts from scattered operations to an organised and sustained capability.
Recommended Stories
list of 2 items
- list 1 of 2Yemen’s government says Houthi attack on al-Makha kills at least four
- list 2 of 2Houthi attack on port kills four eroding truce with Yemen’s government
For years, the Houthis were able to use drones as one of the most important weapons of asymmetric warfare. They were able to monitor their opponents and strike their gatherings, command centres and facilities far from the lines of contact, while government forces were mostly in a position of defence and interception.
Today, the equation is no longer that simple.
Forces affiliated with the government have announced in recent days the use of drones against Houthi positions in Marib, al-Jawf, Taiz, Hajjah, al-Dhalea and other fronts – and have shown video of a number of those operations.
It is not yet possible to speak of parity in drone power. The Houthis have years of experience and a more advanced missile and drone infrastructure. However, the government does not necessarily need full parity in order to bring about change on the battlefield.
It is enough for Houthi gatherings, vehicles, artillery, reinforcements and command centres to become vulnerable to strikes for them to be forced to change their patterns of deployment, movement and supply. In war, forcing the enemy to change its behaviour is in itself a military achievement.
It would be wrong to say that the Houthis have moved onto the defensive. They are carrying out broad offensive operations: they have struck Marib and Hadramout, repeatedly targeted al-Makha (Mocha), escalated against Saudi Arabia and once again moved their operations to the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb.
But there is a difference between the group being on a strategic defensive and beginning to act on some fronts as though it must prepare for a possible attack.
Here, the geography of the recent strikes becomes more important than their number.
Marib, Taiz, al-Makha and the western coast are not random fronts; they represent key gateways for any potential ground war.
Marib is the gateway to the east and one of the government’s most important military and political centres of gravity. Striking camps and movements there not only causes losses, but can also expose deployments, defences, response speed and sources of reinforcement.
Taiz is the central and coastal junction. Activating its fronts can pin down large forces and prevent their easy redeployment towards the western coast or other fronts.
Al-Makha and the western coast carry a different significance. South of the city lies Bab al-Mandeb and to the north the road extends towards Hodeidah. Therefore, the repeated targeting of al-Makha with missiles and drones can also be seen as a test of a front that could become very important if a ground operation begins along the coast.
When we combine what is happening in Marib, Taiz, al-Makha, al-Dhalea, al-Jawf, Saada and Hodeidah, it becomes difficult to view each front as a separate incident.
This does not mean that the decision for a ground war has been made, but it does mean that the parties have begun to act as though this possibility must be taken seriously.
For this reason, the most important indicator in the coming period will not be the number of missiles or drones, but the movement of forces and reserves, and the transfer of ammunition.
When this movement begins to concentrate on a specific axis, we will have moved from testing the front to preparing the front.
It is precisely in this context that the recent statements of Presidential Leadership Council Chairman Rashad al-Alimi should be understood.
Al-Alimi offered the Houthis the option of laying down their arms and participating in the political life of the country, but he also said that from now on, no Houthi action would go without a response or comprehensive deterrence. He defined the strategic objective as restoring state institutions, stressing that sustainable peace is based on the state’s monopoly over arms and sovereignty.
If these statements hadn’t been accompanied by action, they could have been seen as escalating political rhetoric only.
But what gives Al-Alimi’s latest message its weight is what is happening on the ground: government drones have entered the confrontation openly, artillery is operating on more than one front, military readiness is increasing and the government is speaking more clearly about deterrence.
The real test for the government would be whether these moves turn into a sustained operational doctrine, whereby any Houthi attack incurs a direct cost, or the old pattern is maintained where government forces absorb strikes and issue limited responses.
All of this is happening within a larger regional context. The turmoil in the Strait of Hormuz and the US-Israeli war on Iran are raising the strategic value of the Red Sea. The less secure Hormuz becomes, the more important Saudi energy and trade routes to the west become.
Here, the value of Bab al-Mandeb automatically rises as a power card in the hands of the Houthis.
The geographic equation is highly complex: Iran can exert pressure on Hormuz, the Houthis have the ability to threaten Bab al-Mandeb and Saudi Arabia is strategically positioned between the two corridors.
In return, Riyadh is working on arrangements to protect the Red Sea, while Yemeni government forces are showing greater activity on the ground.
This may lead to a formula different from the previous war: Yemeni forces taking on the bulk of the ground confrontation, while Saudi Arabia and its partners provide support, deterrence and protection for maritime routes.
The danger is that everyone is now approaching the brink of war: the Houthis are testing how much pressure they can exert on Saudi Arabia, the Yemeni government, and international navigation. Meanwhile, government forces are testing new tools and their ability to regain the initiative and Saudi Arabia is trying to build a new deterrence, while the US-Iranian confrontation continues in the background. This widens the margin for strategic error that could lead to an open war.

Reality Check: As the election nears, Haaretz debunks Israeli politicians' biggest lies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
14:32:00 UTC
23:32:00 KST

Politicians have lied since the dawn of time. But it seems like during the outgoing Knesset term, Israeli ministers and lawmakers took it even further, making false claims more confidently and more brazenly than ever before. They did so by promising a "total victory" in the Gaza war and claiming to pursue hostage deals even as those efforts were being undermined behind the scenes; by launching baseless attacks on the judicial system to erode public trust; and by inventing security threats to frighten the public and justify controversial military actions.
Those in power have repeatedly tried to reshape Israelis' perception of reality. Haaretz's Reality Check project aims to set the record straight: to cut through the spin and present the facts as they are.
Click the lie to reveal the truth
Most Israelis reject Oct. 7 state probe
Benjamin Netanyahu
Opinion polls show a majority of Israelis support a state commission of inquiry
Benjamin Netanyahu has done everything he can to prevent an investigation into his own failures and those of his government that led to the October 7 massacre. Throughout the war, the prime minister consistently rejected calls to establish a state commission of inquiry, arguing, among other things, that such an investigation could not take place while the campaign against Hamas was still underway.
That argument did not stop senior IDF officers from accepting responsibility for the failures and resigning, nor did it prevent the military from completing a series of hard-hitting operational probes. Netanyahu, meanwhile, found time to submit a detailed 55-page account of the events to the state comptroller, including what amounted to an indictment of the security establishment and its senior commanders.
Alongside his opposition to an inquiry during wartime, Netanyahu also attacked the idea of a state commission of inquiry in and of itself. In a speech to the Knesset in November 2025, he claimed that "a vast majority" of Israelis did not want such a commission and would not accept its conclusions. Yet opinion polls conducted both during the Gaza war and in its aftermath consistently showed that a clear majority of Israelis supported establishing a state commission of inquiry.
A poll published by Channel 12 News in November 2024, for example, found that 79 percent of the public supported establishing such a committee. A poll published by the Institute for National Security Studies about a year later, in October 2025, found that 74 percent of the public supported establishing a state commission of inquiry, compared with 17 percent who opposed it. A December 2025 poll by the Israel Democracy Institute found that 55 percent of the public supported establishing the committee.
In a March 2025 speech to the Knesset, Netanyahu argued that such a commission would be "a commission whose conclusions are already written in advance" and would come entirely from "one end of the political spectrum."
"It is important and vital to investigate in depth everything that happened to us on October 7 and what preceded it, but this investigation has to gain the confidence of the people, or the confidence of an overwhelming majority of the people," the prime minister said. "For that reason, we demand to form an objective, balanced and independent commission of inquiry. Not a commission of inquiry whose conclusions are already written in advance. Do you think that we don't understand this? We want an unbiased, real commission of inquiry."
In December 2025, Netanyahu turned his attention to Supreme Court President Isaac Amit, who under Israeli law is responsible for appointing the members of a state commission of inquiry. He suggested that Amit would assemble a politically motivated panel whose conclusions would lack legitimacy. Netanyahu's allies also floated a proposal that would give politicians control over the appointment of the commission's panel, while expanding the scope of the inquiry to include events dating back to the Oslo Accords.
At the same time, a series of alternative proposals sought to undermine the existing model for a state commission of inquiry. Public figures on the right proposed a commission whose members would be evenly divided between coalition and opposition appointees. President Isaac Herzog suggested that Supreme Court President Amit determine the panel's composition in consultation with his deputy, the conservative Justice Noam Sohlberg. Other proposals were floated calling for a "special state commission of inquiry" whose members would be appointed by Netanyahu and his ministers, the very officials it would be tasked with investigating.
The bottom line is clear: Nearly three years after the greatest disaster in Israel's history, Netanyahu has blocked the only mechanism capable of investigating what went wrong and who was responsible.
Jonathan Lis
Netanyahu ordered Gaza border sealed when Oct. 7 attack began
Benjamin Netanyahu
According to sources and the transcript of his first red phone call, no such order was given
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu claimed in July that, as soon as Hamas launched its October 7 attack, he made sure the Gaza border was sealed to prevent kidnappings. But, according to sources familiar with the events and a published transcript, he issued no such instruction during the first conversations he held that morning.
The sources said the order was not given during his initial WhatsApp call. Nor did he issue it during his first conversation on the secure 
"red" line about 10 minutes later, a call whose transcript was later made public.
Speaking on comedian Ben Ben Baruch's podcast earlier this month, Netanyahu said: "In that [first] conversation or the one immediately after, I had only one question: did we close the border with Gaza? I was very concerned they would take hostages."
He repeated the same account in a later interview on another podcast.
"The first thing I [asked army officials and] wanted to know was, 'Did you close the border with Gaza so they wouldn't go back in with hostages?'" he said.
According to the sources, Netanyahu received his first briefing via WhatsApp at 6:29 A.M. His military secretary at the time, Maj. Gen. Avi Gil, informed him that Hamas had launched a surprise attack and that rocket sirens were sounding across Israel, but provided no additional details. Gil said he was still gathering information and would brief Netanyahu again over the secure line. The call lasted less than a minute and, because it took place over WhatsApp, no transcript exists.
The second conversation, over the secure "Red Phone," took place at 6:40 A.M. The transcript contains no instruction to seal the border. Sources familiar with the matter added that, at that stage, Netanyahu was still unaware of the scale of the attack and had been caught by surprise, which is why he did not issue such an order.
The conversation opens with Netanyahu trying to assess the scope of the attack.
"What happened? Why did they open fire?" he asks at the outset. Then he asks, "What are they shooting?" and "Is the shooting across the entire country?"
Gil replies that it is a "wide-ranging operation, if not a war in Gaza," updates that there is concern about Hamas members infiltrating Israel and concludes: "We are at war."
Later in the conversation, Netanyahu mentions the lack of early intelligence warning. "We have no indication [of a possible attack], I see nothing in the intelligence," he tells Gil, who replies: "We'll need to check later how they surprised us."
Netanyahu then moves on to operational steps. He asks to consider an immediate strike on Hamas leadership, to assess "the scope of the attack," to examine if extensive reserve mobilization is required and to prepare for an IDF General Staff meeting within two or three hours.
It is only at this stage that Netanyahu first raises the possibility that the attack was intended for abductions. "Could this be intended for abductions?" he asks, and Gil replies, "That's what we're thinking."
Even after this exchange, there is no record of a directive to close the border. Instead, Netanyahu orders, "We need to see if we can take down [Hamas'] leadership immediately, [to check] if something is available."
At the end of the call, Gil says that he will hold a round of talks with the heads of the defense agencies and will return to update the prime minister.
Josh Breiner
Top court chief appointed himself to role
Nir Barkat and Avihai Boaron
Isaac Amit was lawfully appointed by the Judicial Selection Committee
On January 27, 2025, the day after Justice Isaac Amit was elected president of the Supreme Court, Economy Minister Nir Barkat appeared on Channel 14 and declared: "Something extraordinary happened yesterday: the judge appointed himself." Likud MK Avihai Boaron made the same claim in an interview with the channel that day, saying, "A Supreme Court justice, deputy to the president, came with his friends, and in practice appointed himself."
In reality, like all his predecessors, Amit was appointed by the Judicial Selection Committee. His appointment complied with Israeli law and followed the seniority system in place since the state's founding, under which the longest-serving Supreme Court justice becomes the court's president.
Since then, the claim has been echoed by a growing list of coalition politicians, following a longstanding delegitimisation campaign conducted by Justice Minister Yariv Levin, architect of the judicial coup, against Amit's appointment, as he is considered an activist judge.
Amit was appointed 15 months after former Supreme Court President Esther Hayut retired. During that time, the court operated without a permanent president for the first time, after Levin, as chair of the Judicial Selection Committee, refused to hold a vote on the appointment.
At the same time, while boycotting Amit's appointment, Levin advanced legislation – set to take effect after the next election – that would overhaul Israel's judicial appointments system, and place the panel under the control of politicians, in what is widely regarded as a blow to democratic due process.
Only after the High Court of Justice ordered the committee to convene did it do so, with Levin boycotting the meeting. In the ruling ordering Levin to convene the committee to appoint a Supreme Court president, Justice Yael Wilner wrote that it was unacceptable for the appointment of the head of the judiciary, "one of the symbols of the State of Israel," to be delayed for more than a year "simply because the minister opposes the [president] selection procedure ratified by the legislature."
Afterward, the justice minister said he did not recognize Amit's appointment as Supreme Court president. "The appointment of the Supreme Court president through the unlawful usurpation of my authority as chair of the committee is fundamentally flawed and illegal," Levin wrote after the vote.
In June, Levin said that "the High Court justices themselves convened the Judicial Selection Committee through an unlawful order and 'appointed' Amit themselves." At the Knesset's opening ceremony in October last year, Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana referred to Amit only as a "Supreme Court justice," rather than as court president, prompting controversy.
Under Israel's Courts Law, the president formally appoints the Supreme Court president following the Judicial Selection Committee's selection. The committee chooses the president under the seniority system that has been in place since the state's founding, under which the longest-serving Supreme Court justice is appointed court president.
In the committee vote held in January 2025, Amit defeated Supreme Court Justice Yosef Elron. He received the support of five members of the Judicial Selection Committee: Supreme Court Justices Daphne Barak-Erez and Noam Sohlberg, Israel Bar Association representatives Muhamad Naamneh and Yonit Kalmanovich and opposition MK Karine Elharrar.
The coalition's representatives – Justice Minister Yariv Levin, Settlements Minister Orit Strock and Otzma Yehudit MK Yitzhak Kroizer – boycotted the vote. But because the appointment required only a simple majority, their absence did not prevent it from going ahead.

Hungary uses sunken barges to raise Danube River to keep nuclear plant going
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
14:30:45 UTC
23:30:45 KST

Hungary is sinking two barges to ensure a key nuclear power plant stays online, Prime Minister Péter Magyar said Saturday.
Europe’s summer of extreme heat has caused the Danube’s water level to hit record lows, affecting power production at the Paks nuclear plant. Nuclear power stations are typically built by rivers and along coastlines so they can use water to cool down reactors.
Hungarian authorities are sinking the two barges to raise water levels so Paks, which provides the country with more than a third of its electricity, can continue to operate normally. The sinking began Saturday morning and Hungarian media are quoting the prime minister saying the water level at the plant has risen by 1 centimeter.
Advertisement
Magyar said on X that the current water level near Hungary's only nuclear energy facility is 122 cm lower than normal and it is projected to drop below 132 cm on Monday, which would force one of the plant’s two turbines to shut down.
On Wednesday, Magyar announced that they would be building a riverbed sill with 150,000 cubic meters of stone and was considering sinking the two 80-meter barges. A sill is an underwater dam meant to slow down the current and raise water levels. Hungary’s Defense Ministry has assigned 100 troops to work around the clock on the project, the prime minister said on X.
Nuclear energy facilities across Europe have been affected by this summer’s droughts and soaring temperatures. Romania shut down a nuclear power plant earlier this week due to the Danube’s water levels.
France — one of Europe’s biggest producers of nuclear power — has seen its fleet of nuclear power plants affected throughout the summer. Le Monde reported authorities had to shut down six of the country’s 57 nuclear reactors as yet another heat wave broiled much of the country. Earlier in the week, a climate change-fueled jellyfish invasion forced workers to bring parts of a different plant offline.
Magyar has also cast doubt on completing an expansion of the Paks plant by a Russian state-owned firm in a deal signed by Magyar’s predecessor, the Kremlin-friendly Viktor Orbàn, citing the water issue.

Young Ukrainian Engineer Brings His 217 MPH Shahed Killer to the US Air Force
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
14:24:51 UTC
23:24:51 KST

- Category

Young Ukrainian Engineer Brings His 217 MPH Shahed Killer to the US Air Force
A young Ukrainian engineer who left his country after Russia’s full-scale invasion has brought a 217 mph (350 km/h) interceptor designed to hunt Shahed-type attack drones to one of the US Air Force’s main flight-testing centers.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defence Blog on August 15, Yehor Balytskyi’s California-based startup Thermopylae Aerospace completed an end-to-end demonstration of its SPART interceptor at Edwards Air Force Base during the “Game of Drones 26-2” event in July.
The demonstration put SPART in front of senior Air Force Test Center leadership, including Brig. Gen. Mark Massaro, commander of the Air Force Test Center, and Chief Master Sgt. Sevin Balkuvvar.
“At 412th Test Wing, Edwards Air Force Base, during Game of Drones 26-2, our lean team completed a successful end-to-end demonstration of SPART, a novel interceptor platform designed to counter big drones asymmetrically,” Balytskyi said, according to Defence Blog.
A 217 MPH interceptor built to hunt Shahed-type drones
SPART is a pneumatically launched, foldable quadcopter developed specifically to intercept larger unmanned aircraft, including Group 2-class threats such as Shahed-type attack drones.
The interceptor uses thermal guidance and can reach speeds of up to 217 mph (350 km/h), with a target flight endurance of up to 20 minutes, according to specifications cited by Defence Blog.
Unlike single-use interceptors, SPART is designed with a partial-reuse capability. If it misses its target, the drone can potentially be recovered and used again.
Thermopylae also designed SPART to operate from a range of host platforms. The interceptor can be integrated with other UAVs, ground vehicles, maritime vessels, and crewed vehicles, allowing it to be deployed as part of different counter-drone configurations.
Balytskyi previously told Janes that Western counter-drone systems often rely on rocket motors and costly components, making them expensive to use against relatively cheap attack drones. Interceptor drones deployed in Ukraine, meanwhile, frequently depend on the skill of individual pilots.
Thermopylae is developing SPART as a lower-cost alternative that could be manufactured and deployed in large numbers. “We built it from the ground up in a very short period of time,” Balytskyi said. “Proud of the team for getting us here.”
From Ukraine to a US Air Force test base
Balytskyi left Ukraine at 17 following Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. He later founded Thermopylae Aerospace in California in June 2025, according to Defence Blog.
Five months later, the startup raised $1.6 million in pre-seed funding from investors including Naval Ravikant and Ukraine-focused venture firm UA1. The company has since expanded from a two-person operation to a team of approximately five.
SPART’s July demonstration took place as part of “Game of Drones,” a recurring testing program organized by the 412th Test Wing’s Experimental Test Force at Edwards Air Force Base in partnership with the Defense Contract Management Agency.
The program brings defense companies and US military engineers together for live testing of small unmanned aircraft and counter-drone technologies. The first “Game of Drones” was held at Edwards’ Rogers Dry Lake in December 2025.
The tests are part of broader Pentagon efforts to accelerate the evaluation, acquisition, and production of unmanned systems. Results can also contribute to consideration for the US military’s sUAS Blue List, which provides a mechanism for vetting small drone systems for military use.
Earlier, Ukrainian drone maker F-Drones delivered 2,000 F10 FPV drones to the US military under the Pentagon’s Drone Dominance Program, becoming the first Ukrainian drone manufacturer authorized to export systems to the United States under the initiative. The program aims to procure more than 200,000 drones for US forces by 2027.

Russia Sends 16 Troops Through a 28-Kilometer Pipe—Only Four Survive
Unknown

23:24:26 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Sends 16 Troops Through a 28-Kilometer Pipe—Only Four Survive
A 16-man Russian assault group spent three days traveling nearly 28 kilometers through an underground pipe toward Ukrainian positions, but only four survived the mission and were later captured by Ukrainian paratroopers.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukraine’s 71st Separate Airmobile Brigade said on August 15 that the Russian troops used an underground utility line to approach Ukrainian positions. According to testimony from one of the captured soldiers released by the brigade, some members of Russian assault units are recruited from prisons, signing military contracts to avoid lengthy sentences.
The group traveled approximately 27–28 kilometers inside a reinforced-concrete pipe around 1.5 meters in diameter. The soldiers spent three days underground and slept inside the pipe during the journey.
One of the prisoners said Russian commanders had told the troops they were being sent to reinforce a battalion and assured them that Ukrainian forces were not present in the forest near their destination.
After emerging from the pipe, the 16-man group came under Ukrainian fire. According to the 71st Brigade, only around eight soldiers managed to reach the forest. Four ultimately survived.
The surviving Russian troops were also left with limited food supplies and had to search for food themselves. According to the prisoner, Russian commanders did not immediately evacuate wounded soldiers and instead continued ordering the assault troops forward despite Ukrainian drone strikes.
The remaining soldiers eventually encountered troops from Ukraine’s 71st Separate Airmobile Brigade and surrendered.
Following his capture, one of the Russian soldiers received medical assistance and urged other Russians not to sign military contracts to fight against Ukraine.
“I would not advise anyone to go to war. No amount of money is worth it, nor are any of the benefits they promise us… To die and go to someone else’s land—for what? For whom? Let them put me in prison. If they hadn’t let me come here, I would never come here again,” the prisoner said in footage released by the brigade.
The 71st Brigade said the footage was recorded with the prisoner’s consent and that its treatment and communication with prisoners of war were conducted in accordance with the Geneva Conventions.
In a separate operation reported on August 15, Ukrainian Special Operations Forces captured three Russian soldiers and killed another during a raid on Russian positions. Operators from the 6th Separate Special Operations Regiment also evacuated a fawn discovered in the combat zone, prompting the unit to dub the mission “Operation Bambi.”

The water level in the Rhine has fallen to a historic low

The water level in the Rhine has fallen to a historic low
Kyiv • UNN
In Germany, the water level in the Rhine near Kaub fell to 6 cm, breaking the 2018 record. This disrupted river freight transport, causing supply disruptions and rising costs.
The water level in the Rhine River in Germany fell to a new record low, significantly disrupting river freight shipping. Deutsche Welle reports, as cited by UNN.
Details
The water level in the Rhine River fell to a new record low, significantly disrupting river freight shipping, as a prolonged drought continues across much of Germany
It is reported that the water-level reading at the Kaub bottleneck near Koblenz fell to 6 centimeters (2.4 inches) on Friday evening, and stood at 8 cm early Saturday.
Before this year, the previous lowest level recorded by this gauge was 25 cm, recorded in 2018.
The gauge shows the depth relative to an assumed baseline near the riverbank, but it is an indicator of the navigable depth at this point, which is approximately one meter deeper.
Most of the cargo previously transported along the Rhine has been shifted to road and rail transport, but these modes cannot fully compensate for the large freight volumes carried by vessels.
For this reason, companies have begun reporting supply disruptions, while chemical manufacturers, utilities and steel companies are warning of rising costs, transport bottlenecks and production cuts.

America In Focus: Inflation cools in July, but so do consumers with their spending
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
14:23:01 UTC
23:23:01 KST

America In Focus: Inflation cools in July, but so do consumers with their spending
The economy, inflation and how those forces could impact the lives of Americans were front and center over the past week. Trips to the grocery store and gas station are more painful than they were last year, and rising costs are impacting the decisions of both households and businesses.
Here’s a snapshot of prominent economic data and news that occurred over the past week and what it potentially means for you.
Inflation cooled last month, but costs remain high
U.S. inflation slowed last month and a measure of underlying price pressures also cooled, suggesting higher oil and gas prices from the Iran war are only having a limited impact on broader costs in the economy.
Consumer prices rose 3.4% in July from a year ago, down slightly from 3.5% in June, the Labor Department said Wednesday. But inflation is still higher than before the Iran war began in February, when it was 2.4%. On a monthly basis, prices rose just 0.1% from June to July.
Wednesday’s report comes as the Federal Reserve is sharply divided over whether it should hike its key interest rate to combat inflation. The Fed kept its rate unchanged, at about 3.6%, at a meeting late last month. But the vote was 9-3, with three dissenters favoring a rate hike.
Significant drop in retail spending catches everyone off guard
Americans unexpectedly cut their spending in July as a boost from government tax refunds faded.
Retail sales slipped 0.6% last month, the biggest drop since May 2025, from a revised gain of 0.2% in June, according to Commerce Department data released Friday.
There was a notable bump in spending in both April and May as Americans dipped into their tax refunds. That affect may have faded last month.
Excluding sales at gas stations and at auto dealers, retail sales in July fell 0.2%. Gas prices bounced back in recent weeks in what appears to be a stalemate in the Strait of Hormuz.
US existing home sales fall in July
Sales of previously occupied U.S. homes slowed again in July as record prices and the highest mortgage rates in a year prove to be an insurmountable hurdle for many prospective buyers.
Existing home sales fell 1.7% last month from June to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 4.06 million units, the National Association of Realtors said Tuesday. That’s slightly above the 4.05 million pace economists were expecting, according to FactSet, and up 0.7% compared with last year.
Home prices continued to rise, hitting unprecedented levels for the month of July, NAR said. The U.S. median sales price increased 2% from a year earlier, to $434,100.
Wholesale price inflation slows
Wholesale inflation dropped last month as gas prices reversed some of their Iran war spike and other costs also cooled, a sign that consumer inflation could grind lower in the months ahead.
The Labor Department’s producer price index — which captures inflation before it reaches consumers — rose 4.7% in July from a year ago, down from a much larger 5.5% increase in June. On a monthly basis, wholesale prices were unchanged from June to July, after they ticked down 0.1% the previous month.
The figures follows the government’s consumer price inflation report, released Wednesday, which also showed a modest cooling last month. Still, consumer prices have risen faster than wages for the past four months, underscoring the challenges many Americans have affording necessities such as rent and utilities. If prices continue to outpace wages, many consumers may be forced to dial back their spending in the coming months.
US unemployment claims rise but remain at healthy level
U.S. applications for unemployment benefits rose last week, but layoffs remain at historically healthy levels.
The Labor Department reported Thursday that 209,000 people filed jobless claims last week, up from a revised 200,000 the week before and higher than the 205,000 forecasters had expected. The four-week average of applications, which smooths out week-to-week-volatitlity, was unchanged at 199,000.
The overall number of people collecting employment benefits the week that ended Aug. 1 dropped by 22,000 to 1.78 million.
Claims for jobless benefits are a proxy for layoffs, and they’ve been at a historically low range of around 200,000 to 230,000 a week for the past year, suggesting that Americans who have jobs enjoy unusual job security. The U.S. unemployment rate is low at 4.1%, as the economy has proved resilient despite a spike in energy prices caused by the fighting with Iran.
Mortgage rates dip slightly, but still up from last year
The average long-term U.S. mortgage rate fell slightly for the first time in six weeks on Thursday, marking a glimpse of relief for prospective homebuyers — although borrowing costs remain steeper than they were a year ago.
The benchmark 30-year fixed rate mortgage rate tumbled to 6.67%, mortgage buyer Freddie Mac said Thursday, down from 6.69% reported last week. Still, by comparison, the average rate was 6.58% at this time in 2025.
Higher mortgage rates can add hundreds of dollars a month in costs for borrowers, limiting homebuyers’ purchasing power. And that can led prospective home shoppers to delay buying, as seen while rates rose over prior weeks. U.S. sales of previously-occupied homes again slowed in July.
Borrowing costs on 15-year fixed-rate mortgages — which are often sought by borrowers looking to refinance a home loan — also fell slightly this week. That rate averaged at 5.96%, down from 6.01% last week. But that’s still higher than a year ago, when Freddie Mac said 15-year fixed-rate mortgages averaged at 5.71%.
Wall Street holds near its record
U.S. stocks traded near record highs despite weak economic data about how much shoppers are spending at retailers. A pullback in spending could keep the Federal Reserve from raising interest rates, which is something Wall Street loves, but it comes with the risk of slow growth and stubborn inflation.
The S&P 500 was virtually unchanged, coming off its all-time high set the day before. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and the Nasdaq composite were both slightly lower.
Treasury yields were mixed in the bond market after a report showed shoppers spent less at U.S. retailers last month than the month before. That surprised economists, who were forecasting another month of growth.

China-Europe Arctic shipping route enters regular weekly operation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
22:22:50 CST
23:22:50 KST

HANGZHOU, Aug. 15 (Xinhua) -- The China-Europe Arctic container express route entered regular weekly operations for the summer season on Saturday, opening a faster and more resilient logistics link between China and Europe.
At around 7 p.m., the container ship Dubai Tower departed from the Ningbo-Zhoushan Port in east China's Zhejiang Province, marking the start of the route's regular seasonal service.
The route crosses the Northeast Arctic Passage before reaching major European ports including Felixstowe in Britain, Rotterdam in the Netherlands, Hamburg in Germany and Gdynia in Poland, according to the operator.
The route completed its first trial voyage in September 2025, reaching Felixstowe Port in about 20 days, nearly halving the time required via the Suez Canal and outpacing the China-Europe freight train.
"The route stands out for its advantages in transit time and supply chain security," said Xin Jianning, general manager of Zhejiang Seaport Logistics Group Co., Ltd.
The Dubai Tower carries high-value-added, temperature-sensitive goods, including energy storage cabinets, power batteries, photovoltaic modules and new-energy vehicle components, mainly from cities in the Yangtze River Delta.
Due to seasonal ice conditions, the route operates mainly from July to October, with at least eight voyages planned this year.
China-EU trade in goods reached 447.8 billion U.S. dollars in the first half of 2026, up 14.2 percent year on year, according to the Ministry of Commerce. ■

SYDNEY, Aug. 15 (Xinhua) -- Australia's New South Wales (NSW) will launch a gun buyback scheme as part of tighter firearm controls introduced after last year's deadly Bondi Beach attack, local media reported Saturday.
The scheme, set to begin on Nov. 2, will make NSW the first Australian state to implement the buyback program announced following the attack, according to the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC).
Up to 274,000 firearms and about 50,000 license holders are estimated to be affected by the state's new firearm restrictions, the ABC reported.
Under the scheme, most surrendered firearms will receive fixed compensation of 450 to 1,000 Australian dollars (about 319 to 708 U.S. dollars), while higher-value firearms may qualify for up to 10,000 Australian dollars (about 7,080 U.S. dollars) each from early next year.
NSW Premier Chris Minns said reducing the number of dangerous firearms in the community would make the state safer.
NSW tightened its firearm laws following the Bondi Beach attack, introducing limits on the number of firearms most licence holders can possess and tighter controls on certain types of firearms.
The federal government has also proposed a national gun buyback scheme, though most other jurisdictions have opposed or not committed to the program. ■

Fresh evidence of Nanjing Massacre donated to Chinese memorial hall
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
22:22:14 CST
23:22:14 KST

NANJING, Aug. 15 (Xinhua) -- A memorial hall in east China's Jiangsu Province said the historical materials it received this year have provided new evidence of war crimes committed by invading Japanese troops during the 1937 Nanjing Massacre.
The Memorial Hall of the Victims of the Nanjing Massacre by Japanese Invaders, located in Jiangsu's capital Nanjing, collected more than 150 sets of artifacts and historical materials, as well as over 100 pieces of archival documents, in the first half of 2026, the memorial hall said on Saturday, which marks the 81st anniversary of Japan's surrender in World War II (WWII).
The newly acquired items, many donated by young students, include private correspondence from Japanese soldiers, battlefield postcards, instructional materials on gas warfare, and compilations of wartime press coverage.
Among them is a collection of private letters written between 1937 and 1939 by a soldier of the Imperial Japanese Army's 16th Division, surnamed Ishikawa. In a letter dated Dec. 20, 1937, one week after the fall of Nanjing, Ishikawa wrote, "A few days ago, we killed over ten thousand defeated soldiers." This letter serves as a firsthand account from the perpetrator himself, recorded at the time of the massacre, and corroborates the diary entries of Azuma Shiro, a fellow soldier in the same division.
Also donated are two instructional manuals on the systematic training of poison gas warfare by the invading Japanese forces.
In addition, Marcus Detrez and Bastien Ratat from France and Zhong Haosong from China made a joint donation of archival materials to the memorial hall. The donated items comprise 861 pages of documents from the French Ministry of Foreign Affairs relating to Japan's aggression in China, as well as over 50 Japanese-language publications, including wartime illustrated magazines and frontline war records.
"These artifacts, historical materials and archival documents reveal the atrocities committed by Japanese forces, including the Nanjing Massacre and other war crimes, from various perspectives. Coming from different sources, they corroborate one another and form an irrefutable chain of evidence," said Meng Guoxiang, a researcher at the Institute for National Memory and International Peace Studies.
The day also saw a ceremony for the fifth cohort of inheritors of the historical memory of the Nanjing Massacre, with new members including Carly Brady, a dual U.S.-Canadian citizen, and Christoph Reinhardt from Germany, among others.
"Since 2022, the memorial hall has issued certificates to five cohorts totaling 44 individuals," said Zhou Feng, curator of the memorial hall. "As this group continues to grow, the historical memory of the Nanjing Massacre will be passed on to an ever-wider audience." ■
