Five years into Taliban rule, Afghanistan plunges into a state of collapse – visualised
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
06:00:49 UTC
15:00:49 KST

‘I married off my daughter so that none of us would die of hunger.” Malika hesitated before saying the words aloud. The 46-year-old lives with her husband and four youngest children (three girls and a boy) in Chihil Dukhtarān, one of Kabul’s poorest neighbourhoods.
Poverty pushed the family to the brink before Malika and her husband made what they describe as the hardest decision of their lives: marrying off their eldest daughter, Maryam, for 200,000 afghanis (£2,270). She was still a teenager.
“God is my witness that during that winter, our food was almost nothing but dry bread and boiled water. Even that was often unavailable, and many nights we went to bed hungry,” she says.
“My poor daughter cried in secret … [but knew] if she refused this marriage, all of us would die from hunger, cold and misery.”
Almost two years on from Maryam’s marriage, crisis again looms for the family. Malika can no longer afford to send her two youngest daughters (aged 12 and nine) to school, so they work alongside their 16-year-old sister in a clothing factory for meagre wages. Her husband’s job is pushing a handcart, but he often returns home empty-handed – one of millions of Afghans out of work in a crippled economy. The dowry money has almost run out. Like many Afghan families, they have one resource left to tap: their girls.
Five years after the Taliban swept back into Kabul, Afghanistan has entered a quieter phase of emergency.
The fighting that once dominated international headlines has largely faded from view, but for millions of Afghans the crisis has only deepened. Nearly half the population requires humanitarian aid and more than 14 million people are expected to face acute food insecurity this year, while rights have been mercilessly restricted, women systematically erased from public life and millions of deportees forced back to an economy unable to absorb them.
An economy collapsing
The economy remains far smaller and more isolated than it was before the Taliban returned to power. Foreign trade has plummeted, and imports have increasingly outpaced exports since 2021, widening the country’s trade deficit.. Government finances have also contracted significantly. The Taliban’s most recent published budget, for the 2023 fiscal year, totalled $2.44bn, less than half the roughly $6bn budget under the previous government in 2021. In 2024, the authorities also abolished Afghanistan’s public pension system as they sought to cope with the country’s fiscal crisis.
Economic output is expanding, yet it is struggling to keep pace with rapid population growth driven by the return of millions of Afghans owing to deportation drives in Pakistan and Iran.
Inflation has added to those pressures. After averaging 3.6% in 2025, it rose to 7.6% by March 2026, driven by increasing food prices, supply disruptions and rising demand, further eroding household purchasing power.
Unemployment has almost doubled since 2021, according to the UN. More than half a million jobs have disappeared and cuts to international aid have hollowed out public spending, while rising food prices have once again squeezed household budgets.
“Five years after the Taliban takeover, Afghanistan is experiencing the world’s worst women’s rights crisis, one of the worst human rights crises and one of the worst humanitarian crises,” said Fereshta Abbasi, Afghanistan researcher at Human Rights Watch.
Years of economic hardship, successive droughts and collapsing international aid have left millions unable to afford basic goods. The numbers are staggering. An estimated 21.9 million people – about 45% of the population – will require humanitarian assistance in 2026. About 11.6 million are children, with 3.5 million under-fives already suffering from acute malnutrition.
But that aid is not arriving. The US, once the country’s largest donor, provided more than $3bn in humanitarian and development assistance between October 2021 and December 2024. But in January 2025, President Donald Trump suspended US humanitarian funding for Afghanistan as part of a pause on all foreign aid programmes, removing a source that had accounted for about 45% of humanitarian support.
The consequences have been immediate. More than 440 health clinics have been forced to close or reduce services because of funding shortages, increasing the proportion of Afghans without access to healthcare from 16% in 2024 to 23% in 2025. Earlier this year, the World Food Programme said it now turned away three out of four acutely malnourished children seeking help because it no longer had the funds to buy food for them.
The annihilation of women’s rights
The humanitarian crisis has unfolded alongside a sweeping assault on women’s rights.
Since seizing power in 2021, the Taliban have barred girls from secondary schools, banned women from universities, excluded them from much of the workforce and public life. In 2022, women were barred from public parks and gyms; in 2024, the Taliban prohibited women from speaking audibly in public, and this year a brutal new marriage law has perpetuated domestic violence and child abuse by effectively recognising child marriage and making it much harder for women to seek divorce.
Zarifa Ghafari, formerly mayor of Maidan Shahr, and one of Afghanistan’s few female mayors, who fled the country in August 2021, says Afghan women and girls have experienced one of the “fastest and most systematic reversals of women’s rights in modern history”.
The consequences are visible across almost every measure of equality. Women’s labour force participation has fallen from about one in six women before the Taliban takeover to roughly one in 20 today. Only 18% of midwives are formally employed, while nearly 80% of female journalists have been forced from their jobs. The UN estimates that excluding women and girls from education and work is already costing Afghanistan at least $84m a year. Afghanistan no longer keeps any records of its child marriage rates, and has also prevents NGOs from gathering data.
But as girls are forced from school and parents struggle to feed their children, rights organisations believe more and more are being pushed into child marriage – with the economic and gender rights crises compounding one another.
Last year, Nilofar, a 13-year-old girl from Bamiyan, completed the sixth grade (year 7) – the final year girls are allowed to attend school. Her small frame makes her look even younger than her age. Her parents have engaged her to be married to an older relative she has never met.
“My parents tell me that now your education is over, it’s time to get married. Keeping a grown daughter at home is a heavy burden,” she says.
Afghanistan now ranks at the bottom of the Georgetown Institute’s Women, Peace and Security Index for measures of women’s inclusion, justice and security. The UN and human rights organisations have described the systematic dismantling of women’s rights as gender apartheid.
“Millions of girls have grown up knowing only exclusion instead of opportunity,” Ghafari says. “The Taliban are not only harming individual lives; they are depriving Afghanistan of doctors, teachers, engineers, entrepreneurs and future leaders. The damage will be felt for generations.” The rise of child marriage exposes girls to high rates of violence and abuse, as well as the prospect of pregnancy and childbirth at a very young age.
At the end of a crowded hospital corridor in Kabul, Shamim, 17, cradles a child in her arms as she waits to see a doctor. She looks more like a schoolgirl than a mother bringing her child to a hospital for treatment.
When approached and asked about the baby in her arms, she replies quietly, without looking up: “He’s my son.” She was forced, along with all other Afghan girls, to leave the school system in sixth grade (about 12 years old). By age 15, she was married, and less than a year later she was pregnant with her first child. Her marriage brought her family 200,000 afghanis, she says. A small portion went to buying household items, and “they used the remaining amount to pay off their debts”.
Geopolitical tensions rise
The country’s internal crises have been compounded by the forced return of millions of Afghans, mostly from neighbouring Iran and Pakistan.
Since 2023, almost 6 million people have returned after intensified crackdowns on undocumented migrants. The UN expects another 2.7 million returns between May and December this year, placing further strain on housing, jobs, healthcare and schools.
“No country can absorb that much population increase, especially a country like Afghanistan where half of the country is already in need of assistance,” says Mihyung Park, chief of mission in Afghanistan for International Organization for Migration.
Relations with Pakistan have also deteriorated sharply. Islamabad accuses the Taliban of harbouring militants from the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan group – allegations the Taliban denies. The dispute has spilled into armed clashes along the border, with exchanges of fire and airstrikes killing civilians and forcing families to flee on both sides. Repeated border closures have also disrupted trade and livelihoods in communities that depend on cross-border movement.
Yet even as rights have continued to deteriorate, the Taliban has steadily expanded its international reach.
Russia has formally recognised the government and signed a military cooperation agreement, while China and the United Arab Emirates have accepted Taliban-appointed ambassadors. Taliban officials have also met European Union representatives in Brussels to discuss migration, prompting criticism from human rights groups.
“Recognising the Taliban without meaningful progress on human rights risks legitimising a system built on gender apartheid,” says Ghafari.
As governments reopen diplomatic channels, many Afghans fear the world is learning to live with a regime that they cannot escape.
“Stability cannot be achieved by sacrificing half the population,” Ghafari says. “To Afghan women, it sends the message that geopolitical interests are outweighing their fundamental rights and freedoms.”

The 20-year search for a vanishing custard-and-chocolate coloured moth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
06:00:48 UTC
15:00:48 KST

Dave Wainwright first surveyed Wallington in Northumberland for a rare custard-and-chocolate coloured moth in 2004. He parked two miles from the site, hauled a moth trap across, and was bitten by a million flies.
He did not find a single dark bordered beauty that night. The ground was heavily grazed by sheep, and the creeping willow the caterpillars depend on was “quite well plucked”.
But he was determined not to give up.
Twenty years later, walking the same Northumberland estate with project officer Charlotte Rankin and National Trust rangers, Wainwright finally found what he had been looking for since he started the job: a population of dark bordered beauty moths, the first recorded at the site since 1952.
“It was a pretty amazing feeling,” he says. “That particular site had been recorded before, but 74 years ago. I surveyed the site about 20 years ago and couldn’t find it … actually finding it after that much effort was really fulfilling.”
The dark bordered beauty is a moth with lemon-yellow wings and a deep chestnut border, sometimes described as custard-and-chocolate coloured. It is also one of the rarest moths in England.
Until this summer, Strensall Common in Yorkshire was the only known site where it survived in the country, and even that population has been collapsing. Hundreds of moths were recorded 20 years ago. The numbers record last barely reached double figures, hit by climate breakdown and a wildfire that tore through much of the reserve.
Wainwright, who is head of conservation in England at Butterfly Conservation, has spent years chasing that narrow margin across some of the country’s landscapes.
“I’ve been to a lot of remote places, particularly in Northumberland, Yorkshire and Cumbria,” he says. “I always felt the dark bordered beauty would be there. I had a sneaking suspicion, but whether or not I’d actually find it, I didn’t know.”
Looking back at that fruitless night in 2004, he now thinks the moth may have been there all along, hidden in plain sight in willow scrub too battered by grazing to support it. “It must have been there,” Wainwright says, “which makes it all the more rewarding.”
The site looks very different now to how it did back then. Where the willow was once cropped bare, there is now lush vegetation and wildflowers. This is the result of years of work between the National Trust and Fiona Goodfellow, a tenant farmer who manages the land as part of a nature recovery project spanning the estate’s 20 sq miles (5,200 hectares).
The discovery came out of a £300,000 grant awarded to Butterfly Conservation last year by the Elgol Fund for Nature to study how rare species across the north of England were coping with climate and human pressures.
For Wainwright, what makes the find matter is not just the science. It is what it means for a species he had feared was running out of time.
“Because I thought we were going to lose [dark bordered beauties] as a species,” he says, when asked why he calls this a highlight of his career.
“You don’t want a species to go extinct on your watch … you feel really powerless. It’s gratifying just knowing that the species isn’t as far down the road to extinction as we feared.”
One of the main challenges in conserving the species is that its caterpillar only eats two plants: aspen and creeping willow.
However, Wainwright still remains wary of moving too fast. The moth has survived at Wallington for more than 70 years without anyone intervening on its behalf, and he would rather understand exactly why the habitat works before anyone starts changing it.
“We wouldn’t want to rush into major changes,” he says. “You could do more harm than good by modifying it without knowing what you’re doing.”
Wainwright explains that as of right now, the work is mostly watching.
Butterfly Conservation is also in the early stages of a captive breeding programme, already planned in partnership with Yorkshire Wildlife Trust at Strensall Common. There is a longer-term hope of introducing the moth to new sites once the right conditions can be created.
Wainwright has spent his career doing the work of finding out what is actually out there and “putting dots on maps”, often in places barely anyone visits. He argues that this is important so that conservation money goes where it is needed most.
It is slow, forensic work, chasing eggs and caterpillars to work out what a moth needs to survive. But every so often, it pays off.

‘Watch your spending, use free perks’: an insider’s tips on student money
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
06:00:48 UTC
15:00:48 KST

Over the past two years university student Erin has been giving Martin Lewis a run for his money when it comes to hunting down the best hacks, tips and tricks to save cash and earn money.
The 21-year-old has seen Oasis for free; earned tickets to race days; made money from selling secondhand clothes (£200 in one weekend alone); and enjoyed cut-price treats with friends.
On Thursday, tens of thousands of young people found out if they had achieved the grades for the course of their choice. Now, as they celebrate, or hurriedly activate, their plan B, the day-to-day costs of student life probably aren’t uppermost in their mind. But perhaps they should be: research from Nationwide Building Society reveals that money mistakes dominate students’ list of regrets.
From failing to budget and track spending properly, overspending on nights out and relying too heavily on their overdraft, to blowing their entire student loan payment in the first few weeks, six of the top seven mistakes students have made are related to money.
“Our research shows just how much more financial pressure today’s students feel compared with previous generations,” says Tom Riley, Nationwide’s director of retail products.
Erin, who is about to start the third year of a psychology and cognitive neuroscience degree at the University of Nottingham, says going to university has “taught me loads” about managing money.
“Before I started, I’d worked and saved, but when that student loan lands in your account, it can feel a bit like free money,” she says. “It’s easy to fall into ‘girl math’ logic and justify little extras that quickly add up.”
She says that working before university and during the holidays “definitely gave me a better sense of what things actually cost”.
Erin sets herself a budget and has a rule that if she needs to go over it, she has to dip into the savings earned from her job, which, she says, focuses the mind on whether she needs to spend that money.
Her view is that wherever possible, the money she is saving “is not money I can spend [as] that is undoing all the good work I’ve done”.
To cut spending, she makes the most of discounts and deals, and joins with friends to maximise the benefits. She, and some of her friends, have Nationwide FlexStudent bank accounts, which offers a £10 Just Eat voucher every month for the first 12 months.
In her first year, she says, they pooled their vouchers and had “floor picnics” in their halls of residence, where they would all sit and share their takeaways.
It was, she says, “a life-saver because we didn’t have great cooking facilities and were on really limited budgets … It was a nice way to treat ourselves”.
Saving money has not meant missing out on a social life, as she has found ways to get into gigs and events that do not involve spending.
As a brand rep for a company that organises days out at racecourses around the UK, she gets a free ticket and transport to any events she has promoted. Tickets can be pricey for these “race day” outings, which are popular with students. She had to post a promotional message on her social media and send a link to three group chats, and she earned commission on any ticket bought via her link.
Signing up with an agency for voluntary work at events has also got her into gigs and festivals for nothing. “I got to see Oasis last year for free,” she says. “I think I did an eight-hour shift scanning tickets.” Her shift finished just as the support act ended, so she was able to watch the band’s entire set. “I was front row – that would have cost a lot of money,” she says. Her stint included a staff meal voucher.
Last year, she volunteered at Truck festival in Oxfordshire. Typically, she says, with volunteering at a festival, you may have to do two or three shifts over the weekend, but still get plenty of free time to enjoy the event.
Her savings pay for things she cannot get for free: this year the big thing she was saving for was the college ski trip. “Every bit I saved I put towards that.”
Here are her money-saving tips:
Think in hours, not pounds Before buying something, work out how many hours you would need to work to pay for it. “A couple of cocktails on a night out can easily be the equivalent of more than an hour’s wages from a summer job. It’s a good reality check and makes me think twice about the impulse purchases.”
Volunteer for freebies and perks There are lots of firms that recruit volunteers for festivals and one-day events – Erin signed up with Festaff and Wicked Events.
Turn fashion into a side hustle Erin snaps up quality pieces from charity shops and similar, some of which she upcycles before selling them on platforms such as Vinted, along with her own items that she no longer wants.
Look out for opportunities A lot of universities have brand ambassador programmes. Students often act as brand reps for nightclubs, as well as other events and venues.
Pool rewards with friends You could combine discounts and deals with housemates or friends to get better value and reduce everyday spending.

====================================================================================================

China Focus: Japanese abandoned WWII chemical weapons continue to threaten public security in China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
13:54:34 CST
14:54:34 KST

HARBIN, Aug. 15 (Xinhua) -- The latest leak involving abandoned Japanese chemical weapons in northeast China's Jilin Province, which contaminated two Japanese personnel during disposal operations, has renewed concerns about the lingering dangers of wartime chemical weapons still buried in China.
As Saturday marks the 81st anniversary of Japan's unconditional surrender in World War II (WWII), the incident has drawn renewed attention to Unit 516, the invading Japanese army's clandestine chemical warfare unit headquartered in Qiqihar, northeast China's Heilongjiang Province, during WWII.
Experts noted that Japan has yet to provide China with critical information regarding Unit 516 and the chemical weapons it abandoned at the end of the war. Some high-risk munitions remained undiscovered, and deterioration of their containers increases the risk that toxic agents could seep into soil and water sources.
At a press briefing on June 4, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning disclosed that on May 26, two Japanese personnel had their arms contaminated with toxic agents during a disposal operation in Jilin when the abandoned Japanese chemical weapons ruptured. The Chinese side immediately provided on-site medical treatment before rushing them to a hospital. After receiving treatment, they returned to Japan on May 29.
The incident was far from unprecedented. According to China's position paper submitted to the Fifth Review Conference of the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC), abandoned Japanese chemical weapons have caused more than 2,000 casualties in China since the end of WWII.
This year marks the 81st anniversary of the end of WWII and of victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression. The 14-year war was the longest and largest fight against foreign aggression for the Chinese people in modern times. It came with great sacrifices -- 35 million casualties among the Chinese military and civilian population -- before Japan ultimately surrendered in 1945.
Scars left by the war have yet to fully heal, and dangerous remnants from the war continue to threaten communities.
In particular, the Japanese military incorporated arsenic into its chemical weapons both to stabilize mustard agents under extremely cold conditions and to enhance their lethality. Arsenic does not naturally break down in the environment. During excavation, investigators have found many shells already corroded or even ruptured. Ongoing deterioration could allow large amounts of toxic liquid to seep into the ground, experts noted.
Such contamination could permanently pollute local soil and groundwater, increasing long-term cancer risks and threatening nearby communities for generations.
Heilongjiang has been one of the provinces most severely affected by abandoned Japanese chemical weapons. Qiqihar City, where Unit 516 was deployed during the war, is considered the epicenter of the problem.
"Unit 516 was responsible for developing a wide range of chemical warfare agents, including mustard gas, Lewisite and chlorine gas, all of which were used in combat," said Wang Tianjiao with the Qiqihar Museum.
"Qiqihar was used as a major base for Japan's chemical warfare program, so virtually every type of abandoned Japanese chemical weapon could potentially still be found here," Wang added.
The city has seen some of the worst toxic exposures over the years. On Aug. 4, 2003, construction workers unearthed five drums containing mustard gas at a building site. The leak resulted in injuries to 44 people. Some victims have since died, while many survivors continue to suffer severe pain and illnesses.
A long-term follow-up medical study published on the website of the U.S. National Center for Biotechnology Information found that severe autonomic failure, such as hyperhidrosis, pollakiuria, diarrhoea, diminished libido, and asthenia, appeared in almost all victims from the incident. Polyneuropathy occurred in 35 percent of the victims and constricted vision in 20 percent of them, among other malfunctions. Many continued to suffer from severe post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and depression years after exposure.
In the years following the 2003 incident, abandoned Japanese artillery shells were discovered repeatedly at construction sites and disused factories across Qiqihar.
On July 30, 2010, a group of school kids in Qiqihar were found fiddling with three rusted shells, with fuses still attached to two of the shells. The terrifying discovery sent local police into an intense excavation that lasted over eight hours. By the end of the operation, they had recovered 359 artillery shells of various types from a disused factory. The shells were later identified as abandoned by Japanese invaders.
Shortly afterwards, another 63 shells were uncovered at a construction site and later identified as abandoned by Japanese troops. Thanks to the prompt response of local police, the danger was neutralized without any casualties.
Wang estimated that Unit 516 abandoned roughly 200,000 chemical munitions at the end of WWII. Some were buried underground, while others were dumped into the Nenjiang River. "Unlike germ warfare weapons, effectiveness of which diminishes over time, chemical weapons remain highly toxic for a long time," he said.
Japan has continued to withhold information on the locations, quantities and types of these abandoned weapons, as well as details about Unit 516, hampering efforts to recover and destroy them.
Historical records indicate that abandoned chemical weapons are scattered across numerous burial sites in widely varying quantities. Their small size and varying burial depths make them especially difficult to locate.
Under the CWC, Japan was required to complete the destruction of all abandoned chemical weapons in China by the end of 2007. However, the deadline has already been postponed four times.
Furthermore, legal efforts to seek accountability have also met setbacks. On Sept. 21, 2012, the Tokyo High Court rejected an appeal by victims of the 2003 Qiqihar chemical leak incident seeking state compensation from the Japanese government.
While acknowledging that the abandoned Japanese chemical weapons had caused the injuries, the ruling denied the Japanese government's liability for inaction, citing the lack of clarity over the locations where the chemical agents had been abandoned and the inability to prevent the incident from occurring.
Twenty-three years after the 2003 incident, many of the original 44 victims have died. Those who remain continue to suffer debilitating long-term health problems.
Hao Yanzhi, whose wife Niu Haiying was among the victims, said his wife's immune system has steadily weakened over the years. The youngest victim of the incident dropped out of school at an early age and has endured chronic pain and poor immunity for more than two decades.
Many survivors say they do not know whether they will live long enough to hear an official apology from the Japanese government. ■

‘Hi Mali, hi Liel’: meet the Israeli cop who found the missing mother and daughter — and went viral
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
05:53:29 UTC
14:53:29 KST

“Hi Mali, hi Liel. I’m Walter, the police representative in South America, OK? From the Israel Police Intelligence Division.”
Those were apparently the first words in Hebrew that Mali and Liel Yahalomi had heard in nearly a week, and they were captured in a video released by the Israel Police to mark the end of a disappearance that had gripped Israel.
“I want to ask you a few questions. We were very worried about you, OK?” the officer continued. “I’m going to get everyone off the bus, and then we’ll talk, OK?”
The discovery of the mother and daughter alive brought relief after days of uncertainty over what had happened to them after they left Israel for Prague and suddenly dropped out of contact. They had continued to Vienna, apparently traveled through Frankfurt and eventually reached Buenos Aires, where they were located.
Their failure to board a scheduled flight from Prague back to Israel had intensified the search, while relatives said the abrupt loss of contact was completely out of character. With their whereabouts unknown as they moved across Europe, the case drew widespread attention in Israel and prompted fears among some that the disappearance could have involved a crime or a terrorist attack targeting Israelis.
Instead, the search ended thousands of miles away in Argentina.
And almost immediately, attention in Israel turned to the man behind the voice in the police video.
His name is Walter Alejandro Kogan, an Israel Police representative in Latin America and the officer who helped bring the search by Israeli police and its Lahav 433 national investigations unit to a successful conclusion.
Kogan’s brief Hebrew exchange with the women quickly went viral in Israel, inspiring memes about an officer whose face was not even visible in the clip. Some social media users jokingly speculated that “Walter” was a name he had adopted for his overseas posting.
It was not.
Who is Walter Kogan?
Kogan, a resident of the southern city of Be'er Sheva, spent years in more conventional police work before moving into international law enforcement.
He previously served as the investigations and intelligence officer at the Arad police station in southern Israel, with the rank of superintendent. He was later promoted to chief superintendent and appointed the Israel Police representative for Latin America.
In Arad, a desert city west of the Dead Sea, Kogan handled property crimes and several cases that made Israeli news, including break-ins at rooms at the Milos Hotel at the Dead Sea and burglaries at synagogues belonging to the Ger Hasidic community.
He was also involved in the investigation of a Bedouin Israeli man accused of committing an indecent act against an 11-year-old girl at a shopping mall in the city.
His current job is markedly different.
When Kogan introduced himself to Mali and Liel, he said he was from the Israel Police Intelligence Division, the operational body responsible for managing the force’s representatives overseas, providing professional direction and coordinating investigative and intelligence activity against crime.
Unlike his operational work in Arad, much of Kogan’s current role is built around international cooperation and law enforcement diplomacy.
Police attachés and representatives abroad effectively serve as an overseas arm of the Israel Police and National Security Ministry. They provide official operational and intelligence links between Israeli police and law enforcement, security and intelligence agencies in the countries where they serve.
Representatives typically cover several countries within a geographical region. In the search for Mali and Liel, Israeli police representatives in Europe were also involved.
Their regular work includes coordinating intelligence and operations against organized crime groups and Israeli criminal targets operating overseas. They also assist investigations into crimes with direct implications for Israel, including international drug trafficking, money laundering and human trafficking.
Police representatives can also become involved in extradition proceedings involving suspects wanted by Israel or other countries and in international legal assistance, including arranging witness testimony or questioning suspects abroad for investigations being conducted in Israel.
International police cooperation between Israel and Argentina has long included exchanges of information aimed at combating transnational organized crime. Argentine authorities have publicly described such cooperation as covering crime prevention, investigations and the exchange of intelligence.
Kogan himself has previously been publicly identified in Argentina as representing the Israel Police during a major international investigation into child sexual exploitation that involved authorities across eight countries.
From police diplomacy to a missing-person search
Since taking up his Latin American posting, Kogan has met police officials across the continent as part of efforts to strengthen cooperation and information-sharing.
On April 29, Bolivian police said Deputy Commander and Chief of Staff Juan Román Peña Rojas held a coordination meeting with Kogan, whom they identified as the Israel Police attaché for Latin America. Bolivian authorities said the meeting focused on strengthening cooperation and exchanging security expertise.
In April 2025, Kogan met police officials in Argentina — the country where Mali and Liel would eventually be found.
Local authorities said at the time that they had shown him how the city’s comprehensive security system operated. Kogan expressed interest in a program for locating and recovering property, they said, and the sides agreed to share expertise and strengthen cooperation.
Earlier this year, Kogan also met Interpol representatives in Paraguay, who said they presented the Israeli officer with the border-control system used at a major international crossing. Paraguayan officials said such contacts help strengthen operational capabilities and develop joint strategies for safer and more efficient border management.
Those relationships are the less visible side of a police attaché’s work. The job usually involves coordination meetings, intelligence exchanges, extradition cases and cooperation against cross-border crime.
This week, it involved finding two Israelis whose disappearance had become a national story back home.
Kogan may hardly have expected that his posting in Latin America — or a few sentences spoken in Hebrew on a bus — would make him an overnight social media sensation in Israel.
After finding Mali and Liel, he questioned them briefly to establish that they were safe and determine whether there was any indication that a crime had been committed.
There apparently was not.
With the search over and no suspicion of criminal conduct involving the mother and daughter, police allowed them to continue their journey.
For days, Israelis had been asking where Mali and Liel Yahalomi had gone. In the end, the answer came from an Israeli police officer on the other side of the world, beginning with a few reassuring words in Hebrew:
“Hi Mali, hi Liel. I’m Walter.”

Myanmar says over 300,000 Rohingya refugees verified for repatriation as exodus enters ninth year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
05:53:02 UTC
14:53:02 KST

Myanmar says over 300,000 Rohingya refugees verified for repatriation as exodus enters ninth year
BANGKOK (AP) — Myanmar’s military-backed government said Saturday that more than 300,000 Rohingya refugees living in camps in Bangladesh are former residents of western Rakhine state and that it will accept their return once security conditions improve.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs statement comes as the Rohingya refugee crisis enters its ninth year, with hundreds of thousands of refugees still living in camps in Bangladesh after fleeing Myanmar in August 2017 when the military launched a crackdown following attacks by a Rohingya insurgent group on guard posts in Rakhine.
The operation drove more than 700,000 Rohingya across the border into Bangladesh, joining hundreds of thousands of others already living there for decades in the wake of waves of previous violence perpetrated by Myanmar’s military.
The scale, organization and ferocity of the operation led to accusations of ethnic cleansing and genocide from the international community, including the U.N.
Myanmar, formerly known as Burma, does not recognize the Rohingya as one of the country’s 135 lawful ethnic minorities, instead referring to them as Bengalis to imply they are natives from Bangladesh and are illegally settled in Myanmar.
Myanmar said it had verified 426,545 of the 828,824 refugees on a list provided by Bangladesh as of the end of July, and determined that 308,797 of those verified were former residents of Rakhine.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs said 113,507 people could not be verified and that 4,241 people were found to have been involved in what it called terrorist activities.
The statement said it will continue working with Bangladesh to receive verified former residents when the security situation in Rakhine becomes more stable.
The ministry also rejected claims that more than 1 million people were displaced from Rakhine, saying that more than 540,000 people crossed into Bangladesh after the violence in 2017 while more than 200,000 remained in northern Rakhine.
Myanmar and Bangladesh agreed to a two-year repatriation process in 2018. However, security in Myanmar worsened following an army takeover in 2021 that ousted the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi, triggering widespread armed resistance. Plans to repatriate the refugees have not succeeded.
The renewed chaos brought about by fighting between the Rakhine-based ethnic Arakan Army group and the military over control of the region in 2023 forced more refugees to flee toward Bangladesh and elsewhere in a desperate move to save their lives. The Arakan Army controls much of Rakhine after capturing territory from the military in recent years.
In recent years, poor conditions in refugee camps, steep cuts to foreign aid and the lack of safe prospects for returning to Myanmar have led to an increasing number of Rohingya refugees attempting to make the dangerous ocean crossing to Malaysia and Indonesia on rickety boats.
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said in late July that Myanmar had agreed to take back 5,000 Rohingya refugees currently living in Malaysia as part of a repatriation program.
However, an official from Myanmar’s foreign ministry, Han Win Aung, told The Associated Press at the time that the repatriation program was focused solely on verified Myanmar nationals currently held in detention centers in Malaysia and rejected reports that the government would accept Rohingya.

Exhausted health workers in Congo struggle to keep up as Ebola outpaces contact tracing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
05:53:02 UTC
14:53:02 KST

Exhausted health workers in Congo struggle to keep up as Ebola outpaces contact tracing
NIZI, Congo (AP) — Every day, community health worker Gédéon Banga Ngbape and his team fan out across communities in eastern Congo looking for people who may have crossed paths with the country’s fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.
The workers investigate dozens of alerts, search for those exposed to suspected or confirmed cases and try to get anyone showing symptoms into care before the virus spreads further.
But the surveillance system is increasingly failing to keep pace with the virus. Between 60% and 70% of new Ebola cases are being detected among people who were not already being monitored as contacts, meaning health workers may only discover infections after patients become sick and have had opportunities to expose others.
“If surveillance does not work well, the entire response suffers,” Ngbape said. “Surveillance is the engine of a response.”
The outbreak has killed over 2,200 people out of more than 4,700 cases, according to the latest government figures. This death toll has been reached almost three times faster than in the 2014-16 Ebola outbreak in West Africa — the worst in history. That outbreak claimed over 11,000 lives.
“We are chasing the virus; the virus is ahead of us,” said WHO regional director for Africa, Dr. Mohamed Yakub Janabi, this week.
U.N. humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher on Friday announced an additional $30.5 million in emergency funding to help tackle the Ebola outbreak.
Response teams work long hours, often without pay
In Nizi, Ngbape’s surveillance teams say they receive an average of 60 to 70 alerts a day. They move through communities to investigate suspected infections, follow people who have been in contact with suspected or confirmed cases and direct those showing possible symptoms to health facilities.
The work can stretch deep into the night.
“I leave in the morning at 8 and return around 11 p.m., sometimes midnight,” Ngbape said. “I still have to follow up and plan the next activities. I feel really tired, but what matters to me is always being of service to the community.”
He did not say how many days a week he works or how often he is able to take time off.
Community health workers who go door to door face risks of their own. Ana Ndroy Kasime, a community health worker in Nizi, said she visits homes to educate residents about Ebola and reports suspected cases to health officials. But she said workers like her lack basic protective supplies.
“When we go door to door, we don’t have protective equipment, like boots, disinfectant and other supplies, even though we are at risk,” Kasime said. “We buy disinfectant with our own money.”
The current outbreak, caused by the rare Bundibugyo Ebola virus, is unfolding in some of the most challenging conditions imaginable. There are no approved vaccines or treatments for the Bundibugyo virus, though trials are underway. Strikes by some unpaid health workers, threats by rebel groups, anger from long-traumatized communities and misinformation asserting that Ebola isn’t real have significantly hindered the response.
The gaps are especially consequential in Nizi, one of the most affected health zones in Ituri province, which accounts for about 90% of Congo’s Ebola cases and 80% of its deaths.
“We started surveillance with fewer workers,” Ngbape said. “The challenges are enormous,” he added.
On Thursday, health workers at the Nizi Treatment Center went on strike and the facility temporarily closed. Ngbape said the health workers have not been paid in over three months.
The head of Africa CDC, Jean Kaseya, on Thursday called on Congo’s government to pay the outstanding salaries, saying money was available and that paying workers was the government’s responsibility.
The government says payments are delayed because it’s verifying worker payroll lists after finding unrelated names had been added and while it shifts payments from cash to mobile money.
Kasime said community health workers like her have received their payments, but at about $50 a month, she considers the amount inadequate for the work and risks involved. She said other Ebola response workers should be paid quickly.
“They are making sacrifices and taking risks,” Kasime said. “If these workers decide to stop working, the epidemic will spread further into the population.”
Insecurity and displacement put contacts out of reach
Surveillance workers in Nizi often struggle to get around, making it harder to investigate alerts and follow contacts across the health zone, Ngbape said. Frequent population movements linked to mining and people fleeing armed conflict add another complication, as people can move before surveillance teams are able to follow up with them.
Poor and sometimes impassable roads can also make remote areas difficult to reach, while insecurity restricts where health workers can safely operate. It remains unclear how many communities in the province are currently inaccessible to surveillance teams.
Dozens of rebel and militia groups operate across eastern Congo. The Allied Democratic Forces, which is tied to the Islamic State group, is among those active in Ituri. The insecurity has forced some health and aid workers to leave remote Ebola hot spots for the relative safety of the provincial capital, Bunia.
Violence affecting the Ebola response has also come from residents. At least a dozen attacks on health facilities and workers were recorded as of mid-July, according to local health authorities. In one incident, residents attacked a hospital in Nyakunde and entered a nearby Ebola treatment center, forcing patients and staff to flee before operations resumed the following day.
Many residents’ anger is caused by misinformation about the virus and bans on traditional burials — when families prepare the bodies and people gather for a funeral, which can lead to further infections.
Ngbape, however, said his surveillance teams in Nizi have not been attacked.
He said cooperation has improved as residents have become more familiar with the surveillance teams and their work. Ngbape also said he does not believe people in Nizi are widely concealing suspected infections, though population movements and limited transportation can still make contacts difficult to follow.
For Ngbape, maintaining that surveillance is critical to preventing individual infections from developing into wider chains of transmission. The long hours and limited resources have left him exhausted, he said, but not ready to stop.
“I am here to save the lives of the population,” he said.

Little penguin found dead with H5 bird flu on Victoria’s Phillip Island
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
05:52:57 UTC
14:52:57 KST

Australia’s first case of the deadly H5 bird flu in a little penguin has been confirmed on Victoria’s Phillip Island, only days after the state government announced it would begin vaccinating the species.
Confirmation of the virus in the little penguin will spark a race to vaccinate thousands of birds, with the government announcing on Saturday it would begin the rollout on Monday.
The government did not provide the exact location where the bird was found, but said it was not inside the island’s famous penguin parade area.
A spokesperson confirmed the little penguin had died.
There are about 40,000 little penguins on Phillip Island, making it the world’s biggest colony of the species and a major tourist attraction.
Environment advocates have been concerned about the potential for mass deaths of little penguins if the virus reached the island.
Euan Ritchie, a professor in wildlife ecology and conservation at Deakin university, said the detection of H5 bird flu in the much-loved little penguin population was “devastating”.
“Phillip Island is home to a diverse array and significant populations of native wildlife, including Australian fur seals, eastern barred bandicoots, and recently reintroduced bush stone curlews,” he said.
“Governments must provide whatever resources are needed to help wildlife survive through and recover from this bird flu outbreak.”
On Wednesday, the Victorian government announced plans for the world’s largest H5 bird flu vaccination program of wild birds.
The government said it would vaccinate up to 5,000 little penguins across populations at Phillip Island and at Melbourne’s St Kilda beach. While vaccinating wild birds is challenging, it was considered possible in Victoria’s wild little penguins because they generally return to the same burrows at Phillip Island and St Kilda each night.
But vaccination requires the delivery of two doses with a gap of a few weeks between each dose.
The detection on Phillip Island will spark concern that it may be too late for some little penguins to develop immunity.
Victoria’s chief biodiversity officer, James Todd, said he understood Victorians would be worried about the detection of the deadly virus in a little penguin.
“We know that the detection in a little penguin on Phillip Island is of concern,” he said.
“But we are proceeding with vaccination of the little penguin colony on Phillip Island and at St Kilda as a meaningful way in which it can help mitigate the impact of H5 on those populations.
“We know that little penguins are iconic and highly valued by Victorians, and for that reason, we are working as a priority to protect those colonies.”
The state’s chief veterinary officer, Dr Graeme Cooke, said Agriculture Victoria and Phillip Island Nature Parks “activated plans” to vaccinate little penguins as soon as the federal government authorised the vaccines for priority native bird species.
“Agriculture Victoria is working closely with Phillip Island Nature Parks to support vaccination of little penguins from Monday,” he said.
“While the first detection in a little penguin is a concern, vaccination of little penguins on Phillip Island remains a meaningful way to help protect this important colony.”
The Victorian government said there had been two further detections of H5 in greater crested terns, one at Lakes Entrance and the other at Dromana on the Mornington peninsula.
Todd said the Lakes Entrance detection was significant because it showed the virus was continuing to move through wild bird populations across Victoria.
On Saturday, the NSW government also confirmed the fifth detected case in the state, in a tern found at Eden on the far south coast.
The government said it would increase surveillance in the area as a result.
There have been two other confirmed cases in local birds in the state, one at Narooma on the state’s south coast and one at Wentworth in the far south-west. All of the confirmed cases in local birds have been in greater crested terns.

“Public awareness regarding personal data and privacy protection has also improved,” she told a radio programme.

Indonesia hit by second powerful earthquake in one day as death toll rises to 47
A magnitude 6.9 earthquake struck Indonesia's western Sumatra island late on Saturday, the US Geological Survey said. The quake followed a powerful 7.7 magnitude quake that hit the country's eastern Flores island earlier the same day, leaving at least 47 people dead and several others trapped beneath collapsed buildings.
Rescuers combed through debris for survivors on Saturday after a powerful earthquake struck off Indonesia's eastern Flores island, killing at least 47 people, according to disaster officials.
The national disaster management agency (BNPB) raised the death toll from 40 late Saturday, and rescue official Fathur Rahman said 50 people were injured in the 7.7-magnitude quake.
Suharyanto, who leads the BNPB, said earlier that people were trapped in several buildings.
"These will be the initial targets of the disaster response teams," said Suharyanto, who like many Indonesians uses one name.
Nearly 160 houses, dozens of educational and health facilities and other public buildings were damaged when the earthquake struck the popular tourist island in Indonesia's east, the BNPB reported.
The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies said preparations were under way to bring aid to some 2,000 people in temporary shelters.

Rescue official Fathur told AFP the focus was on locating victims who may be buried under rubble, but rescue efforts have been complicated by landslides cutting off roads.
Many Flores inhabitants were left without electricity and telecommunications.
Residents in Nagekeo, an area close to the epicentre, raced for higher ground as the sea retreated early Saturday – a possible sign of an approaching tsunami, AFP journalists witnessed.
While a tsunami warning was lifted, authorities urged people not to return to damaged buildings for fear that aftershocks may bring them down.
Hundreds remained outside hours later as dozens of aftershocks shook the island, the strongest measured at a magnitude of 6.1.
Waves of up to 1.6 metres (5.2 feet) were reported in some coastal regions of Flores, according to Indonesia's BMKG geological agency.

The epicentre of the shallow quake was located just off the north coast of the island, US and Indonesian authorities said.
The affected areas have few, if any, high-rise buildings.

Indonesia experiences frequent earthquakes due to its location in the Pacific "Ring of Fire", an arc of intense seismic activity stretching from Japan through Southeast Asia and across the Pacific basin.
Flores was struck by a 7.7-magnitude earthquake in 1992, which triggered a tsunami and resulted in around 2,500 deaths.
A devastating 9.1-magnitude tremor in 2004 struck off the coast of Sumatra and triggered a tsunami that killed 220,000 throughout the region, about 170,000 of them in Indonesia, in one of the deadliest natural disasters in recorded history.

====================================================================================================

Crowds at Mont Blanc: will hiking soon require reservations?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
05:30:02 UTC
14:30:02 KST

The Tour du Mont-Blanc is one of Europe’s most popular long-distance hiking routes, a 170-kilometre circuit through France, Italy and Switzerland that some 80,000 people walk each year, creating mounting problems.
On particularly popular sections of Mont Blanc, hiking groups are now so close together that there is hardly any distance between them. At the same time, not all visitors show respect for nature. Local residents are complaining and consider the situation untenable.
"Today we're moving along in single file. People can only see the backsides of those in front of them. That's hardly ideal," said the mayor of Saint-Gervais-les-Bains, Jean-Marc Peillex, speaking to Swiss public broadcaster SRF. He is calling for access to the route to be restricted from next spring and for this to be enforced through checks and sanctions.
Saint-Gervais-les-Bains is on the French side of the Mont Blanc massif, in the Haute-Savoie department of the French Alps.
The town is an important starting point for tours in this area. The French access route to the Tour du Mont Blanc (TMB) also runs through the region.
In future, anyone doing the Tour du Mont Blanc will have to reserve a place in a hut or an authorised bivouac zone. A bivouac zone is an officially designated area where hikers or mountaineers are allowed to spend the night outdoors on a temporary basis or pitch their tent.
Unlike in a hut, there is usually no infrastructure there, or only very basic facilities.
"If that is not possible, you postpone your plans to the following year," suggests Peillex.
Only a small part of the Tour du Mont Blanc runs through the municipality of Saint-Gervais. However, the other municipalities along the French section of the route are working together on the new rules and want to ensure that they come into force next spring.
Switzerland opts for coordination
Switzerland currently has no comparable plans to restrict access. Joachim Rausis, mayor of Orsières in the canton of Valais, also sees a need for action, but does not speak of pronounced overtourism. "There are warning signs, and we need to regulate things. But above all we need coordination between Switzerland, Italy and France," says Rausis.
One thing is clear: the huge influx of visitors is also creating difficulties for mountain guides. "You have to reserve hotels and huts a year in advance. For someone self-employed, that is almost impossible," because as a self-employed mountain guide you rarely have clients who book a year ahead.
The debate highlights a fundamental problem of mountain tourism: how can the international popularity of the Alps be reconciled with the protection of nature and the interests of local people? A reservation requirement could slow the flow of visitors, but at the same time it would call into question the traditional idea that the mountains are freely accessible to everyone.
A mandatory reservation system would not be entirely new on Mont Blanc. On the French normal route to the summit, overnight stays in the Nid d’Aigle, Tête Rousse and Goûter huts already have to be booked via a special reservation system. The names of all participants must be provided, and the booking confirmation must be shown during checks.
The Goûter and Tête Rousse huts were open for the 2026 season until recently, but have been temporarily closed since 11 August 2026 because of the risk of rockfall.

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday said India had faced a series of crises over the past 10-12 years, including the COVID-19 pandemic and wars in Ukraine and West Asia, but maintained that a citizen-first approach helped the country navigate the challenges.Addressing the nation from the ramparts of the Red Fort on India’s 80th Independence Day, Modi said the country emerged from the pandemic only to confront a tense global environment.“In the last 10-12 years, we have faced many dangers. As soon as we emerged from Covid, there was news of wars that started to arise from Ukraine side and West Asia. An atmosphere of tension prevailed. God knows what all the predictions the predictors made!,” he said.PM Modi also accused some people of deliberately creating anxiety by spreading rumours about shortages of essential supplies during the pandemic.“Some people gain joy in keeping the nation terrified by spreading rumours that vaccines will not be available, petrol, diesel, and fertiliser will not be available in the country. Claude creator's quarterly revenue grew 14-fold amid the AI race
Kyiv • UNN
The maker of the Claude chatbot reported revenue of more than $11.5 billion in the second quarter, compared with $787 million a year earlier. The company is preparing for an autumn IPO in cooperation with Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs.
Anthropic PBC is informing potential investors that its revenue in the second quarter increased at least 14-fold compared with the same period last year, according to relevant documents, Bloomberg reports, writes UNN.
Details
The creator of the Claude chatbots reported preliminary revenue of more than $11.5 billion for the latest completed quarter, compared with $787 million for the corresponding period in 2025 and $4.73 billion in the first quarter of this year, according to the documents. In the second quarter of 2026, Anthropic reported positive adjusted operating profit, the documents show.
Discussions are ongoing, and the figures may be revised. An Anthropic representative declined to comment.
The rapid growth comes as the company battles its longtime rival OpenAI to win corporate customers. Once considered an underdog in the artificial intelligence race, Anthropic has seen a surge in the number of professionals using its software to optimize tasks, including coding.
Anthropic’s annualized revenue, or run rate, exceeded $47 billion in May. OpenAI’s annualized revenue run rate exceeds $40 billion, the publication reports, although the two figures may be calculated differently.
The company is meeting with investors ahead of its potential mega-IPO, people familiar with the matter said in July. Anthropic has confidentially filed an application for a listing and is working with Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs Group Inc. and JPMorgan Chase & Co. on the IPO, the publication reports.
Anthropic aims to take advantage of ample financing opportunities in the public market to maintain its lead over OpenAI and others, as artificial intelligence companies spend hundreds of billions of dollars developing state-of-the-art models.
An IPO this autumn would allow Anthropic to debut not only ahead of OpenAI but also DeepSeek, a Chinese artificial intelligence firm that is capturing an increasing share of the technology market. DeepSeek is preparing for an IPO and could file an application as early as this year, people familiar with the matter said.
The race for leadership in AI has spurred the IPO market: according to Bloomberg, $256.4 billion was raised this year, excluding shell companies and other financial instruments. That is the highest annual figure since 2021.

Ancient Egyptian princesses were skilled archers, trained with weapons, controversial study claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
05:15:14 UTC
14:15:14 KST

Ancient Egyptian princesses buried with weapons may have been trained to use them while alive, according to a controversial study published in the journal Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology in July.
Researchers examined six mummies found at the Dahshur funerary complex in the 1890s. The mummies, belonging to royal individuals from Egypt’s Middle Kingdom, date to nearly 4,000-years-ago.
“Members of the royal family, especially the women, were active participants in skilled, physically demanding activities such as archery and hunting,” said Lead author Dr. Zeinab Hashesh. “This conclusion is supported by the way their bones developed to sustain heavy muscle use, which corresponds directly to the weapons discovered in their tombs.”
The six, four of whom are believed to be daughters of Pharaoh Amenemhat II, were rediscovered in 2020 in the Egyptian Museum after being lost for decades.
After analyzing the mummies’ muscle attachments, researchers suggested that pronounced areas in their upper limbs indicate “repetitive, high-intensity actions like pulling a bowstring or stabilizing a weapon.”
Hashesh added that the conclusion explains the presence of weapons in the princess’s burial chambers, as they are traditionally associated with men.
Princess Ita, Princess Khenmet, Princess Itaweret, and an anonymous woman provisionally identified as Princess Sathathormeryt, were all buried with bows and arrows. Ita’s coffin also held a dagger.
The two other mummies, Princess Noub-Hotep and King Hor, were buried with similar items.
“Princess Ita was a young woman aged between 28 and 34 with strong upper-body muscle attachments, suggesting she habitually used weapons like maces or daggers,” explained Hashesh. “Princess Khenmet was a woman in her late 30s or 40s who showed signs of thinning bones, but had very robust ligament attachments. Princess Itaweret was a young woman aged between 20 and 34 who survived broken ribs and foot fractures; her skeleton shows she was a skilled archer.”
Experts challenge study's claims
However, bioarchaeologists not involved in the study shared with Live Science that “skeletal changes cannot reliably indicate a specific activity,” adding that “age, body size, genetics and other repetitive movements can produce similar results.”
Sonia Zakrzewski, a bioarchaeologist at the University of Southampton who was not involved in the research, told Live Science in an email that the identities of the skeleton’s relies on 19th-century labels, which means that “we cannot be certain how reliable they really are.”
She added that while the attachment sites on the bones are pronounced, there is no way of proving that it was caused by archery, only that the muscles “appear to have been repeatedly used.”
"We cannot say therefore that these skeletal changes necessarily are associated with the use of weaponry," Zakrzewski said, especially since the researchers did not also study any “control” groups from the time period.
"It would be very useful to know how much such side differences exist in contemporaneous Egyptians, whether royal or not," she noted.
No clear reason why princesses buried with arrows
Additionally, she told Live Science that there is no clear reason as to why the princesses were buried with items like arrows.
"Archery is a highly asymmetrical activity,” Scott Haddow, a bioarchaeologist at the University of Turin not involved in the study, explained to Live Science via email. Finding the pronounced sites on both sides of the remains “does not make a particularly strong case for these individuals practicing archery.”
Haddow added that the individuals’ ages could also explain the differences, as “muscle-attachment sites are influenced by aging, as well as by body size and genetics.”
Other experts told Live Science they believe the researchers might be reading into the appearance of the weapons too much.
"Although the presence of funerary artifacts (e.g., arrows, daggers) makes the princesses' involvement in such activities plausible, the authors provide limited biomechanical or biomedical evidence to substantiate this claim," French anthropologist Sébastien Villotte told Live Science in an email.
Villotte, who works at the French National Center for Scientific Research, added that "a more robust approach would involve comparing these individuals to non-elite contemporaries from the same region and period.”
“This would help determine whether such degenerative changes (at these locations) were common in the general population (who were unlikely to engage in the same activities) or truly indicative of elite-specific behaviors."
However, despite the lack of control group and other uncertainties, Zakrzewski told Live Science that the importance of examining the remains should not be disregarded as “it allows us to sort of put flesh on the bones and understand more about their lives.”

Deity-inscribed tombstones, sarcophagi unearthed at ancient Egyptian burial site
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
05:15:04 UTC
14:15:04 KST

Some 20 limestone tombstones, several sarcophagi, and a collection of funerary amulets were discovered during excavations at the Tell El Deir archaeological site, Egypt’s Tourism and Antiquities Ministry announced two weeks ago.
The sides and backs of the tombstones are decorated with religious symbols and godly imagery, including that of a griffin, Agathodaemon, and Isis-Thermouthis.
Agathodaemon is a lesser serpent demon in ancient Graeco-Egyptian religion, as well as in classical Greek mythology. Isis-Thermouthis is a combination of the Egyptian goddess Isis, the sister and wife of Osiris, and Renenutet (Thermuthis), the Egyptian goddess of grain.
The appearance of the two dieties on the tombstones points to joint Greek and Roman influence on ancient Egyptian heritage and funerary practices.
Further, the decorations allow archaeologists to identify the social status of the tombstones’ owners.
Not only a burial place
Additionally, the Egyptian archaeological mission operating at the site uncovered a collection of pottery incense burners, decorated lamps, and funerary amulets, as well as several barrel-shaped style anthropoid ceramic coffins.
Secretary-General of the Supreme Council of Antiquities Dr. Hisham El-Leithy explained that the discovery “opens new horizons for understanding the development of cemeteries in the Nile Delta."
He also said that the finds show that Tell El Deir as “not merely a burial place, but was an integrated funerary center.”
According to Leithy, the finds provide extensive insight into ancient Egypt’s funerary and burial customs from the Late Period (664 BCE until 332 BCE) and through the end of the Roman era.
Egypt unearths underground tombs in ancient coastal city
In early July, a collection of 18 tombs and numerous artifacts were unearthed during archaeological excavations ahead of construction of a visitor’s center in Egypt’s ancient city of Marina El Alamein.
Marina El Alamein, which flourished between the Hellenistic period until the Byzantine era, is located on Egypt’s northwestern coast, about 100 kilometers west of Alexandria. It is believed to be the city of Leukaspis mentioned by the Greek geographer Strabo.
The site was discovered in 1986 during construction work in the Marina area. Since then, extensive archaeological excavations and studies have uncovered one of the best preserved ancient coastal cities in Egypt.
Of the 18 tombs discovered in July, 11 are carved entirely into the rock, a style of tomb known as a hypogeum, explained Mohamed Abdel Badie, head of the Egyptian Antiquities Sector at the Supreme Council of Antiquities, while the other seven are made of limestone aboveground.
Some of the tombs are also very well preserved, with chamber entrances sealed by stone slabs that had not been opened since ancient times.
Eman Abdel Khalek, leader of the archaeological mission, added that a 2.5 meter long granite sarcophagus had been uncovered with its original lid still in place.
The skeletal remains found inside are currently being studied.

How a Sudanese refugee became a head teacher in a Chadian camp
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-15
05:14:40 UTC
14:14:40 KST

How a Sudanese refugee became a head teacher in a Chadian camp
Displaced by Sudan’s war, Sahra now leads a refugee school where education offers children safety and hope.
Adre, Chad – Sahra remembers growing up in el-Geneina, the capital of Sudan’s West Darfur state, determined to outperform the boys in her class.
After sitting her national examinations in 2005 and 2006, she decided she wanted to become a teacher. She volunteered in classrooms while pursuing a university degree, eventually specialising in education administration.
Then, in April 2023, war between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) tore apart the life she had built.
The conflict has devastated Sudan, forcing millions of people from their homes. Chad, which shares a long border with Sudan to the east, has received a large share of those fleeing the fighting.
Sahra is now among nearly one million Sudanese refugees who have crossed into Chad, helping make it one of Africa’s largest refugee-hosting countries.
In eastern Chad, thousands of families arrived to find little more than open ground and trees to shelter under. For many children, there was no school to return to.
In 2024, Plan International and partner organisations established a primary school in one refugee camp. The school now has 1,059 pupils and 30 teachers – Sahra is the head teacher.
Teachers, administrators and child welfare workers have been recruited from the refugee community, allowing people who fled Sudan to help provide services for families displaced alongside them.
Leading from the front line
Chad was already facing a serious education crisis before the latest influx of refugees from Sudan. More than two million young people cannot read or write, and, according to the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), three out of four pupils nationwide are taught by people whose own education ended at secondary school.
The refugee influx has added pressure to an education system already short of classrooms, teachers and basic facilities.
“Illiteracy is very dangerous,” Sahra says. “I want the children to be optimistic about the future because education prevents them from early marriage and violence.”
To accommodate the number of pupils, the school runs two shifts, one in the morning and another in the evening. Lessons cover mathematics, science, history, geography, Arabic and French.
But teaching in exile comes with its own difficulties.
Sudanese teachers have had to adjust to Chad’s curriculum while working across language differences. Chadian children may speak local dialects, while many Sudanese pupils speak Arabic.
“The teaching syllabus in Sudan is easy, but the one in Chad is difficult for us,” says Oummalnas, a teacher who fled el-Geneina in 2024. She teaches mathematics and Arabic.
“We need more workshops to improve our teaching skills and adapt to the Chadian system,” she said.
Protection beyond the classroom
At first, Sudanese and Chadian kids sometimes struggled to get along. Over time, those tensions have eased. The children now learn and play together outside school.
Plan International also provides safe spaces where under-fives can play, socialise and receive psychosocial support in the absence of formal kindergartens.
“We don’t separate education from child protection. It’s an integrated approach that helps create harmony,” said Kefa Mayange, Plan’s Emergency Response Manager for Chad.
For parents in the camp, school is as much about safety as education.
Charfadine arrived with his family during the heavy rains of 2023. Back in West Darfur, his children went to school regularly until the conflict forced them to flee. Three of them now attend primary school in Chad.
“We are happy when they go to school here [in Chad] because it’s a receptive place. It protects them from the violence coming from criminal groups,” he told Al Jazeera.
His hopes remain tied to the country they left behind.
“My ambition is for my children to be teachers to teach coming generations in Sudan and doctors to treat illnesses,” he said.
But not every child has made it into a classroom.
Nasradine, another parent, says hundreds of unaccompanied youngsters who lost their parents while fleeing Darfur remain out of school and wander around the camp.
“If those children remain outside school, our camps will be in danger,” he said. “This group could turn to crime and make our place unsafe. We just want help for those children to go to school.”
A struggle against scarcity
For mothers such as Roukhaya and Zenab, memories of their escape from el-Geneina remain vivid. They walked for about 10 hours to reach the Chadian border.
Yet both say life in Sudan, despite the war, had once felt more manageable than life in the camps.
Roukhaya’s children entered formal schooling for the first time after arriving in Chad. But she has watched older teenagers drop out because there are no high schools or vocational training opportunities for them.
Keeping younger kids in school is a daily struggle, too.
Azraa, a Mobile Unit Supervisor with Plan International, and her colleagues go tent to tent, encouraging parents to keep their children in class. In families with six or seven children, parents may send only two or three to school while the others stay behind to collect firewood, fetch water or look for casual work.
Every Friday, community centres hold awareness sessions reminding families that education remains important, even in displacement.
These efforts are happening despite a severe shortage of resources. Kefa says the refugee response in eastern Chad remains one of the most underfunded humanitarian responses in the world.
Children make up more than half of the refugee population, yet the 2026 Sudan Regional Refugee Response Plan received only 17 percent of the funding it required, leaving an 83 percent shortfall. Education remains among the least supported sectors.
At Sahra’s school, the shortage is visible every day.
There are no flush toilets, no electricity and no accessible facilities for children with disabilities. Pupils sit packed together on the ground or share benches.
Teachers and parents are asking for basic improvements: solar panels for lighting, a mobile health clinic, school meals and enough desks for pupils.
Abakar Mahamat Nour, an Education Officer with the Economic and Social Development Agency (ADES), a Chadian nongovernmental organisation supporting education and emergency relief, says the arrival of Sudanese teachers has created an opportunity for solidarity across the border.
“Chad and Sudan are like brothers; we share families,” he told Al Jazeera. “Having people like Sahra coming from Sudan to teach our children is a benefit for our country. They help our students gain new cultural perspectives and build new friendships.”
She lost the life she had built as a teacher and education administrator in West Darfur. In exile, she has found herself doing what she had planned to do all along: teaching children.
“Refugees have skills, experience, and dreams,” said Kefa Mayange, Plan’s Emergency Response Manager for Chad. “Like Sahra, we see them as leaders.”
Note: Full names have been withheld for safety and privacy reasons.

Berk Kutay Gokmen
15 August 2026•Update: 15 August 2026
The US Army has temporarily suspended all Apache helicopter training flights following a crash earlier this week near Fort Hood, Texas, that claimed the lives of two soldiers.
“Army leaders directed a temporary stand-down of AH64 Apache training flight operations,” the army said in a statement. “The stand-down will remain in effect until we have a better understanding of the root cause of the accident.”
Investigators with the Army Combat Readiness Center arrived at the crash site Thursday and will oversee the investigation.
The AH-64 Apache is an attack helicopter designed to carry two crew members, with the pilot seated in the rear and the co-pilot and gunner positioned in the front, according to the army.
Chief Warrant Officer 2 Deontre Huey, 34, and Warrant Officer Seth Olmstead, 25, died in the crash, according to a statement from Fort Hood.
The soldiers were assigned to Bravo Company, 1st Battalion, 227th Aviation Regiment, 1st Air Cavalry Brigade, 1st Cavalry Division at the base.

PM sets global goals on I-Day
NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday urged India's micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) to seize the opportunities created by the country's free trade agreements (FTAs) and take Indian products to markets across the world.Addressing the nation on the occasion of India's 80th Independence Day, PM Modi said India's growing global stature and the FTAs signed with around 40 countries since 2014 had opened major opportunities for domestic businesses, particularly MSMEs."We have to reach the world. Everything that India produces should reach the world market," PM Modi said, highlighting textiles, machinery, pharmaceuticals and seafood as sectors with considerable potential to expand their global footprint.The Prime Minister, however, stressed that Indian businesses would need to meet international standards and focus on quality if they were to compete successfully in global markets.Pointing to the scale of India's ambitions, PM Modi called for a greater number of Indian companies to emerge as global leaders. He asked why India should not have 50 companies in the Fortune 500 within the next decade and said the country should aim to have an Indian bank among the world's top five.
He also set out ambitions for Indian pharmaceutical companies to feature among the world's top five, while calling for globally leading Indian firms in sectors such as law, ratings, consulting and accounting.PM Modi said the country's textile industry, stretching from Ludhiana in Punjab to Tirupur in Tamil Nadu, had the potential to significantly expand its global presence. He also pointed to India's fisheries and seafood sector as another area that could benefit from the export opportunities created by FTAs.The Prime Minister said India had the talent, capabilities, linguistic strength and a long history needed to compete on the global stage. He urged businesses to build brands that could earn international recognition and turn India's economic rise into a stronger global corporate presence.
"India's technology companies should be a scoreboard in the world," he said, stressing that the creation of globally recognised Indian brands should be treated as a national goal.The PM also highlighted India's stable political mandate, vibrant democracy, strong judicial system and constitutional framework, saying these factors had contributed to the country's growing recognition and respect around the world.

AI, jobs, free coaching & sports: What PM Modi offered Gen Z on Independence Day
TOI News Desk / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 15, 2026, 16:40 IST

Text Size
Small
